The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the preeminent leader among the scriptural divisions; it reveals the wondrousness of the fundamental and the manifested traces, and therein the true nature of all living beings is made manifest.

Thus, the Great Task of the King of Awakening is completed. For this reason, those who study its commentaries on the phrases and sentences find that it is not only the principles that are difficult, but the text itself is no less so.
(I, the fool), having planted roots of goodness in the past, have heard and lectured upon it many times; this was due to my innate disposition.
Tao Mei sometimes listened and sometimes lectured; whenever there were difficult passages, he privately composed annotations.

What he valued was to live apart from the crowd in seclusion during the twilight years of his life, so that when unrolling the scrolls, he would be spared the toil of deep contemplation yet still grasp the essentials of exegesis.

As for the secret keys for opening up the provisional teachings and manifesting the remote purport of the fundamental, he exhausted the essentials of the three-part structural divisions and fully elucidated the four categories of analysis.
The essential purpose of this work is now clear; none dare presume to interfere with it. Regarding the annotations provided here: where citations are abbreviated or omitted, they have been expanded;
where references point back and forth between sections, they have been indicated; where errors in transcription or calligraphy occurred, they have been corrected;

where the meaning of the scriptural text or its contextual relations were unexplained, they have been immediately elucidated; where erroneous or obscure points were present, they have been clarified; and as for the wording...
For those of rare acquaintance with phonology and glossaries, I have divided this work into ten fascicles and placed it among my ritual commentaries to prevent forgetfulness.
Should two or three disciples in the mountains be able to read it, they may thereby understand the intent of these present annotations; it will also serve as a slight aid to its circulation.
As for the minor merit of sparing others the labor of searching for references, and regarding those points where I have left doubts unresolved: [text continues].

I have examined the texts but have not yet seen [the complete version] and await future generations; should it one day fall into the hands of a learned and elegant scholar abroad, he will know that I am judged by this and that I am censured for this.
Preface by Youyan of Jie’an in the first year of the Yuangong era of the Great Song dynasty, the Wuma year (1078 CE).

By the Śramaṇa Youyan of Chicheng. Preface to the "Introductory Chapter."

The teaching-body (*śāstra-deha*) consists of one reality and three designations, serving as the basis for the two [categories]. These are sound, name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*).

Names are established based on syllables, and phrases are established based on names; thus, it is known that names and phrases entirely depend upon syllables. Therefore, syllables are the basis (*āśraya*), while names and phrases are that which depends (*āśrita*).
The term *dòu* (逗) is fundamentally derived from *dòuliú* (逗遛), meaning "to halt" or "to stay. Master You’s *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states:
"The term *dòu* means 'change'; it refers simply to the alteration of the phrasing according to each sentence. Thus, a *dòu* is merely a sentence used to complete the expression of the words.

The meaning of "long" and "short" applies generally. According to the ancient exegesis, the two gates of *honji* (original ground) and *suijaku* (traces) constitute the long sense, while the three divisions of introduction (*nyōhō*), main body (*shinjū*), and circulation (*rutsū*) constitute the short sense.
This is likely because the distinction between long and short is made based on where the force of the meaning comes to an end.

For instance, in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, four characters are treated as one phrase and eight characters as two phrases; this is called a "smaller sentence-body" (*myō shōshin*), which represents the short sense. Four phrases [constitute one...]
The sixteen-character phrase "many bodies are long" (*bahv-ātmakatva*) refers to the meaning of length; this is merely an instance of the general pattern for interpreting the meaning of phrases.

If one wishes to understand the current sutra and its commentary, one must examine the force of the meanings and establish precise limits to distinguish between long and short, as can be known by following this precedent.
Regarding the essential nature of the aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The Muni taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*).

Their essence consists either of speech or names; both are subsumed within the aggregates of form and formations. This is because the body of words (*vyañjana-kāya*) is first apprehended by the eyes and ears, and thus is subsumed under form (*rūpa*);
subsequently, it flows into perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), and is thus subsumed under formations (*saṃskāra*). Now, following further the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*:

The treatise briefly sets forth the essential nature of form (*rūpa*) and the essential nature of formations (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the essential nature of form, that treatise states: "Form refers to the objective sphere traversed by the eye and the object-condition for visual consciousness;

it consists of derivative matter from the four great elements. If its substance is manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*), it is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and is characterized as visible and resistant.

This is the essential nature of form. Regarding the essential nature of formations, it refers to those formations that are dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Furthermore, they are distinguished as follows:

The twenty-four [factors] are: the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the state of non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and the sets of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*). These twenty-four dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are each explained in detail within the treatises.

Regarding the explanation of names, phrases, and phonemes: a "name" (*nāman*) is a provisional designation established for the intrinsic nature of phenomena such as the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*); it is a conceptual appellation that expresses their essence.
A phrase (*pada*) is a collection of names that manifests defilement and purity; it is the nature upon which speech relies.

A phoneme (*vyañjana*) is the nature upon which the former two rely. (The above is the main text. Furthermore, regarding the practitioner who does not correspond [to the teaching], the commentary asks:
"How is it known that *dhāraṇī* is not a phenomenon associated with the mind? The answer is: "For example, even if a person who has attained *dhāraṇī* harbors anger in their mind," and so forth.
Nor did he ever deviate from following people as a shadow follows a form.
The people of that capital, when they spoke, their words formed elegant compositions; this refers to the "Dushi Renshi" (The People of the Capital) in the Mao Commentary on the Book of Poetry.

The poem says: "The people of that capital wear fox-fur robes, yellow in hue; Their countenances remain unchanged, and their speech is composed in elegant verses. This refers to those enlightened kings. (From the Mao Shu).

Regarding the regions of fortified cities and walled towns, they were called "du" (capitals). In ancient times, during the era of the enlightened kings, those among the capital's inhabitants who practiced the conduct of a scholar wore fox-fur robes that were a deep yellow;
they sought only warmth and comfort. Their movements and countenances were constant, and their speech was governed by rules and measures.
They detested the extravagance and licentiousness of the present age, yet did not reproach themselves for their own transgressions.
The *Shiqian* commentary on the *Jianye* [entry] explains that it is also called Jiankang, which was referred to as the "Capital of Ye" (*Yedu*) during the Jin and Song dynasties;

it is the present-day city of Jiangning. It was formerly known as Yangzhou. After the Sui dynasty conquered Chen, the name plaque of Yangzhou was moved north across the Yangtze River to Jingzhou (present-day Jiangling).
Therefore, the text below states that the journey between Jing and Yang covers nearly ten thousand *li*.
Refuting the ancients does not fully account for my own position.
Regarding the provisional application of practice and teaching, there are two types: first, that which concerns practice; second, that which concerns teaching.

Concerning practice, there are name, essence, purpose, and function. Concerning teaching, there are name, function, essence, and purpose. Furthermore, the fivefold profundity primarily applies the function according to practice.

Although this discussion concerns the characteristics of the teachings (*jiaoxiang*), it is actually an exposition of the intent behind the text by means of the practices and the provisional teachings.
Regarding the "intent of the arrival" (*laiyi*)—whether [the teaching] exists or does not exist—the *Sūtra Commentary on the Devadatta Chapter* states:

"The intent of the arrival of this chapter is to cite how ancient Buddhas propagated the sūtras to transmit benefits without error, thereby clarifying that the present propagation of the transformation [of beings] is verified by the past."
It is not in vain that he has come to exhort those of the present. Furthermore, the *Commentary on the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers"* (*Shenli pin shu*) states:

"In this section, because ten kinds of great supernatural powers are manifested for the purpose of entrusting the profound Dharma, it is named the 'Chapter on Supernatural Powers'. The *Ji* (*Record*) states: "This specifically clarifies the purpose of its arrival;

as for the other chapters, some lack such a purpose. Regarding the resolution of difficulties: for instance, in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa," a person from the North said, "The Buddha..."
Regarding the stupa for Śāriputra, it has already been briefly mentioned in the commentary [on the *Lotus Sūtra*], stating that this is merely a matter of human sentiment.

As for the other chapters, either there is no explanation for the removal of obstacles, or the intended meaning is brought forth within the explanation of the title; for example, in the commentary on the "Emergence from the Earth" chapter, the four *siddhārtha* (purposes) are employed.
Having thus explained the title, he concludes by asking: "From where does it come, and by what causes and conditions has it gathered?
Now, because this chapter is explained through various meanings to manifest the understanding of the four *siddhāntas*, it is called the "Chapter on the Emergence" (*Niraya-parivarta*).
Regarding the mutual presence or absence of the explanation of names (*shiming*) and their meanings (*yì*), as stated in the *Shu* (Commentary) on the "Chapter on Retaining" (*Chihpin*):

"Because one receives the mandate to propagate the sutra, it is called 'Retaining' (*chi*"), yet the meaning of "retaining" is not explained; this is an explanation of the name without an explanation of the meaning. Furthermore, the *Shu* on the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" (*Fasheng Gongde Pin*) states:
"'Merits' (*gongde*) refers to the merits of the purification of the six sense faculties and internal and external adornment," yet the term "merits" itself is not defined.
These two characters explain the meaning rather than the name itself.
To explain the meaning while retaining the name is as stated in the *Sūtra Commentary on the Chapter of Never-Disparaging*:

"Internally harboring the understanding of 'never-disparaging,' externally revering the object of 'never-disparaging,' embodying the practice of 'never-disparaging,' and appropriately employing the teaching of 'never-disparaging' toward others. Thus, one acts as [Never-Disparaging].
This refers to the category of "light" (qīng).
Regarding the phrase "the Academy for Nurturing the Aged" (xuéshè yǎnggōng), some say that "gōng" should be "lǎo," meaning the Rites of the State for Nurturing the Aged.
The *Lìjì* states: "The Lord of Yú nourished the state elders in the Upper Xiáng and the common elders in the Lower Xiáng; the Lord of Xià nourished the state... [text fragmentary].
The aged were housed in the Dongxu (Eastern Order), while the common aged were housed in the Xixu (Western Order).

The people of Yin housed the state elders in the Dongjiao (Eastern Academy) and the common aged in the Yuxiang (Academy of Yu). One should know that *xiang*, *xu*, and *jiao* are all names for schools;
the practice of housing the aged embodies the principle of the Son of Heaven attending to the Three Elders (*sanlao*) and Five Venerables (*wugeng*) within the Great Academy (*taixue*).

Regarding the "prostrating doubts" (*fúyí*) and "prostrating difficulties" (*fú nàn*), the intention behind the prostrating doubts is fully explained at the end of the verses in the *Maitreya-Asking-Mañjuśrī* (Maitreyaparipṛcchā).

As for the reason why doubt is not treated as the primary cause, the preface (*biexù*) consists of four parts: first, the gathering of the assembly; second, the manifestation of auspicious signs (*xiàngruì*);

third, the arising of doubt; and fourth, the questions and answers. However, within the commentary (*shū*), only the emission of light and the manifestation of auspicious signs are taken as the cause, while the questions and answers are [treated as the effect].

It is titled "Preface" (*xu*) rather than being ordered by the other two [categories], for which reason its intent is expressed: because doubt and thought are both present, and because the assembly is sparse, it is called "Setting Aside" (*zhi*).

"Quotation" (*yin*) is also a type of song; it refers to discourse such as that found in the *Wenxuan*, where Shi Jilun has the "Song of Longing for Home" (*Sigui yin*) and Ban Meng... [text fragment].
Both Sthiramati and Guṇamati each have their own expositions on the meaning and principles [of the text].

They provide an interpretation based on the term *vaṃśa*, which means lineage or succession—referring to descendants such as sons and grandsons who receive their names in relation to their grandfather.

If one were to interpret it as "ancestral lineage" (*pūrvavaṃśa*), then the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) would be the descendant, while the "Main Body" (*Maulī-bhūmi*) would be the progenitor; thus, the descendant would come first and the progenitor would follow.
Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*) briefly remarks that this is laughable.

Furthermore, regarding the confusion between "Zhangcao" (草) and "Zhangcao" (草), some claim that because the two characters for "Zhangcao" are similar, one mistakes "Zhang" for "Cao"; this explanation is incorrect.
The text itself states: "Furthermore, being confused about 'Zhangcao,' one takes 'Nong' as 'Hu. This clearly indicates that the person did not recognize the character "Nong" as meaning "to call."
The character "jiǎn" (簡) means "to reduce"; it does not refer to one who cannot recognize a chapter or a cursive script (*zhāngcǎo*).
As for what is called *zhāngcǎo*, it refers merely to a cursive transcription; thus, the *Weizhi* states: "Cursive script (*cǎoshū*) first arose during the time of Emperor Zhāng of the Han dynasty;

the author's name is unknown... (and so forth). It is correct that those who practice cursive script today call it *zhāngcǎo*. Regarding the practitioner Zhōngxíng mentioned in the present record, I previously saw him...
In the commentary, the character *lòng* (哢) was hastily written and misread as *hū* (呼); thus, it was rendered as "to call and dissolve" (*hūxiāo*), which is even more laughable.
Yìnchè made the same error.

Generally, when translating scriptures, there are distinct roles for those who assist the translators, such as the reader of the Sanskrit text, the interpreter of terms, the scribe (*bishòu*), and the editor (*rùnwén*).
This sutra was translated twice; because Master Xie participated in the translation during the time of Masters Yan and Guan, it is called the "Supplementary Translation" (Bǔzhù).

When Master Dao’an arrived, he divided it into three parts: the Section on the Causes and Conditions of the True Teaching, the Section on the True Exposition of the Teaching, and the Section on the Practice and Propagation of the Teaching.

One must recognize that among the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Piṭakas, each serves as a primary host; within the Sūtras, the Vinaya and Abhidharma are further treated as guests, and the same applies when the Vinaya and Sūtras treat one another as such.

This is what is meant by beginning from the shallow and proceeding to the profound, like the waxing moon. The initial practice of the Six Pāramitās is like the beginning of the moon; thus it is described in the *Lalitavistara*.
The Sūtra states: "Advancing in virtue is like the waxing moon.
To claim that the first six meanings lack the sense of partial development is an error.

By supplementing what precedes and following with what comes after, the foundation of the treatise is established. Although it was composed during the Buddha’s lifetime, it was prepared in advance as a prophetic record.

In the *Mei shu*, the phrase "the six feet" (ṣaḍpāda) was misunderstood, leading to the erroneous claim that it refers to the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma-śāstra*. Consequently, the *Jñānaprasthāna* was mistakenly taken as the "body," subsuming the preceding six "feet.
Now, one who divides a text into sections must first establish the general and then the specific; for example, the "one body" is the general, while the "four limbs" are the specific.
If one follows the error of the ancients in dividing the sections according to the *Prakaraṇapāda*, one would instead place the specific first and the general second, thereby causing [confusion].
The preface distinguishes between the specific and the general, serving as a comprehensive supplement to what preceded and what follows; this is evident here.
As for the name "Jingzhong" (Within the Mirror), the famous King Yishao (Wang Xizhi) once visited the lake and sighed, saying, "My life has been like a journey within a mirror all day long.
Ancient eminent monks took this place as their own name.
Borrowing terminology to serve as an illustration for the refutation, it is not entirely identical to that [previous case].
The *Śāstra* states: "Whether exceeding or falling short. In the *Analects*, when Zigong asked which was more virtuous between Shizi and Shang, the Master said:

"Shizi exceeded; Shang fell short. The commentary notes: "Both failed to hit the mean; this resembles the ancient practice of varying the number of ritual stages according to whether they were elaborate or concise."
In both advancing and retreating, one cannot hit the mark.
First, regarding the single [section] which is a collective summary of the four: "First" refers to the general clarification that [the categories] reach only up to four.

If one does not lose [the meaning] and does not deviate, it allows wisdom to expand; if one loses [the meaning] through brevity or causes a deficiency in the significance, it constitutes a deviation. If there are four...
When the specific classifications of the fetters (*anuśaya*) accord with the capacities of sentient beings, they are termed "neither lost nor erroneous.

However, one must not attempt to resolve the meaning of these specific texts by applying the principles of expansion and abbreviation found in the general exposition; for within these specific sections, one is simply adopting the meaning of the "middle way" (*madhyama*).
Within each of these subtle [teachings], the four intentions and ten subtleties are also fully present; thus, each is appropriately termed "abiding in the middle.

For example, in the single explanation of the *nidāna* (causal conditions), it naturally attains the state of abiding in the middle. Now, as for each of the ten subtleties abiding in the middle, this is because they fully incorporate the four categories to explain the intended meaning.
The ten [categories] also enter into the four [truths], as they are collectively explained under the name "the four intentions" because they occupy a central position.
First, regarding the contemplation of the mind, there are generally two explanations: first, the contemplation of dharmas produced by causes and conditions within the mind;

these are the world (loka) as emptiness, the person (pudgala) as the conventional (saṃvṛti), and the antidote as the ultimate (paramārtha). Second, the contemplation of the four *siddhāntas* within the mind.

The "thorough inclusion" refers to the three [teachings] beginning with the *nidāna* (causal conditions). What are these? Observing one's own mind and the capacities of sentient beings as the object constitutes the *siddhi* (universal suitability);
illuminating and comprehending them moment by moment constitutes the *pratipatti* (correspondence). This is the inclusion of the *nidāna*.

The four *siddhis* correspond to the Empty (*śūnya*), the Provisional (*upāya*), the Distinct (*vibhinna*), and the Middle (*madhyama*)—that is, the Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*). This is the inclusion of the Four Teachings. The first three *siddhis* represent the traces of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*). First...
The single meaning is entirely the fundamental awakening; this encompasses both the fundamental and the derivative.

The four categories—person, principle, and so forth—are to be understood by analogy with what has been explained. Regarding the four aspects of the Great Matter, they are not anything other than response and stimulus, up to the four aspects of contemplating the mind, each of which individually and collectively encompasses all things.
The three categories of provisional teaching (*kyōkyō*) and so forth must also be described exhaustively; one should likewise apply this analogy to say:

the provisional teaching of the Great Matter, the origin and trace of the Great Matter, the contemplation of the mind regarding the Great Matter; the Great Matter of provisional teaching, the origin and trace of provisional teaching, the contemplation of the mind regarding provisional teaching;
the Great Matter of the origin and trace, the provisional teaching of the origin and trace, and the contemplation of the mind regarding the origin and trace. Indeed, it is thus.
This means that when one perceives the meaning of the four categories as mutually interpenetrating, all things are entirely wondrous.
To cling to a stump while remaining in ignorance—as the Master Han said: "A man of Song was plowing in a field when a rabbit ran into a stump, broke its neck, and died;
he thereupon abandoned his plowing to guard the stump, hoping to catch another"—those who today borrow such analogies yet lack penetrating insight are just like this.
It is likewise so; yet those who remain in ignorance have long claimed that the five thousand [monks] rose and departed, fearing the profound meaning of the scriptural symbols.

Now, I maintain that this is merely the error of those who offer partial interpretations of the sutra. In the present sutra’s "Expedient Means" chapter, the eternal life [of the Buddha] surpasses all other doctrines, yet ancient masters still claim that his lifespan was extended through supernatural powers and ultimately returns to impermanence. Is this not like waiting by a stump? Why is this so?

The sub-commentary below states: "If the masters of both past and present do not yet know that the Master’s original and manifested traces are uniquely transcendent among all teachings, how much less so his disciples?
Moreover, this section of the sub-commentary explains the single topic of the original and manifested traces; it is but a small fragment of the ancient [text]."
How can it be said that one has attained [the middle way] if only the fourfold explanation is fully met to be called "abiding in the middle"?

If that were so, the meaning of "abiding in the middle" in each individual instance mentioned in the preceding text would not be established. However, while the fourfold explanation collectively constitutes the middle way as a whole, each individual instance constitutes the middle way as a particular;
one should not doubt the particulars on account of the whole.
Regarding the explanations of "near" and "far," one should apply discernment.

In terms of their commonality, they are identical; in terms of their specific functions, they differ. When a supernatural transformation (*ṛddhi*) manifests within oneself, it is common; when it takes on forms to respond to sentient beings, it is distinct. Regarding the conditions of a mirror:
when the object arises from the observation, the cause is proximate and the condition is remote; when the observation arises from the object, the condition is proximate and the cause is remote.
[Sparse].

The various doctrines, principles, and contemplations regarding the Three Jewels, the threefold inclusion of the four teachings, and their correspondence with the Three Jewels can be understood [from this].

Furthermore, within the context of "bestowing" (*śe*) and "opening" (*kai*), the provisional application of emptiness and the provisional (*prajñapti*) is "bestowing," while the identity of emptiness and the provisional as the Middle Way is "opening."
The original and the trace each have three aspects: the abbreviated original and trace in the Trace Gate, and the abbreviated original and trace in the Origin Gate;

these are summarized according to the teachings. This refers precisely to the meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding one’s own cultivation of the six perfections. It is illustrated by the analogy of one who wishes to obtain a fatless sheep, using only a wolf to frighten it away;
as the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "The Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka first cultivate emptiness, whereby the wolf subdues the sheep of afflictions."
One who has not yet severed the fetters lacks the "fattened body" of the merit of the six perfections; this is the first *koṭī*.

When the fat of afflictions is eliminated and the merit becomes increasingly fattened, this is the second *koṭī*. Properly emerging from the stage of expedient means to benefit sentient beings is the third *koṭī*.

Regarding the "retention of delusions" (*kleśa-avasthāna*) in the seventh stage for the purpose of moistening rebirth, this refers merely to the cultivation of habitual tendencies. As for the "seventh stage," the *Zhi guan* (Contemplation) states:

"Many people cling to the sutras which say that one cultivates 'emerging from the conventional' (*niryāṇa*) in the eighth stage; or that one cuts off the fetters (*saṃyojana*) in the sixth or seventh stage to equal the Arhat, and only then cultivates 'emerging from the conventional.
This is but one perspective, and it is not necessarily the whole truth. However, the Buddha distinguished these for those of the three capacities [of practitioners]. Below...
Only by severing the roots [of afflictions] can one emerge from the conventional; thus it is judged that this refers to those of inferior capacity.

Those of middling capacity, having severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), find their cycle of birth and death somewhat relaxed, and they spontaneously sever the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya*) at the second stage (*bhūmi*);

from this point onward, they are able to enter the conventional. Those of superior capacity, upon first hearing the Buddha’s wisdom, are immediately able to realize and penetrate that both views and thoughts are empty.
Since he acts as a refuge for sentient beings, why must he emerge from the provisional [teachings] only at the seventh stage?
It is close; even today he should act as a worldly being. Prior to the present sutra, he was merely emerging from the recent past.
In every thought-moment, the three mysteries reach the body and land of every thought-moment; all are explained as arising from the Buddha’s benefit to sentient beings.

For instance, regarding "accordance and opposition" and so forth—whether through transformation by accordance or transformation by opposition, or through various forms and various lands—each and every one serves as a condition for sentient beings to enter into reality.
As the subsequent text states: "In every thought-moment, he constantly acts as a single Buddha for the sake of sentient beings."
This refers to the "vehicle of mature liberation. The traditional interpretation by scholars as "the meaning of observing the mind" is incorrect.
That sutra previously followed a gradual approach; now, upon examining the commentary on the lower section of the original sutra, it states:

"How can one who cannot arise, abide, go, or come, and lacks speech, be called a 'good man practicing the conduct of an infant'? The sutra says: "What is meant by 'practicing the conduct of an infant,' good man?"
The inability to arise, abide, or engage in speech is called "infant"; the Tathāgata is also like this.
"Unable to arise" means that the Tathāgata never gives rise to the characteristics of dharmas. "Unable to abide" means that the Tathāgata does not cling to any dharmas.
"Unable to come" means that the Tathāgata’s bodily actions are without movement. "Unable to go" means that the Tathāgata has already reached Great Nirvāṇa.
As for those who cannot speak, although the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for all sentient beings, in reality there is nothing preached. Why is this?
That which can be preached is called a conditioned dharma (*saṃskṛtadharma*); the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is not conditioned. Therefore, [there is nothing preached].
The "large characters" (*akṣara*) are the *Tathāgata-garbha*. Furthermore, the "infant" (*bāla*) refers to these large characters.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he speaks of the large characters, namely *ba-ho-ho*. *Ba* signifies the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and *ho* signifies the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

This is called the infant. *Ho* is named impermanence (*anitya*), and *ba* is named permanence (*nitya*). When sentient beings hear this, because it is the Dharma of permanence, they sever [their doubts].
Impermanence is called the conduct of an infant.
It is because they do not know that suffering and pleasure are universal. As a sutra says: "Furthermore, an infant does not distinguish between suffering and pleasure, nor between day and night.

As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, an infant does not perform actions of great or small magnitude;

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that while the various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stages have not yet been abandoned at the time of [attaining the path of] seeing, they are collectively designated as "one set of nine" when one reaches the foot of the tree; this refers to the nine grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) belonging to the nine stages.

It is said that the position of the Tripiṭaka masters is that Bodhisattvas on these [lower] stages are equal to ordinary beings (and so forth). The general intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is that [afflictions] are severed all at once (*yugapat*).

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* state that the afflictions of the lower eight stages have already been completely severed prior to the initial cultivation of dhyāna;

only the nine grades of cognitive afflictions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception remain. Because their faculties are superior, they do not [sever them] again by means of the nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Furthermore, one further cultivates the concentrations of the lower eight stages (as discussed at length). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) evaluates this, stating: "Now, by adopting a single interpretation, we harmonize and reconcile the two treatises so that they are equal.

The *Abhidharmakośa* takes the position that when one has already severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) during the time of cultivating dhyāna, there is nothing further to sever. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, relying on other schools, maintains that although afflictions may be severed while still under the influence of outflows (*sāsrava*), this is not yet called 'severance' in the true sense;
rather, it is only upon reaching the Bodhi tree that one severs the [afflictions] of the eighth stage, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)."

That which is associated with the [uncontaminated] stages (bhūmi) is termed "untainted" (anāsrava); however, because they are distinguished by their respective categories (nikāya), the application of the term differs between the two treatises.
Its essence is inferior wisdom;

that is to say, it consists of relish (āsvāda), power (prabhāva), maturation (vipāka), qualities (guṇa), number (saṃkhyā), time (kāla), and measure (parimāṇa). As stated in the opening verse of homage at the beginning of the *Abhidharmakośa*: [text follows].
The *Commentary on the Exposition of the Treatise on the Extinction of All Kinds of What is Suitable* (*Sarvākāra-yukti-nirodha-śāstra-vyākhyā*) states:

"All kinds" (*sarvākāra*) refers to the objects of non-afflicted ignorance. "Kind" (*prakāra*) means category; that is to say, regarding each individual object, there are aspects such as taste (*rasa*), power (*vīrya*), and maturation (*vipāka*).

"Taste" refers to the flavor of phenomena (*dharma*), or tastes such as suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth. "Power" refers to the power of phenomena, such as their capacity for benefit or harm. "Maturation" refers to...

Regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), when they reach the stage of maturation, there are qualities (*guṇa*), which refers to their functional efficacy; number (*saṃkhyā*), such as one, two, and so forth; quantity (*parimāṇa*), such as large and small;
location (*sthāna*), such as distant and near; time (*kāla*), such as past and future; similarity (*sāmānya*), which refers to resemblance; and difference (*viśeṣa*), which refers to distinction.
However, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* identifies these as non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*). If one were to define their essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are ten in total.
The two schools take only inferior wisdom (*hīna-prajñā*) as the essence of non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭa-ajñāna*).

Regarding the four characteristics of the cause for the two types of excellence: one tradition holds that when the potter encountered the former Śākyamuni, he made offerings with three things—grass, a lamp, and honey-mead—and made a vow; this is the cause for the [attainment of] the Tripiṭaka. This is the summit of the Form Realm, the Ultimate of Form (*Akaniṣṭha*), which is the dwelling place of Maheśvara.

The four contemplations of the mind are explained by analogy with what was previously stated.

Regarding the "possession of two": the old interpretation held that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is itself the middle and the provisional (*prajñapti*) is itself the middle; however, within this context, these remain distinct.

If one speaks of the "perfect middle," it possesses both the two [aspects of] emptiness and the provisional. Now, I maintain that "possessing two" refers simply to emptiness-and-middle and middle-and-middle. This is the present case.
Furthermore, this record explains the meaning of "central" by attaching it to specific phenomena as objects of contemplation; thus, it speaks of two types of "middle. What is their intent?

Previously, regarding the provisional teachings (*kyō*), there was a middle between having an essence and lacking an essence, and a middle between the fundamental and the manifested, or between the principle and the phenomena, or between permanence and annihilation.

Now, through the revelation of the truth (*kaiken*), that which has an essence and that which lacks an essence are fundamentally identical in principle, and the fundamental and the manifested, or permanence and annihilation, are no different from emptiness.
That which is the "middle" is precisely the middle between non-substantiality and the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

That which is the "middle of the middle" is the middle between substantial existence and the fundamental principle. Because within emptiness there is this principle that subsumes the meaning of the middle, it does not speak of the provisional.
Regarding those who explain "dispelling evil" as dispelling the evils of the three miserable realms, or as protecting the Dharma by dispelling the evil of those who destroy it:

I now maintain that humans and devas each have their own respective abiding realms. If one is unaware of this and rashly gives rise to contempt based on outward appearance and dress, the present inclusion [of these beings] among the assembly of those who hear the teaching serves to dispel the evil of such ignorant contempt.
Furthermore, regarding the two pairs of meanings, they should be understood as vehicles—that is, the two pairs of vehicles.

While the wording is general and the intent inclusive, the subsequent sutra text speaks only of "revealing one's origins" (fa-ji) in the case of śrāvakas, stating that they "internally conceal the practice of a bodhisattva.
As for those who are humans or devas, the sutra contains no mention of "revealing one's origins"; therefore, we now employ the general term "internal concealment" to include them as well.
Regarding the passage [in the *Yuanjue jing shu*] stating, "When a person possesses a fundamental basis, the old [delusions] are eliminated" (and so forth):
as for the Bodhisattva who "overflows the basis," since he has already realized that basis, we shall not discuss him here.

Through the clear contemplation of conditions (*pratyaya*), one illuminates the profound correspondence between object and wisdom (*ālambana-jñāna*) to clarify the contemplation of conditions. If the object gives rise to wisdom, then...
The proximate is the condition and the remote is the cause; if wisdom illuminates an object, then the condition is proximate and the cause is remote.

Among the various teachings that reveal and manifest [the truth], viewing emptiness and the provisional as identical to the middle is called the "contemplation for disclosing the provisional" (shiquan guan); viewing emptiness and the provisional as identical to the middle is called the "contemplation for manifesting the real" (xianshi guan).
Regarding the contemplations of the fundamental and the manifested: the concealment of the trace refers to the contemplation of emptiness and the provisional;

the manifestation of the trace refers to the contemplation of the Middle Way. Thus, the master and disciple differ. Originally, a nun received the precepts from the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*); therefore, the monks were the masters and the nuns were the disciples.
Recently, due to royal decree, one receives the precepts directly from the community of nuns. If this is the case, it constitutes the "original method" (*mūladharma*).
Among the bhikṣuṇīs, there were no great bhikṣuṇīs capable of transmitting the Dharma; thus, among the twenty-four patriarchs recorded in the *Chuan fabao ji*, there was no bhikṣuṇī.
Although they constitute one of the four assemblies when gathered in the congregation, [they were excluded from this lineage].

The six supernormal powers, the wisdoms, the eloquences, and the three emptinesses—namely those of Maudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Pūrṇa, and Subhūti—are respectively correlated with the supernormal powers and so forth.
Regarding the seven meanings, there are only three; even if a "first meaning" were to exist, according to the intent of the *Mahā-śāstra*, it is entirely subsumed within these three.
Because of the distinction between the Great and the Small, the three teachings are discussed alternately in terms of their relative magnitude.
One must understand that they encompass both the beginning and the end: first receiving the three provisional beginnings, and later entering the ultimate reality of the final stage.
Alternatively, the three [teachings] may be considered as originally being the three, all of which are received at the outset.
Alternatively, there is a sequential entry into the three teachings.
Therefore, it is said that the *Tripiṭaka* (Three Baskets) has one additional character (*yi*).

In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), the similarities and differences are such that at the time of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, they are identical; in places such as the *Avataṃsaka*, they are identical with the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* precepts.

They share the same path and the mind of omniscience; they share the same Middle Way and untainted right view; they share the same sequential entry into the path; and they share the same liberation through transformation.

Regarding the four means of integration, they perform the same service: first, through the integration of giving, they cause sentient beings to give rise to the Bodhisattva practice of the two kinds of giving—material and Dharma.
Regarding the two types of affectionate love: first, the bodhisattva gathers [beings] through kind speech by using gentle words to instruct and transform sentient beings;
second, the bodhisattva gathers [beings] through beneficial conduct by practicing what benefits sentient beings. Fourth, the bodhisattva gathers [beings] through common purpose:

because they perceive the faculties and conditions of sentient beings with the Dharma-eye, they manifest various forms and emanate shadows according to what beings delight in, engaging in the same activities as them.

Regarding the traces [of the Buddha] in the preceding teachings, they are again the same number as before; he manifested traces to establish the Śrāvakas of the *zhì* (access) and *tōng* (penetration) vehicles, who are merely named "abiding in the fruit" and so forth.
As for the "preceding number," it refers to the four types listed above.
Furthermore, "should" (應) and "ground" (地) should be pronounced with the departing tone (*shēng*).
The two characters "ground" (地) and "abide" (住) occur frequently here.

The confusion caused by "arrogance" (上慢) is the same as the previous count; those who are arrogant often overstep their bounds and cause confusion. [They employ] transformations and shared activities.
This is also as previously stated: they are merely termed "those with overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).

To clarify fully, their three types of mindfulness differ from those of outsiders; while the mindfulness of outsiders takes the nature of true reality (*satyadharmatā*) as its object, yet differs by taking only the views of annihilationism and eternalism as objects, the common foundations of mindfulness take uncontaminated dhyāna (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) as their object, differing from outsiders who take only contaminated dhyāna of relishing (*sāsrava-āsvāda-dhyāna*) as their object.

Regarding the objects of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are internal and external distinctions. Unlike outsiders, who take only the four Vedas as their objects, [the Buddhist practitioner] takes these three types of mindfulness in relation to the four *siddhāntas* (ultimate aims):

the mindfulness of the world (*loka-smṛtyupasthāna*) corresponds to the worldly aim (*loka-siddhānta*); the mindfulness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-smṛtyupasthāna*) corresponds to the ultimate aim (*paramārtha-siddhānta*);

and the common mindfulness (*sādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*) corresponds to the therapeutic aim (*prātipakṣika-siddhānta*). The ultimate truth is for the person, while the world is the therapeutic. These details are as extensive as described in that text.
In the past, from the initial stage up to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the majority were those within the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), who were mostly "greatly superior" (*da duosheng*).
What is explained in this present commentary refers to those who have already received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the eight aspects; thus, they are called "greatly superior.

Furthermore, the three meanings of the Separate Teaching explained in this commentary are presented from the perspective of the path of teaching (*shikyo*); if followed from the perspective of the path of realization (*zhengdao*), it is identical to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

(1) the aggregates, (2) afflictions, (3) karma, (4) the mind, (5) death, (6) the son of a deva, (7) roots of goodness, and (8) samādhi.
The nine spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and the tenth, awakening (bodhi).
Regarding the "alms-seeker" (bhikṣu) and the "terrifying of Māra," these may be understood according to the standard exegesis; they are explained by means of the Madhyamaka.

The contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā) actualizes the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), while the contemplation of the conventional (prajñapti-vipaśyanā) actualizes the relative truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Through the contemplation of emptiness, one realizes that afflictions are themselves awakening; through the contemplation of the conventional, one realizes the fetters.
The name "Frightening Māra" refers to liberation through karma. Pure livelihood consists of:

eating from the four directions (referring to acting as a messenger); eating from the mouth (referring to practicing medicine or divination); eating from above the mouth (referring to astrology and lunar calculations);
and eating from below the mouth (referring to agriculture). Excluding these [unlawful means] is called pure livelihood.

The three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) are so called because the clear knowledge of past lives brings understanding of past events and engenders great wearying detachment; the clear knowledge of the divine eye brings understanding of future events;
and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vidyā*) is called "clear knowledge" because it severs delusions through meditative contemplation.
To clarify the intent of the teaching, its characteristics are set forth in the *Xuánwén*: "In the milk, there are three types—distinct, round, and entering-into-distinct-and-round two-truths;
two coarse and one subtle. In the curd, there are only two-truths, which are purely coarse. In the fresh butter, there are seven types: two-truths, six coarse, and one subtle.
In the mature butter, there are six types: five coarse and one subtle. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, there is only the single round [truth]; its two-truths are exclusively subtle."
The reason for not using a coarse title and instead designating it as "Sublime" lies in this very point.

Regarding the term *quan* (詮): it should be written as *quan* (銓). In the *Hanshu*, Ying Shao states that *quan* refers to the balance scale (*quan-heng*). Wei Zhao states that *quan* refers to the weights on a scale;
one uses the weights to align with the scale to determine lightness and heaviness. As for *liang* (量), it refers to the bushel (*dou*); by means of it, one can know quantity.
The two characters "shao" (few) are used metaphorically.
To observe the mind through the preceding Two Truths is precisely the Middle, which is True; it is precisely Emptiness, which is Provisional and Conventional.
The Ten Precepts are the dharmas produced by causes and conditions, which are precisely the Pratimokṣa restraints such as non-deficiency; they are precisely Emptiness, the Path, and Samādhi.
The "equal precepts" are the precepts praised by conventional wisdom; they range from the middle way to the ultimate. According to the number [of phenomena], one generates understanding:

regarding these enumerated dharmas, one may generate an understanding of them as causes and conditions, arising and ceasing, and in combination; or one may generate an understanding of them as being numbered yet not numbered;
or one may generate an understanding of them as being unnumbered yet numbered; or one may generate an understanding of them as being neither unnumbered nor non-unnumbered, yet numbered.
It is not that the four teachings do not have different enumerations of "solutions" (explanations);

rather, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that even those who have not yet awakened the aspiration [for enlightenment] are still called Bodhisattvas— this refers to all sentient beings by virtue of their inherent nature (li-xing).

In future lives, those who cultivate the fields will extinguish suffering; thus, birth for me has been exhausted, the accumulation of karma has been severed, the holy life has been established through cultivation, and cessation has been realized—what was to be done has been accomplished.
When the Buddha arrived at an araṇya, he spoke to the bhikṣus, as recorded in the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*:
"In the past, fifty *li* from the city of Vārāṇasī there was a mountain. Within that mountain were five bhikṣus who entered the city for alms each morning and returned to the mountain after midday.
Eventually, they became so weary that they were unable to settle into dhyāna. The Buddha then manifested as a wandering practitioner and went to their location."
He comforted them (as follows): "Do not beg for alms tomorrow morning; I shall provide you with offerings.

The next day, the Buddha sent food to them, and after the five men had eaten, they all attained arhatship (and so forth). Thus we know that the Tathāgata is not merely one who is worthy of offerings (saṃbhuñjati), but is also one who shares in those offerings (sambhoga).
That which is to be countered consists of the suffering and its origin—the causes and effects of birth and death—which are the objects of counteraction.
Now, both aspects are combined: the former was explained with reference to the "lesser" [teachings] and the latter with reference to the "greater.
Through the three wisdoms that neither break nor do not break, the three delusions are thoroughly and completely destroyed.
There is no thief who does not steal; the thief of birth-and-death steals the True, while the thieves of the mundane steal the Conventional.
Regarding the "Eight Winds," the Master of Nanshan explained them as follows: gain brings joy, while decline brings distress; disparagement incites anger, while praise brings delight;
flattery gratifies the emotions, while sarcasm breeds resentment; encountering suffering leads to dejection, while meeting with pleasure gives rise to indulgence.

The subsequent section explains why the mind attains mastery: it is because all fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*) have been exhausted. The remaining three phrases should be explained accordingly.
The *Shouji qushi men lun* (Treatise on the Door of Gathering and Grasping) lists sixteen phrases in full; the treatise states that both the general and specific categories refer to Arhats.
Regarding these sixteen phrases, the first phrase is general while the remaining ones are specific. It should be understood that there are fifteen meanings of this Arhat:
first, he is worthy of receiving offerings of food, drink, bedding, and robes, as well as honor and respect; second, he is worthy of leading the great assembly to transform and teach all beings;
third, he is worthy of entering villages and cities; fourth, he is worthy of subduing all non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas).
Fifth, one should swiftly observe phenomena with wisdom; sixth, one should teach the Dharma neither too hastily nor too slowly, in accordance with the Dharma, without weariness;

seventh, one should sit in quiet seclusion, refraining from accumulating food, clothing, or any requisites of life, possessing few desires and being content; eighth, one should practice exclusively in goodness.
Ninth, because one should practice without attachment to the various dhyānas; tenth, because one should practice the noble conduct of emptiness (*śūnyatā-ārya-caryā*);
eleventh, because one should practice the noble conduct of signlessness (*animitta-ārya-caryā*); twelfth, because one should practice the noble conduct of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-ārya-caryā*);
thirteenth, because one should subdue worldly dhyāna and purify the mind; fourteenth, because one should give rise to all supreme merits; fifteenth, because one should realize...

Fifteenth, because of the merit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one should know things as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*): that one attains all merits in common with sentient beings for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Regarding the "gate of gathering matters by explaining matters in opposition," these fifteen phrases demonstrate the gathering of ten merits.
Because it can be described as manifest fruit and cannot be described as manifest fruit, [the first] phrase subsumes merit; the second phrase demonstrates this, as in the sūtra:
"All outflows are exhausted, and there are no further afflictions. The third phrase subsumes all merits;
the fourth phrase is the merit of subduing the world, as in the sūtra: "The mind has attained mastery"; and the fifth phrase is the subduing of those who train in the supramundane.
First, the merit of a person is as described in the sūtra: because they have well attained liberation through mind (*ceto-vimukti*) and well attained liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Second, the merit of gathering what has not yet been attained: because they act in accordance with the teachings of the Tathāgata, as the sūtra says, "because their minds are well-tamed.

Third, the merit of gathering excellence: because they are "great dragons among men," as the sūtra says. Fourth, the merit of gathering what is to be done: because they excel in that which ought to be performed.
1. That which is to be performed by means of merit: because one makes offerings, pays homage, respects, and honors the Tathāgata according to the Dharma;

as the sūtra says, "one performs what is to be performed. 2. The sixth is the grasping of fulfilled merit: because one fulfills the stage of training (*śaikṣabhūmi*); as the sūtra says, "the merit that has been accomplished. 3.
The seventh is the grasping of merit that transcends the three phrases: first, the transcendence of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Second... [text fragment].
1. It surpasses the seeking of life, offerings, and honor; 2. it surpasses the lower and upper realms because it has transcended the stages of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*);
as the Sūtra says, "having abandoned all heavy burdens, one attains one's own benefit and exhausts all fetters of existence" (*bhava-saṃyojana*); 3.

it encompasses the virtues of both the lower and upper [realms], as the Sūtra says, "having well attained right knowledge, the mind is liberated"; 4. it encompasses that which should be done for the benefit of others.
The merit of sentient beings is as described in the sutra because they have attained mastery over all minds.

Tenth is the merit of grasping the foremost [qualities], as described in the sutra because they have reached the supreme other shore. In the commentary, fifteen phrases are used to subsume these ten kinds of merit;
since ten of them are primarily phenomena of activity (*vastu-dharma*), it is said that they "grasp the door of activity."
Because they are distinguished from the beginning, one phrase constitutes the opening and five phrases constitute the distinctions.
Excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), among the eighty-eight [defilements], the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*) is removed from each.

Regarding the four floods (*ogha*): the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) consists of all defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) excluding views and delusion; the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) consists of those of the upper realms...
Regarding the two realms, all afflictions—excluding views (*dṛṣṭi*) and ignorance (*moha*)—constitute the "outflow of views" (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*), which refers to the views of the three realms;

the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*) refers to the ignorance of the three realms. In the desire realm, there are two outflows, excluding views and ignorance; one should know that among the afflictions of thought (*klesas*), only greed (*lobha*), pride (*māna*), and the anger (*pratigha*) of the desire realm are mentioned here, as these are merely supplementary explanatory texts.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "The Peak of Existence (*prāntakoṭika*) is that which is universally compliant up to the ultimate. The *Śāstra* commentary explains this as the definition of the term "Peak of Existence":
it is so called because it proceeds from all stages, being universally compliant and increasing until it reaches the ultimate.

That is to say, one enters the first *dhyāna* from the preparatory wholesome mind of the desire realm, proceeding in sequence through the stages up to the Peak of Existence; then, again from the Peak of Existence...

Entering from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) into the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) by way of reverse order, and proceeding down through the successive stages until the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) by way of direct order, continuing in this alternating fashion up to the Fourth Dhyāna, is called "pervasive conformity across all stages" (*sarvabhūmivyāpyanuloma*). This refers to the dedicated cultivation of the Fourth Dhyāna, proceeding from the lower to the middle, and from the middle to the upper;
these three grades are each further divided into three, resulting in the nine levels from the lowest-of-the-low to the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātrādhimātra*).
Regarding the term "birth," when such meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) reaches its ultimate limit, it receives the name "attaining the boundary" (*prāntakoṭika*).
According to the *Śāstra*, there should not yet be the exhaustion of the bonds of the fruit [of Arhatship] among the four great Arhats: Kāśyapa, Rāhula, Piṇḍola-bharadvāja, and Kuṇḍopadhānīya.

Regarding those liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*), there are many instances of regression, as explained in the section on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. If one abandons afflictions through mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*), there is much regression;

however, if one abandons afflictions through untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), there is no regression. As for those who do regress, this generally occurs up to the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*). Regarding the meaning of "regression," there are three explanations.

The Sarvāstivādins maintain that one does not regress from the first fruit, whereas one may regress from the [other] three fruits. This master asserts that [regression applies to] the abandonment of afflictions deluded regarding phenomena (*vastu-moha*).
Because their modes of practice are superficial and false, the Mahāsāṃghikas claim that one may fall back from the first three fruits but not from the fourth fruit of certainty;

this master asserts that one falls back from the first three because the afflictions have not been exhausted. The Sautrāntikas claim that one does not fall back from the first fruit or the fourth fruit, while one often falls back from the middle two;
this master asserts that one falls back from the middle two fruits because they encompass both defiled and undefiled states.

Thus, with respect to the phrase "arhat," these five phrases also constitute a relationship of general and specific; the phrase "exhaustion of all outflows" is general, while the remaining four phrases are specific.
Nirvāṇa is the general term, as it possesses the three virtues.
To describe them separately, there are three types of each regarding their nature and cultivation.
Regarding the eight forms of the "Self-Master" (Īśvara): first, the power of creation; second, the power of creation; third, the power of lightness; fourth, the power of sovereignty;
fifth, the power of possessing a master; sixth, the power of reaching afar; seventh, the power of shaking the earth; eighth, the power of acting according to one's will.
Regarding the body entering the womb and the establishment of the practice of Kāśyapa:
it is like the person falling from a cliff; as the *Guhya-sūtra* says, "Just as a person falling from a cliff is already called a dead man even before reaching the ground."
"Pi" (麩) is pronounced with a slight retroflex "fū" (夫) and is also written as "chao" (麨); it refers to parched grain meal (*kṣaudra*).
To be pure and to accord with one's mind is called "pure" (*śuci*).

Why is it known that the *Jì* (Commentary) and the *Shù* (Sub-commentary) appear to contradict one another regarding the failure to understand the image as empty? The *Jì* states that... [text fragment].

If one perceives the image as empty, it is like a blind person regarding an image with the physical eye and giving rise to attachment toward it; if one realizes the image is empty, it is like opening one's eyes—meaning the eye of wisdom has opened.

In the *Śāstra*, taking the wisdom of non-arising is like the state of non-discrimination of a blind person, while taking the mirror-image is like opening one's eyes, which is like the physical eye giving rise to attachment. Now, in the *Vivaraṇa*, these two explanations are reconciled so that they may be made consistent.

The phrase "not understanding that images are empty" means that the force of the expression has not yet reached its conclusion; it implies that if one understands that images are empty, this constitutes the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and thus one would be like a blind person.
Alternatively, the character "not" (*bu*) may simply be a variant of the character "if" (*ruo*). Let students examine this further.

The mirror is the auxiliary cause; the "mirror" refers to the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas). When the grasping mind conditions these, one initiates accumulated karma, and the future fruit of suffering arises—this is what is meant by the appearance of an image.
By means of this, the fundamental nature of causes and conditions is clarified through the six sense bases. Thus, it is by relying on this that the nature of causes and conditions is elucidated.
Causes and conditions each arise from their own causes and conditions; that is to say, the human cause-condition and the mirror cause-condition.

If one analyzes them exhaustively, there are four causes and conditions. Regarding the human cause-condition, there are two: first, ignorance (*avidyā*) in past kalpas serves as the cause, while body and speech serve as the condition;
second, the parents' craving and desire serve as the cause, while the two drops of red and white [semen and blood] serve as the condition. This refers to others.
The causal conditions for parents arise from the causal conditions of one's own ignorance and the body and speech [of the parents]. Regarding the causal conditions of a mirror, there are also two:
first, the substance of the mirror is the cause and polishing is the condition; second, its luminous clarity is the cause and the manifestation of images is the condition.
This means that the causal conditions for the luminous clarity and the manifestation of images arise from the causal conditions of the mirror’s substance and its polishing.
Although there are four causes and conditions for birth, none of them fail to be like an illusion. Although the current text appears thus, this commentary seems somewhat prolix;
I still suspect that the two characters "causes and conditions" (yin-yuan) in the preceding passage may be redundant.

If it were said that both the person and the mirror are illusions, then since the person and the mirror each arise from their own respective causes and conditions, there would be no need for the aforementioned four causes and conditions.
This is a complex and detailed matter; I fear that errors may have occurred during transcription, so students should examine it carefully.

The matters of delusion and awakening are equal across the ten realms: suffering and its accumulation constitute delusion, while the Four Noble Truths and cessation constitute awakening. This applies from the Buddhas who have attained the realization down to ordinary sentient beings.
Regarding the principle, it begins with the Ten Faiths and ends with the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue).
Regarding "adventitious dust," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "For example, it is like a guest who stays at an inn;

having completed his stay and departed without remaining, he is called a 'guest,' while the resident is called the 'host. Furthermore, it is like the rising sun illuminating the sky; within the void, one sees dust particles quivering.
That which moves is called 'dust,' and that which does not move is called 'space.'"

Regarding the three paths of the various threefold dharmas, these refer to the three paths of the *pariṇāma* (transformation) [realm]. As for the three paths of the *upāya-bhūmi* (land of skillful means), the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary on the Profound Meaning) states:

"Dust-like sands constitute the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*); untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) constitutes the path of karma (*karma-mārga*); and transformation birth-and-death (*pariṇāma-jāti-maraṇa*) constitutes the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*).

Regarding the three paths of the *samyak-vipāka-bhūmi* (land of true retribution), ignorance (*avidyā*) constitutes the path of afflictions; that which is neither tainted nor untainted (*na-āsrava-na-anāsrava*) constitutes the path of karma; and transformation... [birth-and-death constitutes the path of suffering].
The Path of Suffering is easily transformed.
Whether great or small, there is no obstruction to liberation; through great wisdom, the small is liberated.
Whether manifest or obscure, those with prominent faculties are manifest, while those who are stammering and dull are obscure.
He manifested both silence and eloquence: Paṇḍaka was silent and Pūrṇa was eloquent.

Their practices were equal while their principles differed; some say that although the names of these twenty-one venerable ones differ, they are called "equal" because their practice of non-arising is the same.
As for "the principles differing," some say it refers to the difference in the principles of the Three Truths, while others say it refers to the various venerable ones...
Each presides over a single office; the principles may differ, or perhaps it is the practices that differ while the principles remain equal—this is likely a textual error.

These include a single dharma or a single matter, such as the dharmas of the Four Truths or the five sense objects, as well as matters of transformative teaching through inversion or conformity, and matters of divine transformations.

Regarding the gates of contemplation and cultivation: if it concerns the Buddha-land of the Unblinking One (Amitābha), it is generally said that one proceeds from seeing and contemplating through cultivation;
if it concerns the Buddha-land of Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhottamakūṭa), it is generally said that one proceeds from smelling and contemplating through cultivation.

Nevertheless, there is no gate of the three types of wisdom that does not take the Three Truths as its object of wisdom and the Three Contemplations as its essence of wisdom; therefore, it is said that they are not distinct, as detailed below in the text.
Entering the second record on Sublime Joy:
Regarding the *Hetu* (River Chart) discussed in the *Analects*, it says that when a sage receives the Mandate of Heaven, the phoenix arrives and the River produces the chart.
Kong Anguo stated that the "River Chart" refers precisely to the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*). Zheng Xuan, however, maintained that the River Chart and the Luo [Chart]...

The tortoise and dragon [held] the vessel in their mouths and carried it forth, just as described in the *Zhonghou*: the dragon-horse [held] the vessel with its shell marked with red patterns and green color;

the shell resembled the back of a tortoise, measuring nine feet in length and breadth, upon which were inscribed the positions of the lunar mansions and the degrees of the Dipper for regulating the calendar, as well as the records of emperors and kings concerning the cycles of prosperity and decline. This is precisely what is meant.

Regarding the twelve dhūtas—whether they are identical or different: (1) dwelling in the forest (*araṇya*), (2) always begging for food (*piṇḍapātika*), (3) wearing rag-robes from refuse-heaps (*pāṃsukūlika*), (4) eating in a single sitting (*aikāsanika*), (5) moderation in food (*khalupaśyaka*), (6) not drinking liquids after midday (*khalu-paścād-bhakta-khādanīya-pratiniḥsṛṣṭa*), (7) dwelling among tombs (*śmāśānika*), (8) dwelling at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūlika*), (9) dwelling in the open air (*ābhyavakāśika*), (10) always sitting (*naiṣadyika*), (11) following the sequence of alms-round (*sāpadānacārika*), and (12) possessing only the three robes (*traicīvarika*). As for whether these are identical or different, it is according to the Vinaya.
There are those who sit following [the rules] without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food) and who eat only a single morsel;

in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there is no discussion of moderation in eating or not drinking liquids after midday. Regarding sequential begging (*pindapātika*), it does not appear in the *Vinaya*. Furthermore, the *Vinaya* speaks of "patchwork robes" (*nāmakāṣāya*) and the *Śāstra* speaks of "rags from a dust heap" (*pāṃsukūla*);

the *Vinaya* speaks of "begging for food" (*piṇḍapātika*) and the *Śāstra* speaks of "constant begging. Although these two pairs differ in name, their meaning is the same. (The above is the main text.)
Now, I fear that "constant begging" merely refers to begging from house to house in sequence, with "constant sitting" added to make twelve [practices].

These possess ten merits; for now, I shall cite one set of ten merits regarding the *araṇya* (forest hermitage): first, freedom of movement in coming and going; second, the absence of the sense of "mine";

third, acting according to one's will without hindrance; fourth, transforming one's habits through the forest life; fifth, having few desires regarding one’s dwelling; sixth, not being attached to possessions...
The body and life are endowed with virtue; seventh, there is no clamor; eighth, one does not seek gratitude or recompense; ninth, one accords with dhyāna and attains it easily;
tenth, one understands emptiness and attains it easily. For the rest, the details are fully set forth in that [text].
Regarding the statement "movement is not self because it is not autonomous movement," the *Sū* (Commentary) says: "The *Si-li-ji* (Record of Four Examples) states that there is no self.
Now, I shall explain this from two perspectives: first, autonomous movement is the true self, whereas the present [movement] is a deluded self; since there is no such self, it is called 'no-self.
Second, one might fear that the character 'wu' (no) is a scribal error and is merely a [phonetic] character."

I do not have the leisure to fully describe the sequence of all the contemplations (*vipaśyanā*), nor do I have the leisure to demonstrate the contemplation of the mind for each of the twelve ascetic practices (*dhūta*).

For now, I shall merely describe the three contemplations in conjunction with the three topics of dwelling, clothing, and food. Furthermore, according to the preceding text, within the four types of interpretation, one relies on phenomena (*vastu*) to cultivate contemplation;

thus, in this text, it is likewise appropriate to describe the ascetic practice of contemplating causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-dhūta-vipaśyanā*) and the ascetic practice of interpreting through the teachings (*yāna-vibhāga-dhūta-vipaśyanā*).

The contemplations on the original and the trace, the contemplation of *dhūta* (ascetic practices), and the contemplation of the mind through *dhūta* are not currently available for study; students should understand this by analogy.

Regarding "priceless" (*wúqí*), the character *qí* is pronounced with the second tone and the initial *j* (as in *jié*). It means goods or wealth. Because those of the Confucian tradition often adopt the meaning of "invaluable," it is here called "priceless."
*Shēn* (上汝鴆切, 下章刃切; also pronounced *shēn*): This refers to being pregnant. *Báizhè* (白哲; 下旨熱切):
A pure white color. Formerly, Chen Wu, whose courtesy name was Ziqiang, was fair-skinned (*báizhè*) and had a full beard and hair.
The character 鸚鵡[口*雋][口*雋] does not appear in the *Yùpiān*. I suspect it is actually the character 喙 (huì), pronounced with the phonetic 許穢 (xǔ wèi).
Its lips are as red as the beak of a parrot; the *Zuǒchuán* states: "Deep-mouthed and with a false beak."
The latter two must employ the seven purities of the same essence (*ekātmya*), which are the dharmas for severing both *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions). The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:
"Regarding the stage where views within the realm [of desire] are exhausted, it is called 'purity of view' (*dṛṣṭiviśuddhi*) and 'purity beyond doubt' (*tīrṇavicikitsāviśuddhi*);

regarding the stage where afflictions are exhausted, it is called 'purity of discernment' (*pratyavekṣaṇāviśuddhi*) and 'purity of practice' (*pratipattiviśuddhi*)," and so forth. As for "same essence," this occurs only upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*). The *Ṭīkā* further states: "If..."

According to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), in both the mundane and supramundane realms, the removal of afflictions through the views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thoughts (*saṃjñā*) involves a sequence of before and after, which can be easily inferred by analogy.

However, upon entering the stages (*bhūmi*), the principle of the single essence (*tattva*) is not sequential. Within the Separate Teaching, although one enters the stages later, there remains a distinction between the sequence of views and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), from beginning to end, there is no duality. (The above is the main text.)
*Yíngyī* (縈衣): "Yíng" is pronounced with the *shàng* tone, cut by *yíng* (營). It refers to the elaborate decoration of garments and attire. *Ruǎndòng* (蠕動):
"Ruǎn" is pronounced with the *shàng* tone, cut by *rǔn* (而允). The *Huáinánzǐ* says: "Crawling and fluttering. This refers to insects.
Regarding that Buddha, there are three characters here that appear to be errors: "shì" (示) should be "ěr" (爾), and "pǐfó" (彼佛) [should be "bǐfó"]. (The second instance of "pǐfó" is correct).
The characters appear to be numerous.

The "six elements" (ṣaḍ-dhātu) may refer to earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness; however, it is also possible they refer to the six sense organs or the six realms of ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-gati*).
I have not yet verified this in the sūtras.

"Lai-fu-gen" (萊茯根): "Lai" should be written as "lu" (蘆) and "fu" should be written as "fu" (菔), with pronunciations *fu* or *bu*; it is the name of a vegetable that has been vulgarly corrupted into "lu-bo" (蘿蔔).
"Shan-zhi-fa-xiang" (善知法相):
this is likely a scribal inversion; it probably refers to "shan-zhi-xiang-fa" (善知相法), such as the dharmas of goodness (*kuśala*) and so forth.

Regarding the partial and the perfect (*piān-yuán*), as distinguished in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text): "How do the partial and the perfect relate to the provisional and the real (*quán-shí*)? The answer is:

It is for the sake of future evil bhikṣus who will possess impure things and preach to the fourfold assembly that the Buddha has entered nirvana.

One who possesses all the factors of faith—such as faith, hearing the Dharma, and understanding the Buddha-nature—does so because of faith; through faith one advances, and through faith one progresses.

This applies likewise to all the various categories up to morality. Because of morality, there is faith; because of morality, there is effort; because of morality, there is mindfulness, and so on. They receive their names from that which is predominant, and are thus designated as "morality" and so forth.

Regarding "Life": at this point, it is called the stage of Supreme Patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). and the third *kalpa* corresponds to the stage of the Peak (*mūrdhan*). During the hundred *kalpas* of the stage of Lower Patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), one leaves the household life and subdues the Māras; during the stage of Middle Patience (*madhya-kṣānti*), [one proceeds] to the next.
Entering the highest patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) in a single moment: if one discusses this in terms of a hundred eons, it refers to the fundamental lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*);

that it is now called "highest" may be because the three patiences are explained collectively, or because the citations from the *Jùlùn* (Treatise on Verses) differ, or perhaps due to a scribal error.

whether hidden or manifest, ordinary or sage,

the second tier extends eight thousand, the third four thousand, and the fourth two thousand, all calculated in thousands of yojanas.
Outside the city, adorning its four sides, there are four most excellent and delightful parks: first, the Caitraratha Park;
second, the Pāruṣyaka Park; third, the Miśraka Park; and fourth, the Nandana Park.
Each of the four tiers has ten abodes. On the four tiers of Mount Sumeru, there are the abodes of the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods; on the first tier, there are ten abodes belonging to them:
(1) the Elephant-headed gods (*Hastisīsa*), (2) the Always-Indulgent gods (*Sadāmada*), (3) the Lute-bearing gods (*Tūṇava*), and so forth, each having ten abodes.
Three and a half cubits constitute one unit; each cubit is eighteen inches.
The measurements increase twofold in succession: eight cubits for the eastern continent, sixteen cubits for the western continent, and thirty-two cubits for the northern continent.
In the desire-realm heavens (*kāmadeva*), each successive [level] increases by one-quarter of a *krośa*. An increase of one-quarter [of a *krośa*] is four *hasta*;
four *hasta* constitute one *dhanus*, which is also called one *vyāma*. Five hundred *vyāma* constitute one *krośa*, which is also called an *araṇya*.
Eight *krośa* constitute one *yojana*. The height of the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*) is one-quarter of a *krośa*.
The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is two-quarters of a krośa in height; the Yāma Heaven is three-quarters of a krośa; the Tuṣita Heaven is four-quarters of a krośa;
the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is five-quarters of a krośa; and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven is one and a half krośas.
In the heavens of form, a *yojana* is also called a *krośa*.
Among them, the gods of the Brahmakāyika heaven are half a *yojana* in height; the gods of the Brahmapurohita heaven are one *yojana*;
