This passage—“observing illusion and transformation, one sees that afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves the dharma-nature” (*dharmatā*)—is found in the sixth section, within the text on “entering emptiness.
The *Mūla-śāstra* briefly cites the beginning and end of the gradual [teaching], stating:
“Just as a cow has milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and finally the supreme *sarpis* (ghee), so too is the Hīnayāna like milk and the Mahāyāna like *sarpis*. This is the analogy.”
It clarifies that the unsurpassed Mahāyāna is likewise unsurpassed for all śrāvakas and others;
yet, it remains incomplete, as the "milk" analogy in the *Shu* (Commentary) on the Twelve Divisions of Scripture cites only the metaphor itself without corresponding to the thing being illustrated.
Xuánwén also correlates "milk" with the "Small Vehicle," citing a sūtra which says: "Ordinary beings are like milk, and Bodhisattvas are likewise;
because the power of a Bodhisattva’s self-realization is weak, they are identical to ordinary beings, being entirely untransformed, just like milk."
The reason for halting [the teaching] by stating that the profoundly quiescent Dharma at both ends cannot be spoken of rashly is twofold:
first, to inspire longing and admiration in those who are ready to receive it; second, to prevent those who have left the assembly from creating the conditions for slandering the Dharma.
Since the initial passage praises [the practice] by distinguishing it from the two types of cessation (*śamatha*), this is a praise that simultaneously encompasses cessation.

Regarding the objects, wisdom, practices, and stages, as well as the objective realm and essence of self and others: while the objects and wisdom cultivated during the five ranks, the ten levels of faith, and above—up to the stages of entry (*praveśa*) and abiding (*vihāra*)—constitute one's own practice, once these are perfected, one must necessarily transform others; therefore, the present text distinguishes them all to restrict [the focus].
Regarding the grasping of objects and so forth, these pertain to the Buddha in the state of fruition.

Among the six ordinary beings and four sages, from the beginning to the end—whether in the inverse or the direct order—the "objects" (*viṣaya*) refer to everything from the stage of "name-only" up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), encompassing both those who turn their backs in opposition and those who move toward accord. Here, all such cases are excluded; we take only the objects entered by the Buddha in the state of fruition.
Regarding the four categories—such as "accomplishment of both fruit and cause"—all of these pertain to the fruit.

As for the meaning of the phrase "if not accomplished" and so forth, it encompasses everything from the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) down to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Dengjue), and furthermore includes all three teachings and three vehicles, as they are all termed "not accomplished"; thus it says, "and because of all provisional [teachings]."
The principle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* consists of the two gates of the fundamental and the phenomenal (*honji-matsuji*), which are the subtle means capable of opening [the truth].
It is the head of all teachings; the four periods and three vehicles emerge from the One Vehicle.

Regarding the "key point" (*kangen*) of explaining the meaning: "gate" (*kan*) refers to the door-leaf and "point" (*gen*) refers to the bolt (*kōyaku*), meaning the essential locus. This is as explained in the commentary.

Since both the phenomenal and the noumenal aspects of creation point entirely to the nature of mind, it is said that [the opponent] does not understand this present text; how then can they explain the verse?
The "trigger for the arousal of the aspiration" (發心之機) means that the trigger serves as a support and the support serves as an incentive, implying a sense of reliance.
Because the non-constructive reality-mark (實相無作) is like a supporting object, one arouses the bodhicitta based upon it.

The application of expedient means (*upāya*) takes the essence as its basis while responding to conditions to benefit others; this matter relies upon the "root," which refers to the single nature (*ekaprakṛti*).
This is the source of both delusion and enlightenment: to go against it is to turn one's back on this nature and become deluded; to follow it is to realize this nature and bring it into practice.

The principle of the fruition-virtue is fundamentally the fruit-ground where the environment and its inhabitants are interpenetrated, and it likewise relies upon the fundamental nature of the capacities of all sentient beings.
Throughout the completion of a single cycle of transformation, the Buddha-seed has been universally permeated and matured; only today is one finally liberated.
Thus, both phenomenon and principle are perfected, and the capacity for enlightened activity is fulfilled.
At the conclusion of the five periods, spanning more than fifty years, the Great Matter of the Buddha’s intention was finally fulfilled.
This serves to dissolve various divergent views and attain this profound realm, which encompasses ten meanings as seen in the twenty-eight chapters and all the Perfect Sutras;
these have never failed to discuss the locus of reality.
The statement that "the five hundred bodhisattvas who have gathered for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are the five hundred arhats" is what is taught in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Regarding the phrase "those who take refuge in the Buddha-way," Ci'en (Xuanzang) states that these are śrāvakas of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) whose buddha-nature has already been extinguished; they await their own taking of refuge [in the Buddha-way].
The Buddha-way and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* open the assembly; it is not that this person is excluded from the assembly.
Furthermore, even those bodhisattvas who engage in empty talk regarding the sūtras, as well as those bodhisattvas who have not yet attained non-retrogression, likewise cannot know [this].
They should also understand that while the Buddha-nature may be eternally extinguished, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* does not exclude them from the assembly.

The *Shu* (Commentary) is brief and does not cite the specific sections, but provides a general heading for the chapter on the Provisional and the Real, stating: "The true reality of all dharmas (*dharmatā*)";

yet, when it subsequently cites the chapter on the Provisional, it says: "That which is called the suchness of all dharmas (*tathatā*), etc. According to the intention of Guangzhai, if one were to follow the citation of the Provisional, one would further need to cite the Real, saying:
"That which is called the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), such as the causes and so forth."

Therefore, the commentary uses "essence" (*tattva*) as the name; desire is the essence of bondage and attachment, while the essence is the true principle (*tattva*). Because one attains the true principle, one is able to fulfill all desires;
thus, the name "desire" is subsumed under "essence.

He then told his disciples: "The characteristics of lust and delusion are themselves the true nature of reality;
they are without obstruction. Vijayamati did not believe this and fell into hell, where he suffered for a thousand years before being reborn.

The Bodhisattva Xi-gen is now a Buddha in the eastern direction, named Light Surpassing the Sun and Moon Tathāgata.
Regarding the mutual relationship of principal and attendant (*pramukha-parivāra*), there are three meanings: either one Buddha is the principal with his emanation Buddhas as attendants;
or a Buddha is the principal with Bodhisattvas as attendants; or one Bodhisattva is himself the principal with his emanation Bodhisattvas as attendants.
The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Śāstra*) states: "The transforming principal and his retinue both take a single body and an infinite body to serve as principal and attendant to one another."
While they accompany one another, they are not of a single body; they possess mastery over the one and the many, yet they conceal the doctrine of the emanation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).

They merely speak of the mutual relationship between the principal and the retinue, and further state that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* adds four Bodhisattvas to explain the causes and effects of Bodhisattvas.

This ability to add [Bodhisattvas] belongs only to the *trac* (manifestation) Buddhas and their retinues; thus, there is no need to assemble the *shu* (universal) Buddhas. It is simply said that the ten directions act as each other's retinues.

Regarding the principal and the retinue (*parivāra*), it is not stated that the retinue consists of emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*); rather, they are simply referred to as "attendants" (*parijana*). (The above is the main text.
If a Bodhisattva establishes their own principal and retinue, it is as stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*:

"When the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta travels, immeasurable emanations of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta all gather like clouds. Furthermore, in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati...

Regarding the teaching of the Ten Abodes, those who teach the Ten Abodes in the worlds of the ten directions are all called Dharmamati, and so on up to Vajragarbha; the same applies to the teaching of the Ten Grounds.

There must never be a confusion of good with evil. Even in the case of the woman Vāsuladattā, who used desire to attract those she sought to convert—could she possibly have been among the ranks of the base and the lustful?

This refers to those who wish to enter the stage of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Otherwise, one could attain the samādhi of visiting all Buddha-fields by merely grasping another's hand;

When he deluded Ānanda, he also taught the Middle Way. At the time of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda was outside the Śāla grove, being tormented by sixty-four trillion māras. These māras transformed themselves into the likeness of the Tathāgata;

or of the contemplation of impurity, mindfulness of breathing, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four roots of goodness, the three gates of liberation, the stage of no-more-learning, the first bhūmi, up to the tenth dwelling, the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

This extensively expounds the three to reveal the one, and extensively expounds the near to reveal the distant.
How much more so when explaining the "four ones," which surpasses the Guangzhai school; here, the single fruit is exclusively the Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

To clarify that entry into the stages is easy at first but difficult later, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary* cites an ancient interpretation, stating: "The four [kinds of nirvana] always proceed from delusion."

The "mind-nature lineage" (*citta-prakṛti-gotra*) spans from six *kalpas* to eight *kalpas*; this refers to the subsequent "path-lineage of the mind" (*citta-mārga-gotra*) up to the point where Zhanran (Zhang’an) rebuked it, asking, "How does this relate to the Buddha-dharma?

down to the point where it says that "bodhi" cannot be attained by means of the body nor by means of the mind. The Commentary states: "The bodhi of skillful means has no person;

The present text takes the four wisdoms as collectively belonging to the resultant stage in order to refute the errors of past [scholars].

Regarding the four [wisdoms] beginning with "opening" (*ka*) and so forth, which correspond respectively to the four wisdoms: generally speaking, "opening" and the others are considered vertical (*ūrdhva*), whereas if "opening" and the others each possess the four wisdoms, they are termed horizontal (*tiryak*).

The ancients said that the four wisdoms are a single essence complete in itself; now, one must employ the horizontal to correspond to the vertical, matching the wisdom of the path (*mārga-jñatā*) with "opening," the wisdom of the aspects of the path (*mārgākāra-jñatā*) with "showing," the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) with "awakening," and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) with "entering."
Even if one considers cause and effect in relation to one another— such that the two types of wisdom, *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths) and *sarvajñatā* (omniscience),

Specifically, the obstacle to phenomenal wisdom refers to the delusion of "dust-like sands" (*rajas-aṃśu*), while the obstacle to principled wisdom refers to the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The two delusions—the pervasive and the particular—reside together within a single moment of thought. Their essence (*tǐ*) is precisely what is designated as "principle" (*lǐ*). Thus, their essence is identical;

it is the essence that is not principle, which is the phenomenal event (*shì*) rather than the fundamental nature. Master Yuancuo’s commentary states: "This expresses both non-identity and non-separation.
Regarding "it is the essence that is not principle": the essence of inherent virtue (*xingdé*) is itself the unmanifest delusion, for the delusion is not separate from it.

Since nature (*prakṛti*) is also ignorance and not a virtuous quality of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), it is said to be "unreasonable" (*ayoniśas*). Thus, delusion is precisely nature; this phenomenon is not [something other than] that.

This refers to both the general and specific delusions as being the virtuous qualities of nature. To manifest nature is not to be separate from delusion; because it is the virtuous quality of nature and not ignorance, it is said to be "not otherwise.
Therefore, one should know that this entirely employs the intent of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*. Now, in order to cite the scripture to accord with these two points:

Regarding the passage: "That which is unstained yet stained refers to the essence (tattva), which is not logical; that which is stained yet unstained refers to the phenomenon (vastu), which is not [the ultimate].

This is a summary of the "Separation from Attachment" (*li*) within the "Ten Abodes" (*shizhu*). My private explanation differs slightly from the public meaning established by Master Cao;
let us examine this in detail. When the *śāstra* enters into principle, it refers to Prajñā as the "Abode. That sutra correctly explains the meaning of the names of the Ten Abodes:

The fruit is named *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) and the cultivation of wisdom, etc.; these both reside in the cause, just as it is said that "calm abiding and insight are the cause, while eye and wisdom are the fruit.

Now, the reason why this commentary explains them without following a sequential order is to correspond to the three categories of the practitioner, the teaching, and the text of the Sutra that follows.

Contemplating that which is fundamentally unobstructed is the nature of the three wisdoms of *prajñā*, wherein they are fused and not compared. This differs from the preceding stages where obstructions remain;

here, the near and the distant mutually encompass one another. The principle of "one" is the near, while the other three are the distant. This principle is not manifested without the three, nor do the three exist apart from it.
The principle does not hold.

For the *Jielun* (Explanatory Treatise) states that there are four interpretations of the term "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) in the main treatise: first, the meaning of being unsurpassed; second, the meaning of being equal; third, the meaning of being unknowable;

Guangzhai points out that what was previously not understood as "wondrous" refers to the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle.

"Puṣya, my buddha-field shall be pure and flawless, such that men and women shall live separately and be free from lustful thoughts and the like.
Twenty-four *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands] of *kalpas* to the northwest of this place is where the Buddha named Acala resides.

That land is pure and free from lust, anger, and ignorance; those above and below are respectful and compliant, and they all cultivate the purity of the void. All sentient beings in that land are entirely [free from afflictions]."

To the northwest of this place, forty-eight *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands] away, there is a Buddha named Dharmadarśana.

The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, moment by moment free from all residual thoughts, cultivate only the unsurpassed path; they abandon the darkness of the fundamental limit and manifest the Buddha’s light of wisdom.
These Śrāvakas, adorned with their own multitude of virtues, proclaim incomparable teachings to transform and enlighten all people.

The nature of sentient beings (*sattva*) and lands (*kṣetra*) is one and the same; the three thousandfold world-system is this very nature.

Sentient beings are the primary retribution (*pratyātmika-vipāka*), while lands are the dependent retribution (*parigraha-vipāka*). If these are not divided, then sentient beings and lands are distinct; if they are divided, then sentient beings and lands are identical.

As for the "land-body" (*kṣetra-kāya*) mentioned in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it refers to the body of the land, which is precisely the dependent aspect of the primary [retribution]. One should know this.

Regarding the four propositions for each of the five aggregates (*skandha*) across the three periods of time, the *Mahā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Exposition), fascicle 68, states:
"The four propositions such as 'form is the gone' (*gata*) apply likewise to the other four aggregates; together they comprise twenty propositions. These reckon the past period.

The four propositions regarding form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as the other four aggregates (*skandha*), are likewise applied; this reckoning pertains to the future.

Together with the sixty views of the three time periods, and including both existence and non-existence, there are sixty-two views. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), fascicle 3, explains this in great detail; here I shall provide a brief excerpt.
Regarding the four propositions concerning "form as having gone" (*rūpam gatam*): namely, form has gone, form has not gone, form both has and has not gone, and form neither has nor has not gone.

The departure from form is neither departing nor not departing; this applies analogously up to consciousness, which is neither departing nor not departing, including both positions and the negation of both.
Furthermore, the fourfold tetralemma—present form as permanent, present form as impermanent, both, and neither—should be applied analogously.
Moreover, the fourfold tetralemma regarding future form as finite, future form as infinite, both, and neither should also be applied analogously.
In the *Agamas* on the "Views Concerning Past Kalpas and Views Concerning Past Existence," the Buddha told the brahmin Sunetta (and so forth):
"There are sixty-two views. There are eighteen views concerning past kalpas and past existence, and forty-four views concerning future kalpas and future existence; together they comprise sixty-two.
Regarding the 'eighteen,' there are four sets of four propositions plus two fundamental [views]. As for the first set of four propositions, there are twenty views."

Regarding the two views on the formation and destruction of kalpas lasting forty kalpas, the three views on eighty kalpas of formation and destruction, and the four [views] based on swift intelligence—each of these asserts that the self and the world are eternal.
As for the second set of four propositions: first, the calculation that the self and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal;
second, the calculation that [the world] arises from play and laughter; third, the calculation that it arises from loss of mindfulness; fourth, [the calculation] based on swift intelligence.
Regarding the swift-witted one’s explanation of the third tetrad: (1) that the self and the world are finite; (2) that they are infinite;

(3) that they are finite in the upward and downward directions but infinite in the horizontal directions; and (4) [the fourth alternative]. Regarding the swift-witted one’s explanation of the fourth tetrad:
(1) that he neither sees nor knows whether there is retribution for good and evil, or no retribution; and (2) that he neither knows nor sees whether there is another world or no other world.
Third, I do not know and do not see what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. Fourth, being foolish and dull-witted, one answers questions according to others.
Regarding the two fundamental phrases: first, with a concentrated mind, one knows that sentient beings will exist in the future without causes or conditions;

Regarding each gate, the reason for their "double negation" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta) is explained as follows: since the gate that discards both existence and non-existence is harmonious and pervasive, those with sharp faculties and light hindrances should enter it;
since the gate of "both together" allows for the coexistence of existence and non-existence, those with sharp faculties and heavy hindrances should enter it;
and since the gate of emptiness is the threefold provisional nature being empty and void, and the gate of existence is the moment-to-moment arising and ceasing, these may be explained accordingly.

Regarding the three grades of the four teachings, those with lower-grade precepts who are diligent in their practice obtain a human body; those with middle-grade precepts who are diligent obtain a body in the heavens of the desire realm;
and those with upper-grade precepts who are diligent further cultivate meditative concentration (dhyāna) obtain a body in the form or formless realms. Thus are the three grades.
Furthermore, hearing the Tripitaka is considered the Small Vehicle; hearing the Shared and Distinct [teachings] is the Middle Vehicle; and hearing the Perfect [teaching] is the Supreme Vehicle.
Since this is the case regarding hearing the teachings, it should likewise be understood by analogy for the five periods of teaching, both exoteric and esoteric.

To receive this body by being conceived in the womb of one’s parents is the "provisional nature of causal formation" (*hetu-saṃvṛti*). From the moment of conception until the onset of white hair is the "provisional nature of continuity" (*saṃtāna-saṃvṛti*).

To exist as a body in dependence upon what is not a body is the "provisional nature of mutual dependence" (*apekṣā-saṃvṛti*). This refers to form (*rūpa*). For example, when the four subtle elements (*catvāri paramāṇūni*) form a pillar, this is the provisional nature of causal formation;
that its continuity is uninterrupted is the provisional nature of continuity; and furthermore, this pillar exists in dependence upon what is not a pillar.
Furthermore, when length and shortness, or large and small, differ from one another, this is "mutual dependence" (相待假).
The term "designation" (名) applies to both locations; that is, it applies to both the "feeling" (受) and the "dharma" (法) as two types of designation.

Since life and so forth are the dharmas being conceptualized, there is a provisional name upon these conceptualized dharmas; the *Fuxing* (輔行) states that this provisional name refers to "continuity designation" (相續假).

Regarding the brevity and length of kalpas: the second and third dhyānas are said to be "brief" because they are both destroyed by water and wind, sharing a single *saṃvarta-kalpa* (destruction kalpa).
In the three heavens of the second dhyāna, the lifespans are respectively two, four, and eight great kalpas (*mahākalpa*).
In the three heavens of the third dhyāna, the lifespans are likewise respectively sixteen, thirty-two, and sixty-four great kalpas; therefore, it is said that [the first two dhyānas] are brief.
The above concerns the brevity or length of kalpas and lifespans.

Regarding rebirth after these [kalpas], the *Abhidharmakośa* states that at the beginning of the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), sentient beings in the hells merely die and no longer undergo rebirth there.
It further states that if sentient beings possess fixed karma (*niyata-karma*) that must necessarily be experienced as retribution in hell, it cannot be exhausted [during the dissolution].
Karma leads these sentient beings to receive retribution in other realms, hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts;

one should speak in this same manner regarding the destruction by the kalpa-ending calamities. As for those dwelling in the great ocean as animals, they are destroyed first; if they are humans, they are destroyed later.

One who, without a teacher, attains entry into the first dhyāna through the natural order of things, upon emerging from that concentration for the first time, speaks these words:
"For virtuous people, the bliss born of seclusion is most excellent. When others hear these words, they each practice this concentration;
such persons, when they pass away, are all reborn in the Brahma realm. This is likewise said regarding all four continents, and furthermore, regarding Brahma himself.
