The power of the ultimate meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*) and that which precedes it have already been annotated in the first fascicle.
Regarding the various ways in which the Arhats manifest or remain hidden, according to the *Śākyapuṅgava-vaṃśa*,
sixteen Arhats dwell in the four continents and the heavens, protecting the Dharma until the human lifespan decreases to ten years and the calamity of weapons arises.

All the sages have temporarily vanished; when the lifespan of human beings reaches one hundred years, the sages will all emerge together to transform and guide others as before, and their teachings will once again flourish and manifest.

Furthermore, among the arhats, many will enter parinirvāṇa by the end of Śākyamuni’s Final Dharma period, while some arhats will wait until Maitreya appears before entering parinirvāṇa, such as Kāśyapa, who preserved the robe.
This is so; these points concern the principles of concealment and manifestation as fully detailed in the *Nanshan Linggan Chuan* (Account of the Miraculous Responses at Mount Nanshan).

As for the statement regarding "ordinary people," the ancients meant that one transforms a coarse body into a subtle essence; it is incorrect to interpret this as referring to the bodies of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the meaning of "other lands," ancient scholars maintained that the land of "residual existence" (sopadhiśeṣa) exists only within the same dwelling (sahabhū).
This was not understood; for ancient scholars held that the transformation of the coarse body into a subtle substance meant that the residual existence resided only within the same dwelling.
However, the *Lotus Sūtra* and its commentary (*Śāstra*) state that residual existence exists outside the realm (dharmadhātu). Thus, they caused the ancient [view] to be transformed.
The coarse and the remaining explanations are not fully comprehensible;
yet, regarding birth in the five destinies, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "He closes the gates to all evil realms and manifests his body within the five destinies."
Yet he re-enters birth-and-death; as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Because of the sicknesses of sentient beings, I am sick.
If the sicknesses of sentient beings are extinguished, then my sickness is extinguished. Why is this? It is because the bodhisattva enters birth-and-death for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding the passage on "not [attaining] nirvāṇa" in the hundred [verses], the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"For example, suppose one wishes to cross a vast wilderness and perilous path of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, or four hundred *yojanas*. This is the illustration;

the "perilous path" refers to the world, "four hundred" to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), "three hundred" to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), "two hundred" to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and "one hundred" to those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
The *Zhiguan* commentary explains: "Two hundred for the Two Vehicles" further clarifies that Bodhisattvas who emerge from the provisional (出假) do so by exiting from emptiness;
thus, [the state of] nirvana is counted as two hundred, while entering the triple world is counted as three hundred.
Even when encountering a Buddha or an Arhat, Śāriputra still suspected them might be Māras;
upon first hearing a brief exposition of the Buddhas' Dharma, he immediately conceived doubts, thinking it was a teaching of Māra. Thus, his later realization of understanding stated:
"Could it not be that a Māra has manifested as a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind?"

One must write it in white characters within the commentary; since the nine characters [of the main text] should not be treated as small-character annotations, it is said that "one must write them in white characters.
As for the annotator, the text becomes florid and is no longer white. Nowadays, scholars recite the text but do not recite the commentary, claiming they are "reciting the white."
There are three aspects to the code of discipline (*vinaya-saṃvara*): not being deficient, not being broken, and not being pierced. Not being deficient refers to the two hundred and fifty precepts;
not being broken refers to the four *pārājika* offenses; not being pierced refers to the *pāyattika* offenses; and not being defiled refers to the *duṣkṛta* offenses.

Each has its own intended meaning, as fully explained in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*). "Not deficient" (*bùquē*) in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and "not deficient" (*bùquē*) in the *Śāstra* share the same name but differ in meaning.
In the *Śāstra*, "deficient" (*quē*) refers to that which is broken and ruined, rendering it unfit for use; in contrast to the root *sūtra*, it refers to having even slight damage.
This is the explanation found in the *Shiqian*. If the Master of the Nanshan Vinaya takes "unbroken" (*bùpò*) to refer to the four *pārājika* offenses, [the meaning is as follows].
Even if the six precepts are deficient, broken, pierced, or mixed with the meditative path, they are still termed "leakage" (āsrava);

however, because one attains the untainted (anāsrava) meditative concentration and the untainted path upon reaching the four fruits, this is called "concordance with concentration" (samādhi-samprayukta).
Since it is determined to be shared with the path, it is categorized as being within the stage of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who has attained the state of concentration.

Furthermore, regarding the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage, the previous record states that the four fruits of the Hīnayāna are already expedient means, and that Heat, Peak (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*) constitute the true culmination.
Based on this prior statement, it appears that those five thousand who rose and departed possessed the Heat stage.

However, according to what is said here—that those of the "smaller of the small" are merely those with out-flowing (*sāsrava*) states in the four dhyānas, and even these four dhyānas are smaller—this [prior account] is understood accordingly.

Regarding one interpretation, it seems there were no *uṣmagata* (warmth) dharmas prior [to this]. In the previous commentary, it was said, "the skillful means of skillful means," whereas the current commentary says, "the smallest among the small.
These two explanations in the record differ: one says they clung to *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* (summit), while the other says they clung to the four *dhyānas*.

It is difficult to reconcile these meanings; therefore, I shall now explain them through two perspectives. First, among the five thousand people, there were those who had attained *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.
The two explanations exist because of differences regarding the four dhyānas. Alternatively, some may mistakenly take the four dhyānas to be the stages of "warmth" (uṣmagata) and "summit" (mūrdhan).

If one relies on worldly dhyāna to cultivate the sixfold contemplation (ṣaḍvidhābhāvanā), there are those who attain the outflow-free state (anāsrava), such as many of the arhats who frequently fall back.

It is not necessary to rely on the discrimination of "present mindfulness" (pratyutpanna-smṛti) to establish that "desire" (chanda) and "nature" (svabhāva) are identical; it is simply by contrasting the two factors of desire and nature that they are distinguished.
Although the name "desire" does not derive from the past, it can nevertheless be understood in relation to the present and the future.

Since the names "past desire" and "future desire" are also applicable to the present, it is said that "past desire" constitutes the "present nature," and that "present nature" gives rise to "future desire" and so forth.

Nevertheless, following the explanation based on the present: if one speaks of each of the three time periods in terms of faculties, dispositions, and desires, then all desires and thoughts are rendered as being present—namely, past and present desires, up to future and present desires.

The *Shuchao* (Commentary on the Seven Expedients) transmits the tradition that good and evil are recorded as follows: regarding the general nature of good and evil, it is as stated in the *Suizuyi* (According to One’s Own Intent).
That *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) says: "Good and evil have no fixed nature. For instance, when various obscurations constitute evil deeds, one attains the retribution of humans or devas;

once this retribution is exhausted, one falls back into the three miserable realms, at which point one is again considered evil. When the two vehicles emerge from suffering, it is termed 'good,' yet [this too is relative]."
One who can save themselves alone is not a true person of goodness; one should know that for such a person, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are likewise evil.

Even the Bodhisattva of the Six Perfections is called "good" only in comparison; yet though they can provide universal salvation, it is like food stored in a vessel of poison—once eaten, it kills the person, and thus it is still evil.

Even the teachings of the Separate Vehicle (Pṛthag-vāda) are considered "good," yet because they still carry expedient means and cannot accord with ultimate principle, their followers are called people of false views.
The commentary on the ninefold division of the scriptures: *Sūtra* is translated here as "Dharma-source" (*dharmapada*); *Gāthā* is translated as "non-repeated verse";
*Itivṛttaka* refers to the accounts of disciples' past lives; *Jātaka* refers to the accounts of the Buddha's past lives; *Adbhutadharma* refers to the teaching of rare and marvelous events;

*Nidāna* means that when one wishes to clarify the precepts and Dharma, it is necessarily because of a transgression; *Avadāna* uses near examples to illustrate distant meanings; *Veyyākaraṇa* is translated here as "repetition."
The *geya* (verse) and *upadeśa* (treatise)—the latter translated here as "discourse"—these constitute the ninefold division (*navāṅga*).

As for the twelvefold division (*dvādaśāṅga*), one adds the *vaipulya* (extensive), the *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy), and the *anudharmapada* (unasked spontaneous teaching); these are then termed the Mahāyāna.
There are those who encounter the conditions for Buddhahood— such as Mahākāśyapa, who was originally a pratyekabuddha but fell to the level of a śrāvaka upon meeting the Buddha—
and yet refuse to believe, still claiming that a śrāvaka can never become a Buddha.
Therefore, those who attain mutual penetration and receive the transmission of the True [Dharma] have long heard of the Middle Principle;
this true entry into the Middle is because the principle of the Middle does not perish within the True.

This entry of the Middle into the True refers to the many classes of beings—such as devas, ghosts, animals, and asuras—as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "If, in the realm of ghosts, one protects..."
If one enters the void by means of the power of the Dharma and supernatural penetrations, this is categorized within the realm of ghosts born from eggs.

If one descends from the heavens due to the loss of merit and falls into decline, yet the dwelling place they occupy remains adjacent to the sun and moon, this is categorized within the human realm born from wombs.
If one maintains the world, possesses penetrating power and fearlessness, and contends for authority with Brahmā and Śakra, this is categorized within the celestial realm born through transformation.
There is one born from moisture who dwells in the great ocean, wandering through the void at dawn and returning to sleep in the water at dusk; this belongs to the realm of animals born from moisture.
According to the Commentary: "How might one encounter the Buddha? means "In what manner? or "By what means?"
*Kalala* (translated as "impure mixture") has the appearance of congealed cream.
*Arbuda* (translated as "blister") has the appearance of a pustule.
*Peśī* (translated as "flesh-mass" or "knot of doubt") is like coagulated blood.
*Kaṭhina* (羯男) is here translated as "hard and thick," meaning that which gradually becomes firm and rigid.
*Pralamba* (鉢羅奢) is here translated as "position of form," referring to the differentiation of the four limbs.
[The commentary notes: "Xie-li" (邪戾)—"xie" should be written as "xie" (斜); it means crookedness. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, when a dog enters a doorway, its body curves. Now...
The Commentary states: "Those who are 'crooked and perverse' refers to those such as the lame and the hunchbacked.
To pay high homage to the superior while paying low homage to the inferior—namely, to pay high homage to a Buddha-stūpa while paying low homage to one's own teacher’s stūpa—is improper.
When one dies and enters the dark realm of the dead, according to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, one departs alone into the darkness; who then can inquire into right and wrong?"

One immediately dons [this practice] and contemplates it as if offering a single incense stick or a single flower, guiding it with the three contemplations so that it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, performing great Buddha-work and universally tending toward the fruit of Buddhahood;
thus Liang Su said: "To speak of even a hair’s breadth of goodness allows one to glimpse the gate of the Double Mystery."
The commentary states, "dài (殆) does not encompass," where *dài* is pronounced *dài*.
It means "almost" (*jǐ*), as in the phrase "human life is almost lost.

[The text] says that even the sixth stage (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*) is not yet encompassed; if one follows the ancients who name the stages after the dwellings (*vihāra*), it should say that even the seventh stage is not yet encompassed.
The "Earth" [refers to] the eighth stage because it is the stage of the "Childlike Innocence" (*dāraka-satya*).
"Principle and number" (*li-shu*) refers to the meaning of spontaneity (*svabhāva*); the *Hanshu* states, "Principle and number are thus.
Guanzhong is the region of Qin; it was there that Daosheng, Sengzhao, Daorong, and Daohui were born and flourished by virtue of this land.

"Good deeds do not receive retribution" refers to the fact that in the Guanzhong region, there is much talk of the essence of all dharmas being empty, such that one does not receive the karmic fruits of the human or heavenly realms.
If [the teaching] had not yet been opened, it should have been immediately manifested.

The commentary states: "It is like the first basketful of earth for a mountain. (The character *jù* is pronounced with the *qiú* and *wèi* finals; the *Lunyu* says: "For example, in making a mountain, if one has not yet completed one basketful...")
"The basket is stopped, and I am stopped. The commentary states: "A 'basket' (kui) is a wickerwork container for earth.
It refers to the passage in the *Laozi*, the *Dejing* chapter, which says: 'A tree that grows to embrace the arms was produced from a tiny sprout.'"

The Sūtra sets forth these four propositions: there are those who possess the Buddha-nature while icchantikas lack it; there are those who possess the Buddha-nature while those with roots of goodness lack it;

there are those who possess the Buddha-nature while both groups possess it; and there are those who possess the Buddha-nature while both groups lack it. Regarding those who possess it while the other group lacks it:
they possess the nature of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), whereas icchantikas lack the cultivation of goodness, while those with roots of goodness do possess it.

Furthermore, there are those who cultivate evil while being icchantikas, whereas those with roots of goodness do not; and there are those who lack both, because they lack the nature of non-retrogression as they have not yet entered the stage resembling [the path of seeing].
Regarding the three explanations by Xinghuang, although the other two are not essential, I still wish to know them now.
The *Shujie chushi shi suo jie shu* (Commentary on the Various Masters’ Explanations) states: "The icchantika possesses the nature of evil and perverted objects;
the person with inherent good roots possesses the 'enabling cause' (*liāoyin*) of the ten thousand virtues, which is also called the 'conditioning cause' (*yuānyīn*).

Both types of persons possess the 'correct nature' (*zhèngxìng*) or the 'sentient-being nature' (*zhòngshēngxìng*). Those who lack both have no fruit and no causal nature. Hexi said: "The icchantika possesses [the nature]."
The five aggregates of evil are of an unwholesome nature; those who possess wholesome roots have the nature of wholesome five aggregates;
those who possess both have both; those who possess neither have neither; and the nature of the fruit of *nirvāṇa* is wondrously transcendent.

This differs in phrasing from the old interpretation but is identical in meaning. Regarding the three types of explanations provided by Xingxing: first, in terms of various meanings; second, in terms of principle, internal and external.
Third, regarding the internal analysis of the principle according to its various meanings: the principle itself is neither good nor evil, yet it possesses two functions—good and evil.
Those with roots of goodness possess the function of good; those who are icchantikas possess the function of evil.

"Both" refers to having one side of each; "neither" refers to lacking one side of each. Next, regarding the internal and external aspects of the principle: Buddha-nature is fundamentally not something acquired, nor is it something non-existent.
Based on the principle of contingent conditions (*pratyaya*), there is the logic of both attainment and non-attainment. Outside the principle, the icchantika possesses the nature of attainment;
within the principle, the person possessing roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) possesses the nature of non-attainment. Both possess [the nature] and both lack [it], as explained above.
Next, considering only those within the principle: the icchantika is none other than Śunakṣatra, while the person possessing roots of goodness is...

Rāhula, these are the two types of transformative teachings—those of opposition and those of conformity. Those who are icchantikas possess the nature of unwholesome qualities through the transformative teaching of opposition;

those who possess roots of goodness possess the nature of wholesome dharmas through the transformative teaching of conformity. That both exist and both are absent is as explained above (the preceding points are all the interpretations of the ancients;

that Master Xinghuang’s *Threefold Record of Exegesis* does not adopt them refers to the two interpretations: the internal and external relative to principle, and the interpretation based solely on principle. Thus it says "not necessarily what is adopted," for while he speaks in terms of various meanings, the language here in this text is spoken in terms of principle, and thus differs from him).
Zhang’an’s own commentary states: "Now, to clarify how one might establish four propositions based on this text: those who are icchantikas possess only 'submergence';
those who have severed their good roots possess only 'emergence. Both types possess both states and are situated within the Ganges;

both types lack both states and do not reach the shore. Furthermore, if categorized according to the three truths: those who are icchantikas and possess [only submergence] belong to the world of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and are evil."
Regarding those who possess the causes of wholesome roots, both [the person and the cause] exist; regarding those who lack them, both are absent.

The body that is the retributive fruit of worldly truth exists for both when they exist, and is absent for both when they are absent. The Middle Way of cause and effect is explained in the commentary on the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*, specifically in the seventeenth fascicle.
The *Saptasattva-sūtra* states: "In the Ganges River there are seven kinds of sentient beings;
whether for the sake of bathing or gathering flowers, they enter the river. The first person, upon entering the water, sinks;
the second person, having emerged, sinks again; and so on, until the seventh person, who, because of his sharp faculties, remains firmly established in faith and wisdom."
"Attaining the further shore without regression" (and so forth), up to the seventh record below, where it shall be further cited and annotated so that the dharma and the simile are complete.
Regarding the "ruby" (*lohitamuktikā*), the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is named after its cause, as the substance of the jewel itself is red. The *Hanshu* says:

The subtle essence within the pearl oyster fills and empties according to the moon. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that pearls emerge from the bellies of fish, from within bamboo, or from the brains of snakes.
*Vaiḍūrya*, in Sanskrit, is translated as "blue-colored gem."
*Pholi* (頗棃) is translated here as "water-jade" (*shuiyu*) or "crystal" (*shuijing*).
It belongs to the same category as *cānchu* (車渠) and various types of shells. The *Shangshu Dazhuan* states: "The great shell (*dabei*) is like the *qu* (渠) of a large chariot;
*qu* refers to the rim (*wang*) of a chariot. Following this description, it resembles the wheel-rim of a chariot; hence it is called *qu*.
Agate (*musāragalva*) is named for its color, which resembles the agate of a horse; it is produced in reddish-white hues, and when fashioned into vessels, it displays patterns like twisted silk.
According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, there are three kinds of jewels: those belonging to humans, devas, and bodhisattvas.
Human jewels possess little power; they merely have pure radiance and color, capable of warding off the suffering of venomous spirits, darkness, hunger, thirst, cold, and heat.

The celestial ear-jewel constantly follows the celestial body, enabling it to converse with others; it is light rather than heavy, and like the *Rājapraśnīya-sūtra* or the wish-fulfilling jewel (*maṇi*), it can speak.

The Bodhisattva, encompassing the affairs of both humans and devas, enables all sentient beings to know the causes and conditions of birth and death, just as a great bright mirror reflects all things.
The commentary explains that "unintentional offenses" (*asamcetanika-āpatti*) are referred to in the Vinaya as "inauspicious matters," meaning things that ought not to be done.
If one performs such acts, one incurs the retribution of an inauspicious offense; consequently, in the ultimate result, one frequently encounters unexpected misfortunes.
Impure money is so called because it is acquired through impure means; there are eight such types of impurity, namely:
hoarding salt and grain, raising birds and beasts, and engaging in trade for profit. Regarding the making of images, as the Buddha’s regulations state:

a monk who maintains the precepts must not perform prostrations [for such gains]. If he prepares food and drink, he incurs an offense with every swallow; if he constructs a dwelling, he incurs an offense upon entry.
If one enters into a downfall (*āpatti*), such as when making or wearing robes, one incurs a downfall for each instance of wearing them.

One must not mix [prohibited substances] with milk or glue; milk is a fundamental impurity derived from semen and blood, and according to the Vinaya regulations, a healthy bhikṣu should not consume "fine foods," namely milk, curd, fish, and meat.
The *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states that one who is not ill should not seek out such delicacies.

Regarding the offense of consuming [forbidden] food: if the World-Honored One had accepted Nanda’s milk, it would have been merely one instance among the seven sages’ shared transformation of a single stingy Brahmin, as recorded in the *Ruxiang jing* (Sūtra on the Light of Milk).
Furthermore, the aroma of cow’s milk in the Western Land is as utterly distinct from that of this land as heaven and earth;
for example, the cow dung of that land may be used to smear the ground or fumigate the alms-bowl.
"Zhēn-jí" (疹疾): The first character is pronounced with the radical "shèn" (忍). A disease characterized by raised swellings on the skin is called *yìnzhěn* (癮疹). "Mài" (麥):
The second character is pronounced with the radical "gǔ-měng" (古猛). It refers to large wheat (*yìmài* [穬麥]); it should be written as "yìmài."
The "exposed basin" (*lùpán*) refers to a basin for dew; Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty created it, as previously annotated.
It is called the "Chang'an person's call" because the Han capital was Chang'an. Chang'an is the present-day Yongzhou (雍州), specifically the Shuixing Commandery (水興軍).
In the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, King Prasenajit went to the Jetavana Monastery and heard the beautiful sound of a bhikṣu chanting.
Upon seeing a bhikṣu whose physical appearance was dark, ugly, and short, the king asked why his form and voice did not correspond.
The bhikṣu replied: "In a past life, I saw people building a stūpa and, because I resented its height and breadth, I caused it to be made short and ugly."
Later, seeing that the stupa had been completed, he gave up his house-bells to hang as offerings for the stupa; from this, his reputation spread.

That a small cause yields a great fruit is like the case of offering a single flower and attaining non-retrogression—those are actual causes, while this present instance is an opening of the coarse [to reveal the subtle].
The objects may be coarse while the mind is subtle, as in the case of managing one's livelihood and business, all of which do not contradict the true nature (dharmatā).
Both may be coarse, as in the examples of sifting sand to reveal Buddha-images or drawing Buddhas in the sand, which ultimately lead to the fulfillment of the Buddha-way.

Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, although their textual expressions may differ, some say that despite these differences, both treatises merely discuss the principles and meanings of reality in order to refute the two types of grasping and reveal the two kinds of emptiness.

Others say that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is a commentary on the sūtras and frequently discusses the principle of non-arising; as it says, for example: "It is not dependent on a single cause, nor does it arise without a cause. Therefore...

Regarding the teaching of non-arising, this name is established according to principle; it is the school of the Madhyamaka-śāstra that relies on the sūtras and treatises. These works frequently discuss the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), as it is said:

"It is also called a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), and it is also called the meaning of the Middle Way. This name is established according to its meaning. Some say that the ancients clung to the *ālayavijñāna* as the producer of phenomena;
however, within the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, there is a refutation of existence based on principle and a refutation of existence based on meaning, which arises from the [Bhūmi] sections.

Subsuming these two, the objects of calculation do not transcend the nature of self or other; the present school takes the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Jñāna-prasthāna-śāstra*, and refutes them through the fourfold logic (*catuṣkoṭi*) according to their true meaning.

Recently, there was another person who examined the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Jñāna-prasthāna-śāstra* and stated that, according to the principle, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 74, says:
"Phenomena born of causes and conditions have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because they lack intrinsic nature, [they are empty]."

"This is ultimate emptiness" refers to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. Furthermore, Nāgārjuna composed the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* as a commentary on the essential meaning of the Mahāyāna sūtras, opening his treatise with the eightfold negation beginning with "non-arising," stating that "all phenomena do not arise from themselves"; this refers to the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.

Herein, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* expounds the wisdom of ultimate emptiness, while the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* elucidates the threefold wisdom within the one mind; these are all names based upon [the same principle].

Regarding the principle that "the words conform to the meaning," the fourfold contemplation of phenomena extensively refutes all delusions. Now, having already examined the various interpretations of those respective [texts]—like the chrysanthemums and mums [of different schools]—I shall further clarify and elucidate them.
Whether it be the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* or the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, there is none that does not take the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its primary subject matter.

This "subject matter" refers to the ultimate reality (*tattva*). This ultimate reality is fundamentally based on the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*) and is not something arrived at through external inference.

To examine [the self] and find it ultimately empty is to conform to the principle (*yili*). Although the principle is fundamentally empty, sentient beings falsely conceptualize, speaking of "self" and "other";

therefore, the Great Sage employs skillful means to lead them to investigate in accordance with the nature (*xing*) so as to reveal the two kinds of emptiness. This is to conform to the meaning (*yiyi*).
Meaning is simply a discourse on the reasons why the true principle is as it is.

From "Originally, both are empty" up to "this is the contemplation of the inconceivable realm of the nature-attained and practice-attained virtues" constitutes a general outline [of the contemplation].

Although nature is originally empty, because sentient beings dwell in delusion and give rise to attachments within that delusion, it is necessary to discuss it by following its nature through analytical investigation;
thus, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) points to the nature-attained virtues, stating: "Although the preceding section has concluded the establishment of the realm of nature-attained virtues..."
If one does not investigate and examine, how is this different from the "Bird in the Void" Sutra? That sutra says:

"For example, though a lute or a zither possesses exquisite sounds, if there are no skilled fingers, those sounds will certainly not be produced. The Great Master said: "The true mind is applied to the true object," and Jingxi said:

"By practicing the illumination of the nature. These statements all refer to those who practice contemplation; however, for those with sharp faculties during the Buddha’s lifetime, they would hear [the teaching] and immediately practice it.

It is still necessary to further examine and await the subsequent analysis; for the two kinds of emptiness shown in the current commentary (*shu*) and record (*ji*) are precisely the "provisional establishment through causes" (*yin-cheng-ja*).

Therefore, it merely says "awaiting the subsequent. If it is the provisional establishment through causes, one should take the conjunction of the sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) as the basis and contemplate whether this single thought-moment arises from the mind itself, arises from the mind in opposition to the sense organs, or arises from the conjunction of the sense organs and objects.
[The passage] beginning with "The mind arises apart from the sense faculties and objects" (and so forth) concerns the conventional nature of continuity (*prabandha-prajñapti*).

Although one cannot find a [substantial] mind when analyzing it through the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the internal faculties and their preceding causes, we nevertheless currently perceive that there is a continuous succession of arising and ceasing moment by moment.

If the preceding moment has not ceased when the succeeding moment arises, then both would arise simultaneously; if the preceding moment has already ceased when the succeeding moment arises, then the latter would arise without a cause; and if it were both ceased and unceased when the succeeding moment arises, these two contradictions would coexist. Therefore, [the mind is merely a conventional designation].

When one contemplates that the arising of a thought is neither cessation nor non-cessation, and that the subsequent thought arises (and so forth), this is a provisional establishment based on mutual dependence regarding the non-existence of cessation.

As for the provisional continuity of the preceding [thought], if one does not enter [this realization], one still calculates that there is a mind dependent upon a non-mind. Now, when examining this mind:
does the mind arise depending on the non-arising of a mind, or does the mind arise depending on the arising of a mind, or does it arise depending on both arising and non-arising?

"The arising of the mind arises in dependence; it is neither arising from existence nor arising from non-existence" (and so forth, as explained at length in the *Pó fǎbiàn* [Exhaustive Refutation of Dharmas]).
Why, then, does the present text not establish this contemplation? This contemplation refers to the "succession of the conventional" (*prajñapti-anuvṛtti*), intended for those of sharp faculties.

It is simply that, upon the conventional designation established by causes, one realizes that the nature and virtues are fundamentally empty of both self and phenomena; this does not mean that one does not cultivate contemplation.

As noted previously, it is said here that hearing the Dharma seems to pertain to the stage of faith-practice (*śraddhā-carita*), yet it is not without the inclusion of the Dharma-practice (*dharma-carita*);
within this single session, there should be no sixty-four rounds [of conceptual proliferation].

It is not said that there is both emptiness and non-emptiness; however, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states that because the *tathāgatagarbha* exists, one can become weary of the suffering of saṃsāra and joyfully seek the bliss of nirvāṇa, and so forth;
thus, there arise the concepts of the empty *tathāgatagarbha* and the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

Furthermore, because it pertains to practice (*pratipatti*) and principle (*tattva*), it refers to the "Treasury of Practice" (*caryā-garbha*) and the "Treasury of Principle" (*tattva-garbha*). As stated in the sub-commentary below:

"All dharmas tend toward *dāna* (generosity), and there is no going beyond this"—this clarifies the Tathāgatagarbha in terms of practice. "All dharmas tend toward the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), and there is no going beyond this"—this clarifies the Tathāgatagarbha in terms of principle.
Is it because of the power of the practitioner’s roots of goodness that the aspects of words and meanings arise upon the Tathāgata’s consciousness?
Master Ci’en’s Commentary poses the question: "When the Buddha preaches the Dharma, is it called 'Thus have I heard,' or when he does not preach the Dharma, is it called 'Thus have I heard'?

There are two interpretations. First, masters such as Nāgamitra state that the Buddha possesses only three qualities—great meditative concentration, wisdom, and compassion—and has long since transcended conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

The treatise has never claimed that the Dharma is spoken by the Buddha through the power of his compassion, original vows, and conditions; rather, the aspects of words and meanings arise upon the consciousness of sentient beings.
Although these aspects of words and meanings directly depend on the power of one’s own roots of goodness, they are termed "the Buddha’s teaching" because of their strong conditioning.
Furthermore, because they arise through the power of the ear-faculty and one’s own mental transformation, it is said, "I have heard. Thus, the Bodhisattva Asvabhāva says:
Those who hear it perceive that which is directly expressed as non-directly expressed; these gathered appearances constitute the essence of the teaching. To this, he raises an objection:
"If that is so, how can Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak? [The answer is: It is said to be so by the power of their sovereign influence (*adhipati-bala*).

For example, through the sovereign influence of deities and others, one can obtain incantations (*mantra*), treatises (*śāstra*), and so forth within a dream. Therefore, the Buddha also stated that, beginning from his attainment of enlightenment...
From the night of the Path’s attainment until the night of Nirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken therein, nor did you hear anything.

This is as when a mother bites her finger and the child, upon being born, cries out; it is as the words of the Two Parents, Kāśyapa and others, who said that because one is free from conceptualization, it is called "non-proliferation" (*niṣprapañca*).

Does this not mean that teaching the Dharma is also called non-proliferation? It is because, by the power of the original vows of those worthy to hear, [the teaching appears] upon the consciousness of the Tathāgata.
The mutual arising of words and meanings—these words and meanings arise from the Buddha’s roots of goodness for the benefit of others;

therefore, it is called "I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*). (End of the main text. In the sūtras, the teaching is taken as the single seed of the Buddha. Regarding this, Ci’en cites the commentaries of Nāgamitra and Prajñākaramati on "I heard":
they state that this refers to the mutual arising of words and meanings within the consciousness of sentient beings. If this were the case, there would be no need to wait [for the Buddha].

Because the Buddha preached the Dharma and there was something personally heard by him, the preceding text previously refuted this, saying: "If one were not to allow for seeing [the Buddha] at all, then from the very beginning of the sutra, 'heard' (*śruta*) should have been changed to 'asked' (*pṛṣṭa*).
When asked, "What is the consciousness of sentient beings? [Dharmakīrti] replied, "The consciousness of the Tathāgata. When asked, "What is the consciousness of the Tathāgata?

[Śākyabuddhi] replied, "The consciousness of sentient beings. Regarding these two forms of consciousness, what further basis is there to suppress or level them? Furthermore, what other consciousness does the Tathāgata possess? [The answer is: It is the consciousness of sentient beings.

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "By the power of the dominant condition of the Tathāgata’s compassion and original vows, the aspects of word and meaning arise upon the consciousness of sentient beings.

If this refers to the Tathāgata’s own consciousness, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* further states: "By the power of the dominant condition of the listener’s roots of goodness and original vows, the aspects of word and meaning arise upon the Tathāgata’s consciousness.
Thus, one knows that these two consciousnesses mutually respond and perfect one another; therefore, it is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
It is said that through the power of mutual reinforcement, the two consciousnesses become determinate; thus, since the Tathāgata’s various consciousnesses have already been exhausted,
what is now called "consciousness" is merely another name for wisdom— it is simply the wondrous discerning wisdom within the Tathāgata’s mind.
Regarding the refutation within "I have heard" (*śruta*) in the commentary on the section "I have heard": it states that all instances should be corrected to "heard.

Within the objective realm (*viṣaya*), both the cultivated nature (*bhāvanā-dharmatā*) and the innate nature (*prakṛti-dharmatā*) are fully present; the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and paths (*mārga*) constitute the substance, which is precisely the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) serving as the innate nature.
In this particular passage, however, it specifically designates the direct cause as the innate nature.
Right practice consists of generating the bodhicitta, calming the mind, and cultivating the factors of the path as the primary means;

these are called the "auxiliaries to the path" because they assist in opening up the realization of the Way. This distinction between the primary and the auxiliary defines the conditions and the understanding. As the preceding text also states: "One must cultivate the myriad practices, combining the primary and the auxiliary in one's conduct," which is identical to this point.

Regarding the "Teaching on Cultivating Right Assistance": the first six chapters rely on the teaching to open up understanding, while the latter four chapters rely on the teaching to establish practice.

Thus, one should know that both cultivation and nature possess both self and other. As for the interpretation of the text, it may differ; for instance, Dharma Master Xi Shang cites the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Mohe Zhiguan) [to support this].

It is said that the principle-nature (*li-xing*) is fundamentally without nature; this is spoken of by way of the gate of cultivation (*xiu-men*). One must clearly understand the departure from conceptual reckonings (*ji*).

If, within the "Marvelous Joy" [of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*], it is said that both nature and cultivation exist together, and one first infers that ignorance within one's own nature is "other," this is merely an investigation and examination of the mind according to the practice of cessation and contemplation (*shi-guan*).
By means of this arising of the mind, one confronts the characteristics of wisdom-practice (*zhi-xing*) and cultivates accordingly, thereby [eliminating] all delusions.

All matters concerning the inverse cultivation of practice (*gyō*) are termed "other" (*ta*). This master’s intention is that when establishing the fundamental absence of nature (*honmu-shō*) and investigating it according to its nature (*junshō*), there is fundamentally no distinction between self and other;
thus, in both the inverse and the direct modes of cultivation, when one investigates through practice, there is likewise no self or other. These texts are found within the *Hatsushin Shō*.
Furthermore, others have said that both cultivation and nature possess both self and other, as in the statement: "In a single thought-moment, there are the three thousand realms."
If self and other do not exist [independently], how could they not exist within the nature? If one clings to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), this is called attachment to characteristics;

one must further employ the four propositions to break through that attachment to characteristics—this is what is meant by "self and other within cultivation. This is because cultivation and nature are distinguished by means of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).

It is said that there was another Dharma Master who claimed that among the ten vehicles, the first vehicle is nature, while from the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) onwards consists of the remaining nine.

Regarding the vehicles as being cultivation, since the nature of the first vehicle is thus established, one should infer that the nine other vehicles belong to cultivation; the process of investigation is likewise.

Here, the ten vehicles are distinguished as belonging to either cultivation or nature. Although each of the three [ancient] masters' explanations possesses its own significance, they have not yet clearly demonstrated the reasons for the two types of "otherness.
I shall now attempt to set them forth: that which is called "other" refers to ignorance, because the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is primordially present and non-existent [as a separate entity].

This clarifies that what arises subsequently is first true and then false, like a host followed by a guest; therefore, ignorance (*avidyā*) is identified as the "other-nature" (*parabhāva*) among the refutations.
If one claims that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) gives rise to phenomena, this is reckoned as "self" (*sva*); if one claims that ignorance gives rise to phenomena, this is reckoned as "other.
Since the meanings of "both" and "causeless" can likewise be understood, it is said: "First, one examines the nature of phenomena as self," and so forth.

Extending this further, it does not constitute [a complete system]; rather, one further cultivates the ten thousand practices upon the nine vehicles. Regarding what is called "extending the practice for others":

the practices of the nine vehicles arise from the totality of the nature (*xing*). First comes original enlightenment (*benjue*), and subsequently initial enlightenment (*shijue*), just as water precedes waves;

therefore, it is said that one only then extends the practice for others. Within these practices, that which is "broken" refers to: if one initiates practice based on external objects, this is reckoned as self-centered; if not based on objects...
When one engages in practice based on an object, this involves calculating it as "other," whether collectively or without cause; by extension, such views are also refuted.
For one who makes this statement, does it not clarify not only the meaning of simultaneous cultivation and nature, but also the two meanings of "other"?
Together, they infer that the self-nature of dharmas is primordially present.
Regarding the four dharmas, both the Buddha and sentient beings each possess their own characteristics and stages.
As for the specific correspondence: when it comes to the color of the causal seed, because the nature of color is itself the nature of wisdom, this is the revealing cause.

The six dharmas discussed here in relation to the three causes differ slightly from those in the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary). That work’s eleventh fascicle states: "The direct cause is neither identical to nor separate from form (*rūpa*);

the revealing cause is neither identical to nor separate from consciousness (*vijñāna*); the conditional cause is neither identical to nor separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, and the self (*ātman*).
One should know that these six dharmas are nothing other than the three causes. (The above is the main text. Regarding form being the direct cause, this refers to the path of suffering.
Since this is the Dharma-body, comparing that with this— whether due to a textual error or a deliberate correspondence—
the cultivation of the six natures constitutes the direct cause, while the cultivation of the six harmonies constitutes the conditional cause.

Regarding those [teachings], for each of the three virtues and four virtues in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, there is a specific intent. In the second section on Samatha and Vipaśyanā, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is cited as follows:
"By the cessation of this form, one attains the eternal form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

The Dharma-body is eternally blissful, self, and pure. These two virtues are also thus. If one relies on the single mode of transformation—whereby form is transformed into the Dharma-body—the Dharma-body is eternal.

"Delighting in the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna*) into wisdom (*prajñā*), and wisdom being the purification of the transformation of feeling (*vedanā*) into liberation (*vimukti*); liberation is then the self (*ātman*).

Furthermore, based on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the transformation of consciousness becomes permanence, the transformation of feeling becomes bliss (*sukha*), the transformation of perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) becomes self, and the transformation of form (*rūpa*) becomes purity.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), at the end of the eleventh fascicle, further explains this as follows:
The principle is that the separate textual sections on the person and the principle collectively clarify that the three periods of time are subsumed within their essential meaning;
however, because the phrasing of the text simply states "the person and the principle are one," these constitute separate textual sections, which is the same as in the prose portion.
To take the "opening of the provisional" as the first [section] and the "bestowal of the second [jewel]"— which corresponds to the second of the four or three previous sections—
as the second, while placing the first "analogy of the five turbidities" as the second, such that the One Vehicle cannot be preached, is a profound inversion.
Nevertheless, it is first divided into four parts. According to our own school’s view, the analogy of the house on fire is divided into two:
first, the various calamities within the house; second, the Buddha’s arousal of the thought of the One Vehicle. According to the other school’s view, it is divided into two:
third, sentient beings’ refusal to accept [the teaching]; fourth, the preaching of the joy of the Three Vehicles.

Regarding the passage "One should sigh that the Dharma appears rarely," the underlying meaning is not explicitly stated; however, the sub-commentary (*śū*) states that the chapter on "Sighing over the Dharma" is not one of the six similes and is therefore omitted.
Furthermore, within the sub-commentary’s discussion on how each preceding stage should be applied before the various bodhisattvas:
Regarding the fourth of the four distinct metaphors added by Guangzhai, it is simply our own school’s metaphor of the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*).
Guangzhai divides this into two parts, adding one more for "escaping from calamity," thereby resulting in nineteen phrases.

According to the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) below, if the great capacity [of the faculty] moves first and obstacles are subsequently removed, it is as in the *Upāya-paṛiccheda* (Chapter on Expedient Means); if obstacles are first removed and the capacity subsequently moves, it is as in... [the following].
In the "Parable Chapter," the movement of the spiritual capacity and the removal of obstacles manifest alternately as the ear and the eye. Guangzhai did not understand this meaning;

in his commentary, he criticized [the text] by saying, "Guangzhai directly uses the great capacity to correspond to the avoidance of calamity. He thus refuted it, claiming that because the wording of the sutra differs before and after, it does not mean that there is a sequence in the removal of obstacles.
The fifth [section] is divided into five and six; in the current school’s later detailed exposition, it states:

"Śāriputra, you should know that I see the sons of the Buddha," etc. These two lines clarify the movement of the great capacity, serving as the basis for the subsequent parable of seeking the carriage.
Yet Guangzhai divides these two lines into five and six, stating that the first line, "I see the sons of the Buddha," etc., clarifies the Great [Vehicle].

The expedient means for the lesser [capacity] is likened to seeing one's children escape danger; this corresponds to the original [teaching] of the six *paramitas* through a single practice of a respectful mind.
The seeking of the vehicle by the three vehicles is likened to the lesser sons seeking a vehicle; this corresponds to the original [teaching] that the causes have not yet been fulfilled.
It is not that the analogy of "rejoicing" is merely an analogy for escaping danger; if the analogy of "rejoicing" were not the fundamental analogy, it would not be far from being removed.
Now, this fundamental analogy removes the net of doubt below it, and all [doubts] are removed without being far off.

In this omission, where there is prose on "existence" and "non-existence," there is no verse on "firm faith"; whereas in the verses on "praising the Dharma," there is praise for the Dharma but no mention of firm faith.
Thus, there are still four [sections]. It should properly be included in the second part; as stated in the sub-commentary below: "From the time the elder saw the great fire..."
Arising from the four sides, this is the second distinct analogy, which is further divided into four parts: first, the elder seeing the fire; second, abandoning the small chairs and using the carts;
third, bestowing the great carts; and fourth, being without falsehood. Regarding the first, "seeing the fire," there are again four points, though their essential meaning is threefold:
first, the person who sees; second, clarifying what is seen; third, the alarm and fear; and fourth, expanding upon what was previously seen. Thus:
It merely establishes three points of meaning; although the following text extensively clarifies the vision of fire, it should properly be included within the second section on "that which is seen.

The *shu* (sub-commentary) states that the faith and understanding of the four groups were divergent and discordant. The lower record says: "Divergent" means they broke away from [the teachings of] Guangzhai.
He refutes the other masters who have lost the Perfect Teaching (yuanzong). How could the Perfect Buddha require a full three weeks [of practice]?

Even if one allows for differences between the long and short durations, they do not accord with the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Ten Stages), which speaks of two weeks, nor with this present sutra’s account of three weeks; these are merely the expedient teachings of a minor transformation.
First. As the treatise states: "The first is the Bodhi of the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha (*saṃbhogabuddha*). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* states:

"The first is the Bodhi of the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha," as the sutra describes leaving the palace of the Śākya clan and attaining Bodhi at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and so forth. Second is the Bodhi of the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha. Tenth...

The fulfillment of the practice on the stages results in the attainment of Bodhi, as stated in the Sūtra: "Since I attained Buddhahood, immeasurable and boundless kalpas have passed," and so forth—these three points correspond to the Dharma-Buddha’s Bodhi, the unchanging nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, and so on, as in the Sūtra passage:
"It is not as one perceives the triple world within the triple world" (and so forth). Now, in this record, one character should be made into two characters.
Since "Gayā is not" does not constitute a sentence break, it means that Gayā is not the Dharma-Buddha who preached this sutra.
If Gayā is not the Dharma-Buddha, how could that long-lived Sambhogakāya (Reward Body) alone be the Dharma-Buddha? It is an error to claim that the present sutra was preached by the Dharma-Buddha.
The rules for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) are as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "When walking in meditation, one should walk straight, neither too slowly nor too quickly.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that there are five benefits of walking meditation: first, the ability to travel long distances; second, the capacity for contemplation;

third, having little illness; fourth, digesting food; and fifth, attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Additionally, the *Trīṇi-sahasra-vidhi-sūtra* states that there are five places suitable for walking meditation.
First, in a secluded place; second, before the entrance; third, before the lecture hall; fourth, beneath a stupa; fifth, beneath a pavilion. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:

"In order to dispel drowsiness, the Buddha permitted 'walking meditation' (*caṅkramaṇa*). One should avoid ground where there are insects. Cien (Yijing) says: "The land in the Western Regions is damp; they pile bricks to form a path.
Because one comes and goes upon it like weaving on a loom, it is called 'walking meditation' (*caṅkramaṇa*)."

Ignorance is the root; the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the two factors of the past constitute the root, the five factors of the present constitute the stalk, the three factors of the present constitute the flower, and the two factors of the future constitute the fruit.
Both the untainted (anāsrava) true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) and [the path] may be considered forests. Regarding the untainted as the forest:

taking faith through hearing the teaching as the roots, the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) as the trunk, the internal ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*) as the flowers, and the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*) and so forth as the fruits; regarding true reality as the forest:

taking the arising of understanding through names and phrases as the roots, the five stages of practice (*pañca-krama*) as the trunk, the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) as the flowers, and the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) as the partial fruit.

This is the intended meaning of the *Abhidharmakośa* text regarding the absence of odor, taste, and the two consciousnesses associated with them. That verse states: "In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), fourteen [elements] are included, excluding odor, taste, and the two consciousnesses.
The commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains: "Among the realms of form, these two are excluded because they belong to the category of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

Since those born there have abandoned desire for edible food, these objects do not exist; consequently, the two consciousnesses of the nose and tongue cannot arise due to the lack of their respective objects."
Birth is a hindrance because it lacks the conditions for non-arising.
All else is seen within the eighteen *dhātus*, with the exception of odor, taste, the nose, and the tongue; the same should apply to the sense bases (*āyatanas*).
The *Śūramgama-samādhi Sūtra* states that when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he saw some tattered clothing and wished to take it to wash it.
The Heavenly Lord, knowing the Buddha’s intention, immediately took stones from the four directions and placed them at the edge, saying to the Buddha, "These may be used for washing robes.

Regarding the two gates of the Mahāyāna, each has its own intended suitability; when there is no receptive capacity, the transformation through teaching ceases. As the sub-commentary states: "The gate of exhortation is..."
The gate of admonishing the multitude to practice all that is good and refrain from all that is evil consists of three exhortations:

first, following the elder’s reflection, "My own body and hands possess strength"—this corresponds to the aforementioned mindfulness of employing the Mahāyāna by contemplating these matters for twenty-one days;

second, following the further reflection, "My son does not accept [the gift]"—this corresponds to the aforementioned...; third, following the reflection, "I am now old and feeble"—this corresponds to the aforementioned... [and so forth].

Regarding the "unresponsive" (amūka), how can they be saved? There are three [types]: those who might fall away, those who are consumed by fire, and those who are abandoned as a metaphor for the absence of response below;
these are the points where I desist from teaching, thinking, "How could I not preach the Dharma? etc. If one follows the gate of admonition, there are three;
furthermore, the three within the section on faith and understanding are both as explained in the commentary (śāstra).
The preceding passage already categorized the faculties (indriya) by means of four propositions; now, Lu Wei’s record further cites that text:
first, those with sharp faculties but heavy obstructions who hear the Mahāyāna for the first time here in this land; second, those with sharp faculties and light obstructions;

third, those with dull faculties but light obstructions, including those in other lands or pure realms who hear the Mahāyāna; and fourth, those with dull faculties and heavy obstructions, being those in this very land.

Those who remove turbidity and only then hear the Mahāyāna are as follows: among those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, there are four categories. Those with sharp faculties who are hindered by light [obstacles] are exemplified by Śāriputra.
Those with sharp faculties who are hindered by heavy [obstacles] are exemplified by Aṅgulimāla. Those with dull faculties who are hindered by light [obstacles] are exemplified by Lohitaka (Panthaka).

Those with dull faculties who are hindered by heavy [obstacles] are those who cannot attain deliverance within either the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles. If one were to teach and analyze each case according to these four gates:

Those with sharp faculties who are excluded from hearing the light [teaching] enter through the gate of "neither"; those with sharp faculties who are excluded from hearing the heavy [teaching] enter through the gate of "both";

those with dull faculties who are excluded from hearing the emptiness gate enter through the gate of "emptiness"; and those with dull faculties who are excluded from hearing the existence gate enter through the gate of "existence"—all of these can be understood accordingly.
Sixty-four thousand; this is the number of years during which the previous Buddhas appeared in the Bhadrakalpa.
Examining the Vinaya texts and collating them with this passage, the Vinaya states: "When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, Vipaśyin Buddha appeared;
when it was seventy thousand years, Śikhin Buddha appeared; when it was sixty thousand years, Viśvabhū Buddha appeared; [when it was forty thousand years, Krakucchanda Buddha appeared]..."
Regarding the ages [of the Buddhas]: K Krakucchanda Buddha appeared when the human lifespan was thirty thousand years; K Kanakamuni Buddha appeared when it was twenty thousand years;
and K Kāśyapa Buddha appeared when it was ten thousand years. Furthermore, the *Pañca-kaṣāya-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Five Corruptions) provides the same figures for these ages.
As for the present text stating "two," this is likely a scribal error and should read "three."

In the "Chapter on the Transformation City" (*Nirmita-pura-parivarta*) within the *Brahma-vimāna-parivarta*, the Brahmā speaks a warning, saying: "For one hundred and eighty kalpas, time has passed in vain, for there has been no Buddha.
This is from the "Parable Chapter" (*Upamā-parivarta*).

Regarding the ninefold [classification] of the Mahāyāna and the twelvefold division of the sūtras: if one discusses the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna in relation to one another, the Mahāyāna also consists of nine divisions—namely, excluding the *avadāna* (analogies), including the four conditions (*pratyaya*), and including the *upadeśa* (treatises).
There should be those that constitute the Hīnayāna; it is only by including the *avadāna* that they form the Minor Section (*Kṣudraka-piṭaka*).

On the day he was secretly dispatched, he still lacked the intention to work as a hired laborer; thus, the "immediately" (*ji*) in the sutra differs from the "secretly" (*mi*) used in contrast with that [previous state].
In the *Avataṃsaka*, he was immediately dispatched by a bystander, whereas at the Deer Park, he was secretly dispatched by two people.

If one were to explain the text using the common term "secretly" (*mi*), then since he already possessed the intention to work as a hired laborer at the Deer Park, one could not say that he lacked it. One should know that what is called "secretly" here [refers to this specific context].

"Dispatching" (*kai*) is precisely "dispatching-as-immediate" (*soku-kai*), which is why the preceding commentary states: "He secretly dispatched two men to pursue and capture [them] to bring them back.
One should know that "dispatching" is itself "dispatching-as-immediate.

The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) notes that from ancient times, Master Dizang has exclusively employed the "single sound" (*yiyin*) to judge and categorize the teachings; thus, it is said: "Exclusively employing the single sound."

The *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) clarifies the distinction between difference and non-difference. Pureṇa harbored a doubt in his mind: "If the Buddha-nature is seen as permanent, then before it was seen, it must have been impermanent;
if it was originally impermanent, it should likewise remain so later. For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...

Although the three vehicles differ in their white [purity], they share the same Buddha-nature; yet there are distinctions among them:
the śrāvaka is like milk, the pratyekabuddha is like curd, the bodhisattva is like fresh or processed ghee, and the Buddha is like the finest cream (maṇḍa).
For this reason, it is said in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* that there are four natures with their respective differences.
In the *Dewi jiwude jing* (The Sūtra on Attaining Non-attainment), after explaining the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), it states:
"Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, they lack the four unimpeded knowledges. Kāśyapa then addressed the Buddha:
"If Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas lack the four unimpeded knowledges, why did the Buddha say that Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom and Mahākausthila..."
Regarding the four unhindered knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), the Buddha said: "For example, the Ganges has immeasurable water, as do the other four rivers;
though they are called 'immeasurable,' in reality their quantities are not equal. Kāśyapa spoke again:

"As the Buddha previously taught, when a bodhisattva’s knowledge and vision attain the four unhindered knowledges, that bodhisattva’s knowledge and vision find nothing to be attained, nor is there anything [to be attained]."
“World-Honored One, the mind and speech are non-apprehensible; for these bodhisattvas, there is truly nothing to be apprehended.

If a bodhisattva were to have anything apprehended by the mind, they would not be called a bodhisattva, but rather an ordinary person. The Buddha further replied, “A bodhisattva truly has nothing to be apprehended.

"This is called the four perversions. Good son, because Bodhisattvas are free from the four perversions, they attain non-obstruction;
therefore, Bodhisattvas are said to have 'nothing to be attained. That which has nothing to be attained is called wisdom.

Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying: "The Tathāgata once spoke a verse for Cunda: 'Originally non-existent, now existent'—these are the four lines. What is the meaning of this? The Buddha said:

"Fundamentally non-existent" means that I originally lacked Prajñā; because of this lack of Prajñā, all the fetters of affliction are currently present.

if one sees those who practice evil, it is called seeing hell-beings. Why? Because their retribution is fixed. Noble son, all sentient beings will certainly attain bodhi;
therefore, I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. All sentient beings are truly...
In reality, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics do not yet exist; for this reason, I have spoken these verses in this sutra:
"What existed before is now non-existent" (the four lines). There are three kinds of existence: first, future existence;
second, present existence; third, past existence. That all sentient beings shall attain bodhi in a future life is called [future existence].
All sentient beings currently possess the Buddha-nature, yet they are presently bound by afflictions and fetters;
therefore, at present, they do not manifest the thirty-two marks or eighty minor characteristics.
Because all sentient beings severed their afflictions in past lives, they are now able to see the Buddha-nature. For this reason, I proclaim that all sentient beings [possess the Buddha-nature].
"All possess Buddha-nature; even those such as the icchantikas have Buddha-nature.

The *Sūtra on Breaking the Notion of Fixed Nature to Clarify the Absence of [Fixed] Nature* states: "Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external. Although it is neither internal nor external, it is not lost or destroyed;
therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Siṃhanāda Bodhisattva said: "World-Honored One..."
As the Buddha has taught, all sentient beings possess buddha-nature, just as milk contains curd.
The buddha-nature of all Buddhas is like pure *ghṛta* (clarified butter). Why, then, did the Tathāgata say that buddha-nature is neither internal nor external?
The Buddha said: "I do not say that there is curd within the milk; rather, because curd arises from milk, I say that there is curd. ... up to: "For example, suppose there were a person..."
There are pens, paper, and ink which combine to form characters; yet within the paper there were originally no characters.
Because they were originally non-existent, they are produced through the conjunction of conditions. If they had existed inherently, what need would there be for various conditions?
Son of good family, all dharmas are fundamentally without intrinsic nature. For this reason, I have spoken these verses (the four lines). Son of good family, all dharmas arise from causes...

Through conditions they arise, and through causes and conditions they cease. If sentient beings possessed the Buddha-nature within themselves, all sentient beings should possess the Buddha-body just as I do now.
This prediction was made in the past, referring to the mind prior to the vajra-like samādhi.
Therefore, [it is] before the *Vajra* (a phrase break); it is impossible for there to be dharmas in the three periods of time thereafter. The commentary states:
"Based on the fact that from the *Vajra* onwards, the eternally abiding Buddha-fruit is not subsumed within the three periods of time, it is said that such a thing is impossible."
The *Dilun* masters say: "The essence and function of permanent dharmas," etc. The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The *Dilun* people say that permanent dharmas are not something newly acquired;
rather, their original essence and function are complete from the beginning, but they are merely covered by delusive afflictions and only become manifest at a later time.

If this were so, then what was previously hidden should also be manifest later; and since it has already submerged and then reappeared, once it has manifested, it should no longer be hidden, yet it should also continue to be hidden. [The text here appears to be an elliptical critique of this position.]
Manifestation.
Zhiyi’s fivefold interpretation of the first [point] regarding the Three Truths, as stated in the *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "It is based solely on a single phrase:
difference is non-difference, and non-difference is difference; one truth is the three truths. Therefore, it is said that the original three truths are one truth."
Therefore, it is said that "present non-existence" is neither identical to nor different from the three times;

thus, it is said that "there is no place where dharmas exist throughout the three times"—in this way, they are successively shown to be inseparable. This is precisely the case where difference is non-difference and non-difference is difference;
where there is neither difference nor non-difference. This then dispels Kāśyapa’s objection, leaving nothing remaining.
Next, regarding the commentary on "permanent" and "impermanent," it states: "That which is impermanent is also permanent; that which is permanent is also impermanent;
neither permanent nor impermanent. Thus, the clouds of Cunda’s doubts were dispelled and the ice was melted away.

How then can these difficulties and doubts not be eliminated?"
Fourth, regarding the four *siddhāntas*, the Commentary states: "That which is fundamentally existent—'if one exists, all exist'—is the Worldly (*loka*) standpoint.

That which is currently non-existent—'if one is non-existent, all are non-existent'—is the Therapeutic (*prātipakṣika*) standpoint. Combining this existence and non-existence—'all are both existent and non-existent'—is the Personal (*pauruṣeya*) standpoint.
'That there are dharmas existing throughout the three periods of time is impossible' is the Ultimate (*paramārtha*) standpoint. Now, this single *siddhānta* encompasses them all."

Regarding the four *siddhāntas*, which dispel difficulties and resolve doubts, Jingxi says: "If both the doubts and the difficulties of these two types of people are dispelled and resolved, then the capacities of all beings will be harmonized and fully integrated.

Fifth, regarding the four gates: that which is inherently present is the "existence phrase" (*yǒu-jù*) of the gate of existence (*yǒu-mén*); that which is currently absent is the "non-existence phrase" (*wú-jù*) of the gate of non-existence (*wú-mén*). Sound... [text truncated]
To hear that the Pratyekabuddhas also have both distinctions and no distinctions— that is, the phrase "both existent and non-existent" and the gate "both existent and non-existent"—

and that it is impossible for there to be dharmas existing throughout the three periods of time— that is the phrase "neither existent nor non-existent" and the gate "neither existent nor non-existent.
