Pāṭikāputra exhorted him to draw near to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, but Agniveśya said, "What kind of path does this shaven-headed mendicant possess?"

It is because he reviled the Buddha as a "shaven-headed practitioner" that, now that he is about to attain enlightenment, he must undergo six years of asceticism and endure all manner of hardships to repay that karmic debt.
Regarding Sundarī’s slander: formerly there was a courtesan named Mṛgajā, and at that time there was a gambler named...
While Śuddhākṣa was sporting with her beneath a tree, he saw that the deer had assumed the appearance of a woman, wearing exquisite and precious garments;
he killed it, took the clothes, and departed. For this reason, he suffers slander in his present life.
One day, as the Buddha Kinkara was begging for alms in a village, he saw a piece of broken wood, one chiang-er two cun long, protruding beside him.
Knowing this to be a karmic connection from a previous life, the Buddha leaped into the air and ascended as far as the Brahma Heaven;
Kinkara followed him there. As the Buddha descended from heaven, Kinkara also descended with him. Thereupon, the World-Honored One extended his foot, and Kinkara entered through it.
[As stated] in detail: Regarding past conditions, countless eons ago there were two merchants, each leading five hundred traders, who entered the sea to gather treasures.
Later, a sudden flood disaster occurred. The second merchant, having previously completed the repair of his ship, immediately boarded it with his caravan of traders.
The first merchant, however, requested a ship but had not yet obtained one, so he gave [his goods] to the second merchant.
The guests fought over a boat, and with iron spears they pierced the feet of the first merchant, who immediately passed away;
the second guest was the Buddha.
Long ago, in a past kalpa, there was a king named Bandhumat who invited the Tathāgata Vipaśyin to enter his palace.
At the time of the offering, there was a bhikṣu named Maitreya who, being ill, did not go;
he instead sent a request for food. On his way, he passed Mount Vaṃśa. Upon seeing that the food was fragrant and delicious, the King of Mount Vaṃśa became envious and malicious, saying:
"This shaven-headed śramaṇa should eat nothing but horse-grams! The king’s attendants all said: "O Master, this king should indeed eat horse-grams!"
Because of this residual karma, the Buddha and five hundred bhikṣus ate horse barley for ninety days at Icchānaṅgala.
Regarding the past transgression of Vairāḍī killing the Śākyas: in a former age, during a famine, there was a pond outside a village near Rājagṛha;
at that time, the people caught fish from it to eat. Within this pond were two fish, one named...
The two fish named *Kṣāra* and *Bahujihva* spoke among themselves, saying: "We have done him no wrong, yet we have been killed by him without cause;
may we, in a future life, take our revenge upon him. At that time, the fisherman who was gathering fish in Lake Rauruka was the Śākya [Mahānāman];
the fish *Kṣāra* was King Virūḍhaka; and the fish *Bahujihva* was the physiognomist of King Virūḍhaka.
Regarding those with evil tongues:

in the *Piṇḍapātra-śūnya-bhājana-sūtra*, there is no textual passage [to this effect]. However, the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that after the Buddha had completed the *varṣā* retreat at Śrāvastī, he went to a city of Brahmins to beg for alms with his bowl;
at that time, the king issued a restrictive decree forbidding the people of the country from [giving to him].
When it was time for the Buddha’s meal, the people all closed their doors; thus the Tathāgata went out of the city with an empty bowl.

At that moment, an old man who was a servant came out carrying a broken earthenware vessel filled with dregs of rice gruel and discarded it, saying to the Buddha, "If you need this poor food now, you may take it."
In a former age, there were two bhikṣus: one named Ajita (Unconquerable) and the other named Nityapramudita (Ever-Joyful).
In that country, there was an elder whose wife was named Sudarśanā (Exquisite). These two bhikṣus frequented her household;

the bhikṣu Ajita had severed all outflows (*āsrava*) and was fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The elder’s wife provided them with offerings of the four requisites in great abundance.
If one whose mind is focused on making offerings to Nityapramudita becomes weak in resolve, then jealousy toward Nityapramudita will arise;
one will falsely slander the Unconquerable One (Ajita), claiming he consorts with the woman Śubhāṅgī, and that he accepts offerings only out of lustful attachment.
(And so forth. "Nityapramudita" refers to the Buddha; "Śubhāṅgī" refers to Ciñcā-mānavikā, who approached him carrying a bowl and manifesting a protruding belly.
I said previously, "In the past you were intimate with me, and because of that I became pregnant; now I am approaching my time of delivery, and I require ghee and oil.
Then Śakra, fanning the Buddha, transformed himself into a mouse and gnawed the cord of the bowl; suddenly, the bowl fell to the ground.
Regarding Devadatta’s pushing of the mountain: Formerly, there was an elder named Sudatta whose son was named Sumati.
When his father passed away, he had a half-brother named Suyasa-Sumati, who thought to himself, "If this half-brother remains, all our property must be divided.
He then devised a plan to go to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to engage in some discussion with him.
Upon reaching the mountain, he immediately pushed him to the base of a cliff and struck him with a stone; he died instantly.
At that time, King Śuddhodana was the one who required *candana* (sandalwood), the Buddha was Sumati, and Devadatta was Suyasa.
The cold wind sought his clothing, so he rose and went out; however, I have not yet examined other sutras on this matter.

Regarding the back pain under the twin trees: formerly, in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, during a great festival assembly, there were two athletes—one a Kṣatriya and the other a Brāhmaṇa—who were wrestling together at the time. The Brāhmaṇa said to the Kṣatriya: "Do not..."
"I will strike you, and I shall give you wealth. The Kṣatriya bowed in submission, and both men received rewards from the king.
However, the Brāhmaṇa had no intention of repaying his debt of gratitude; this continued until the third time, when he still did not acknowledge the service.

Thereafter, they struck one another again, and the Kṣatriya pressed down on his head with his right hand, seized his waist with his left, and kicked him with both feet, breaking the bones of his spine.
Regarding the "Sugarcane-breaker" Kṣatriya, the Buddha was a Brahmin and Devadatta was that [Kṣatriya].

Although the sūtras do not mention the two afflictions of failing to obtain alms-food and being pursued by cold winds for clothing, there were additionally five hundred arhats who were slandered and suffered from aching bones and joints;
thus, including these, they possessed ten [afflictions], while excluding the arhats, they likewise possessed nine.

Regarding the statement that the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) precede the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), while the seventh [factor] of the latter—concentration (*samādhi*)—is said to precede the seven [factors of enlightenment], this should be analyzed through three propositions:

first, that all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are with-outflow (*sāsrava*); second, that they are all without-outflow (*anāsrava*); and third, that they are both with-outflow and without-outflow.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When one correctly attains the initial wholesome state, there are the wholesome five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) which are with-outflow."
The five outflowing aggregates (*āsrava-skandha*) are themselves the stage prior to the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) factor; how, then, does one cultivate the Eightfold Path at this stage?

First, receiving the Dharma from a teacher and binding the mind to it through mindfulness is called the "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Diligently practicing for the sake of attaining this Dharma is called "right effort" (*samyak-prahāṇa*).

Cultivating within a single state of mind is called the "bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*), and so forth. One should know that these factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) are all with outflows (*sāsrava*). And so forth.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If one cultivates the Eightfold Path after the Seven Factors of Enlightenment, it may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Why is this? Entering the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) by means of the Eightfold Path is itself uncontaminated; furthermore, that which is both contaminated and uncontaminated refers to the intention of the preparatory stage.

The *Fuxingji* (Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*) explains: "That which precedes the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is also contaminated; [this refers to] the Path of Vision."
That which has already passed is likewise untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding this aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), who is it that ages and dies? The *Āgama* states: "The twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) range from ignorance (*avidyā*) to aging and death.
If anyone were to say, 'Who is it that ages and dies? they would give rise to false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and this applies even down to ignorance."
Thus, if one says that there is no one who ages and dies, know that this is false; this is called the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
If one says that aging and death do not exist, know that this is false; this is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
In the Great Sūtra, regarding the section on the gates of Mahāyāna remedies, it says that even using the "Constant" [Sūtra]:

there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who upheld the five precepts and was fully endowed with dignified conduct; he was named King Vimalakīrti of Majestic Virtue. He took profound delight in contemplating the various gates of remedial application (*pratipakṣa*), namely:
suffering and pleasure, permanence and impermanence, purity and impurity, self and non-self, reality and unreality, and so forth.
"One should always delight in observing such gates of remedial counteraction (as detailed in the passage above).
As for the statement in the subsequent text that 'this is also not what was employed by the King Vimalakīrti,' this is likewise incorrect."

This refers to the correspondence between the stage of the five powers (*pañcabala*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Specifically, it is so called because the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) corresponds to right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) to the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*) to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), and the stage of the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) to the five powers. Thus it is said.

The Commentary states that entering the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) within the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*)—wherein "Heat" originally belongs to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) and "Patience" (*kṣānti*) enter into cultivation—refers mostly to the skillful means (*upāya*) for entering the stage of cultivation.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refutes the provisional teachings by stating: "In the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, there are those who have not yet generated the aspiration [for enlightenment] yet receive a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), and there are those who..."

The generation of the resolve for enlightenment and the bestowal of predictions upon others are known by all; why, then, is it said that during the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, one does not know that one will become a Buddha (and so forth)?
That which is called "not knowing" is merely a provisional teaching, and therefore the *Śāstra* refutes it.

It is not meant that they are entirely non-existent; rather, as for the claim made by Kātyāyana and other Buddhas—that the *tri-piṭaka* bodhisattvas do not sever their fetters and are thus rejected by the *Mahā-śāstra*—this is clearly a provisional teaching (*upāya*).
According to the *Āgamas*, it is not the case that there are no *tri-piṭaka* bodhisattvas who actually practice the path in reality.
How can one claim that the two ancient masters understood [the Lotus Sūtra] as teaching only for the two vehicles?
Whether one advances or retreats from these two interpretations, they cite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*’s parable of the Great Garuḍa:

just as a young Garuḍa flies from one Mount Sumeru to another, if its body were to fall to the ground, it would experience the suffering of death; if it had not yet reached the ground, it would experience what is equal to death.
"Those who have reached the ground" refers to those of the four fruits who no longer give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; this is termed "death.

"Those who have not yet reached the ground" refers to those of the first, second, and third fruits, who may or may not give rise to the aspiration; hence they are said to be "advancing and retreating."

There is no longer a sequence of before and after; however, if one were to discuss such a sequence, it would have to be stated as: the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), and so on, up to the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).

The remaining three [patiences] universally encompass all afflictions of the view-division (*darśana-heya-kleśa*); they eliminate [afflictions] extending for three hundred *yojanas*, using the five lower stages as a single unit.

The "one hundred" refers merely to taking two portions each from greed and hatred. As for the three beginning with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), these are fundamentally afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
This is because the *Abhidharmakośa* explains that among the five lower-tier fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya*), four are afflictions of view and one is an affliction of thought (*saṃjñā-kleśa*).

Therefore, in the previous commentary, when the twenty years were explained through the analogy of combining the five lower-tier and five upper-tier afflictions, it was stated that those who sever the [afflictions of] thought are [the ones referred to].

As stated in detail in the *Abhidharmakośakārikā*: "By two, one does not transcend the desire realm; by three, one returns to the lower realms. This is because they encompass the gates and the faculties.

Alternatively, it is said that there are only three [fetters] to be abandoned, because they can obstruct the departure for liberation through lack of aspiration, confusion regarding the path, and doubt concerning the path.

The commentary explains these five as: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); third, doubt (*vicikitsā*); fourth, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*); and fifth, ill-will (*vyāpāda*). These five...

Because they exist within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are called "lower" (*adhobhāgīya*). One does not transcend the desire realm due to two [fetters], and returns to the lower [realms] due to three.

This is because one does not transcend the desire realm due to greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*); even if one were able to transcend it and be reborn as high as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one would return to the desire realm due to the three beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, greed and hatred are like prison guards, while the three beginning with the view of a self-identity are like sentries.

Regarding the statement that the "lower fetters" (avarabhāgīya) refer to lower sentient beings—namely, ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana)—and that they also take the lower realm—the desire realm (kāmadhātu)—as their object:
the first three are able to obstruct the transcendence of lower sentient beings, while the latter two prevent one from transcending the desire realm;

therefore, all five are given the name "conducive to the lower realms. Question: If stream-enterers (srotāpanna) abandon six afflictions, why does the Sūtra state that they only abandon [the first five]?
Regarding the answer to the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*), there are two masters. The first explanation states in verse: "Because they subsume the gateways of the faculties, there are three.

To explain, "subsuming the gateways" means that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) resides in one gateway, namely the gateway of suffering (*duḥkha*). The clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) resides in two gateways, namely the gateways of suffering and the path (*mārga*).
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) pervades all four gateways, namely the gateways of the Four Noble Truths. It is said that by abandoning these three [fetters], those three gateways are subsumed.

Therefore, it is said that by abandoning three, one has already abandoned six. As for the inclusion of the faculties (*indriya*), it means that the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arises based on the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);

the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) arises based on the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) arises based on doubt (*vicikitsā*). Thus, it is said that by abandoning these three types, those three faculties are subsumed;

therefore, having stated the abandonment of three, one has stated the abandonment of six (and so forth). Regarding the five higher fetters (*pañcordhvabhāgīya*), the verse says: "The fetters conducive to the higher [realms] (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*) are likewise..."

The five [factors]—desire for the realm of form (*rūparāga*), desire for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), restlessness in the realms of form and formless (*rūpārūpyauddhatya*), pride in the realms of form and formless (*rūpārūpyamāna*), and ignorance in the realms of form and formless (*rūpārūpyavidyā*)—are explained as follows: (1) desire for the realm of form; (2) desire for the formless realm; (3) restlessness in the realms of form and formless; (4) pride in the realms of form and formless; and (5) ignorance in the realms of form and formless.

Because these five can prevent sentient beings from arising in the higher realms, they are called "higher-tier" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*). This is because the fault of craving (*rāga*) is the most severe among them. Thus, there are two [categories].

*Jie-bie-lun* (End of the Main Text): Regarding the five names and their meanings, the *Xin-shu* does not provide an explanation; my current record states that "defiling them" refers to the verse’s "greed-defilement," which is simply greed.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) pertains to the form and formless realms; pride (*māna*) is the exaltation of one who has attained dhyāna; and agitation (*auddhatya*) is the discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) of one who has emerged from dhyāna.

The severing of a small portion of the afflictions of thought refers to those non-Buddhists who have attained dhyāna; they are able to sever these, which is called "subduing" (vibhava), not "severing" (prahāṇa) in the sense of definitive abandonment.
This is because there is certainly no one who first severs the afflictions of thought and only afterwards severs the afflictions of view.

The fourth and fifth [sections] are combined into one segment. The previous outline divided them into five parts: (1) "Abandoning his father and fleeing" is the parable of the father and son losing each other;
(2) "The father and son seeing each other" is the parable of their meeting; (3) "Pursuing from the side and the two inducements" is the parable of the two methods of persuasion;

(4) "From 'following his heart' to 'mutually recognizing and trusting'" is the parable of fully understanding the family business; (5) this is not a summary of the preceding near and far [distances], but rather takes up the *Vaipulya* [sūtras].
The meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàpǐn) is that the fifth entrustment, the analogy of family property, is precisely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Furthermore, the fourth and fifth [entrustments] together constitute the analogy of wealth (as explained at length). The intention here is that these two inducements represent the intent of the Deer Park period;
if the fourth were merged into the fifth, there would be no mention of the Vaipulya and Prajñā periods within the great structural divisions.
Regarding the "abbreviated text" of the *Sūtra on Requesting the Chariot*: after being exempted from calamity at the Deer Park, one immediately requests the chariot;
yet the sūtra does not separately explain the differences between the capacities and dispositions of the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā* vehicles, hence it is said that the text is abbreviated.

Regarding "receiving, practicing, awakening, and entering," the aforementioned text states that "receiving" refers to the opportunity; "following what is heard" refers to the stage of *uṣmagata* (Heat);

"turning the contemplation" refers to the stages from *mūrdhan* (Summit) up to *laukikāgradharma* (Supreme Mundane Dharma); "awakening" refers to the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*); and "entering" refers to the subsequent fruits. By analogy with the small [stages], the large [stages] should also be understood accordingly.

The phrase "separating the ordinary and accomplishing the holy" (*shuge* / *sekaku*)—where "separate" (*ge*) should be read as "reform" (*kakku*), meaning to reform—refers to manifesting auspicious signs (*shōzai*) to distinguish [the teachings].
In this present sutra, the six auspicious signs collectively manifest the opening of the provisional (*kai-gen*).

Regarding the auspicious signs in that [other] sutra, where the World-Honored One announced his parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second month, the commentary states: "This signifies the Dharma. The second month is the middle spring; "middle" (*chū*) refers to...
The center represents the Middle Way; furthermore, the time when the moon is full on the fifteenth day symbolizes perfect permanence.

Moreover, when the Buddha gathered the assembly—first by means of sound and second by means of light—and once the great multitude from the ten directions had assembled, the World-Honored One withdrew both the sound and the light, causing them to enter through his own mouth;
this symbolizes the cessation of illumination regarding the three obstacles. Therefore, humans and devas wept, saying, "The Sage has passed away."
"The sun of wisdom has now forever set; this also signifies impermanence.
This [statement] refers to the immediate and remote traces that diverge from the present sutra, which explores the intent of the Dharma-body descending to manifest transformation.
That sutra, however, only addresses the matters of the five periods within a single lifetime, as it says: "From cow comes milk," and so on, up to "from clarified butter comes ghee."

Regarding the *Amṛta* (the "Essence"): it describes how, because the faculties of sentient beings are not equal, in this present sutra each of the three faculties has its own realization and understanding, and for each of these the Tathāgata provides a corresponding confirmation;
such [a distinction] does not exist in that [other] sutra.
Regarding the entrustment for the lower regions, there is this present sutra entrusted to the lower regions;
within it, sixty thousand bodhisattvas, each with a retinue equal to sixty thousand Ganges-sands, dwell in the space of the lower regions.
That sutra circulates only in this land.
If the Buddha had arisen from his samādhi and yet could not speak, or if he were unable to provide the testimony that ought to have been given,
why would the compilers of the sutra not have placed this chapter before he arose from his concentration?
Moreover, the commentary explicitly states that Prabhūtaratna came to provide testimony.

The "people" (min) have a certain measure; the people are the mechanism (*jī*). According to the *Avataṃsaka* teaching, there are two types of people: the many at the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*) teaching and the few in other schools;
this is explained accordingly. Regarding the source of assets:
either the principle of truth (*tattva*) is the asset and the stages of practice (*bhūmi*) are what is produced from it, or else cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the asset and...
The "Holy Stage of Assets" (*Zīchān Shèngwèi*) is that from which [this teaching] emerges;
it possesses two meanings. The *Xuánwén* states: "If this were the *Avataṃsaka* of the Place of Quiescence (*Jíchǎng*), it would not be sequential.
Now, according to the *Fǎxìng Lùn*, Bodhisattvas of pure faculties enter the Dharma-realm in three stages: first, the *Prajñā*; second, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; and third..."
The entry into the Dharma-realm through the Prajñā of Nirvāṇa is precisely the ocean-like emptiness of the Avataṃsaka;
furthermore, the time of the Avataṃsaka was long ago, and those of inferior capacity could not enter it as if they were deaf, but now, upon hearing the Prajñā, they are able to gain entry.
How could there not be those in the position of "next-to-be" (upapadya) within the first three teachings?
After the Deer Park, did he not preach the precepts and goodness? To eliminate the filth of views and afflictions was precisely at the Deer Park;

from this point onward, if all were for the sake of world-transcendence, why were the twelve years following [the Deer Park] a period of "precepts of non-action," wherein only six phrases were taught?

The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* was established twelve years later as a comprehensive code of discipline; those who uphold the precepts are reborn in the heavens. How can this be judged as entirely transcending the world?
They have not yet abandoned the narrow path of clinging to the fruit of an Arhat, lacking even the slightest desire to seek a single meal—this is not to wander [in liberation].
This is a major point.
To claim that the *Lotus Sūtra* was judged to be Esoteric Buddhism based on the two envoys' report is incorrect.

That report was merely an attempt to grasp the general tenor of the text; this text itself is precisely what accords with the vow. Although it does not strictly conform to the envoys' report, [the essence remains].

The "appropriateness" (*yathārhata*) of taking up the preceding passage refers to the teaching within the section on cleaning the latrine; the "appropriateness" of taking up both [passages] together is because these two instances of appropriateness are identical.
Therefore, it is said that what was previously seen in the section on signs—where it stated, "This might be a king"—is now here [seen as] a householder.
Regarding the title "The Elder," it follows the sequence of the King; thus, it is discussed next.

As for the *Parivarta* on Bestowing Predictions (*Vyākaraṇa*) in the *Dharmadhātuparivarta*, although no explicit words of prediction are clearly evident there, it may be called a "subsidiary" [section] because various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) exhort and inspire the bodhicitta.

Regarding the term *quàn* (券): the pronunciation is *quàn*. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) explains it as "a contract" (*quàn*). It refers to mutual binding and entanglement (*xiàn*) that results in a sense of obligation;
it is broken down the middle to distinguish the parties. The incisions were originally made with wood to record the number of items, but now iron is used to record the number of objects.
This is what is meant by the "iron contract" (*tiěquàn*) currently bestowed by the state upon meritorious officials as a solemn oath.

"Practicing accordingly and appreciating accordingly" refers to dwelling in the preliminary stage of cultivation; "meritorious cultivation" refers to the eightfold manifestation of attaining Buddhahood, which is called "appreciation.
Having finished distinguishing these differences, the preceding text states: "If one dwells within the stage of the Two Vehicles and turns to teach others, this is called 'twenty years.
The term 'twenty' is the same in both cases, each having its own underlying reason."
In the commentary, the preceding section on "conformity" contains two long passages. Within these, there are two parts: first, from "We, by means of the three sufferings...
up to "...confused and ignorant," which corresponds to the two gates regarding the lack of capacity; second, "knowing those who delight in the lesser Dharma," which corresponds to the abandonment.

There is nothing in the commentary that does not involve relinquishing; even within the prose sections, there are instances where inferior states of mind have not yet been relinquished, as well as gradual progress toward serenity.
According to the sutra, all phenomena are empty and quiescent, and the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are all extinguished without remainder.
The truth of non-arising and non-ceasing is pure and utterly devoid of coming or going;
it is neither great nor small, for its fundamental nature is identical and lacks the distinctions of the three vehicles.

This is called the "fruit of practice," as it does not involve the drawing forth of rebirth and thus is not termed a "retributive fruit. The *Mysterious Text* states that this is analogous to the two vehicles.

the pronunciation of *xiáng* is *rǎng*. To ward off an object with the hand is called *xiáng*; furthermore, to roll up one’s sleeves and extend the arm is also called *xiáng*.
Here, it means to push away that [previous state] and receive this [present state].
The character "chū" (initial) at the beginning is likely a scribal error.
The reasoning [of that passage] is untenable; the intent of the sūtra fundamentally uses the single ground as a metaphor for the single true principle (*ekasatya-tattva*).
Ancient commentators erroneously used the fact that the *ālayavijñāna* contains seeds to represent the single ground, which is why it is said that the reasoning is untenable.
Regarding the phrase "the first person at the beginning of the world of the five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha-loka*), the character for "first" (*chu*) is placed above this clause to read "first,
regarding the five aggregates," etc.
As for "Xie Suzi," the term "Xie" (*xie*) carries the meaning of being "inaccessible" or "unreachable."

As explained in the *Xuanwen* (Profound Text) regarding the interpretation of the Dharma, it cites a sutra stating: "Vimalakīrti contemplates the true mark of the body; his contemplation of the Buddha is likewise.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of the non-differentiation among the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings. This means that while mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are distinct as three, mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are one and thus without differentiation.

By analogy, one knows that the horizontal is emptiness; thus, the vertical is the provisional. The horizontal simultaneously illuminates both emptiness and the provisional, while the horizontal and vertical together negate both emptiness and the provisional—neither horizontal nor vertical.
In Guanzhong, only Master Daoyuan saw that when the sutras speak of gathering sand to form the Buddha-way, he immediately claimed that gathering sand does not [form the Buddha-way].
To claim that receiving the proximate retribution of humans and devas constitutes reaching the Buddha-way in the distant future is incorrect.
This [stage] transcends the three persons of the Tripiṭaka teaching—the Pratyekabuddhas—and the two vehicles of the Shared Teaching.
First, it is because the essence of the seven stages of skillful means is wholesome, and this essence is the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*).
The essential nature is fully present; the provisional is precisely the three thousand realms within that essence.

Each corresponds respectively to those of the various vehicles who are hindered by the four inversions, those of the three paths who are hindered by the six obscurations, Bodhisattvas who are hindered by the four abodes, and followers of the Two Vehicles who are hindered by the five abodes, as well as those of the Separate and Perfect Teachings.

Each medicine and each disease corresponds to the ten realms; the Āgada medicines consist of the categories of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, while the path and the delusions are likewise threefold.
One can recognize the vertical correspondence between the medicines and diseases across the ten realms.

The two meanings of "habitual cause" (*xiyin*) and "retributive fruit" (*baoguo*) are distinct. Mountains and rivers are fundamentally metaphors for retributive fruit; it was incorrect [of former commentators] to use them as analogies for habitual cause.

The *Shu* (Commentary) discusses the Dharma in relation to the mind, where "Dharma" refers to the object-field of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). Therefore, the *Ji* (Record/Annotation) distinguishes the mind by way of its objects of perception (*ālambana*).

Originally, based on the single cause of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are thereby established. If one discusses the mind in terms of dharmas, if there were no six sense objects, there would consequently be no six consciousnesses.

The character *wū* (污) is originally pronounced with the initial *ā* and the final *dū*; however, because the Master of the Record (Jizang) wished to employ it as the character *wā* (窊), he changed it to *wǔ huá*.
The character "切" (qiè) is pronounced as "烏華切" (wū huā qiè).
The characters for "涇" (jīng), "渭" (wèi), "霸" (bà), "滻" (sǎn), "澧" (lǐ), and "澇" (lào) are all read according to their standard pronunciations.

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the self (*ātman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are referred to as the "six. These are neither identical to nor separate from those [five aggregates].

The Dharma, by means of these six dharmas, is neither identical to nor separate from the correct conditions and causes; as the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "Because they are not identical, yet because they are not non-separate;
because they are inherently complete [in principle], yet because they are the fundamental delusion. It is not [the case that they are not non-separate].
"Interspersed" (*jiànròu*) is read with the lower character *nǚ* (女) and the phonetic *jiù* (救).

It refers, for example, to the sixth category of the "Household" (*jiā*) [in the *Abhidharmakośa*], where the earth of mountains, rivers, valleys, and gorges is combined within the three thousandfold world system (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*). This clarifies that this constitutes an interspersing.
In the *Vyākhyā* on the *Sarvajñatā-bhūmi-sūtra*, it is asked: "What is the difference between omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
Some say there is no distinction; others say that the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is omniscience, while the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is the knowledge of all aspects.
The cause is omniscience, and the fruit is the knowledge of all aspects. Briefly stated, it is omniscience; explained in detail, it is the knowledge of all aspects.

The Buddha of All-Knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) possesses a vast and expansive substance within the Great Perfect Middle Way; his substance is great and his wondrous response extends throughout the ten directions, thus his "shadows" (manifestations) are vast and expansive.

The Buddha of Expedient Means possesses a subtle substance as he realizes the Truth; his substance is subtle and he responds only to the six classes of ordinary beings, thus his "shadows" are narrow and limited.
The Dharma taught by the two Buddhas, the Storehouse (Āgama) and the Transmission (Abhidharma), is like rain without lightning or thunder.
Regarding "clouds without rain," the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The response-body (nirmāṇakāya) does not preach the Dharma, as in the cases of Śākyamuni and Prabhūtaratna;
this is because these clouds do not contain moisture."

It is unnecessary to employ the six heavens and four realms described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. In that scripture, the rain falls upon the six heavens and four realms by the Dragon King Vāsava, yet their forms and colors differ:

those in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) are like celestial fragrant flowers; those in the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*) are like *campaka* flowers;

those in Tuṣita are like *maṇi* jewels; those in the Yāma Heaven are like banners and canopies; those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are like wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*); and those in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) are like... [the text here appears to be incomplete].
The sweet delicacies of Uttarakuru are like a necklace; those of Pūrvavideha and Aparagoyānī are both like campaka flowers;
and the pure waters of Jambudvīpa are used as metaphors for the bodhisattva’s wondrous, effortless activity within the Middle Way.

It is sufficient to borrow the Āgamas as analogies, employing only the *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya) where the lightning strikes and the five conditions fail to produce rain as the analogy.

From what is manifested, we know that the grasses and trees are the "manifested" (the effect), while the clouds and rain are the "manifester" (the cause). Since the grasses and trees differ from the clouds and rain, the two must also be distinct.
Among the ten mental factors (*caitasika*) corresponding to the mind, there are two: concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the various treatises such as the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā) and the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, which discuss the causes of habituation (*vāsanā-hetu*) and retribution (*vipāka-hetu*), it is said:

"The arising of afflictions (*kleśa*) in this life is called the cause of habituation; the formation of karma is the cause of retribution. The arising of afflictions in a future life is called the fruit of habituation. If [this refers to] sensation (*vedanā*), it is named...

Regarding retribution-fruition (*vipāka-phala*), if it refers to supramundane causes and effects, as in the case of the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) arising in those of the Two Vehicles, they repay their conditioning cause (*abhyāsa-hetu*) by obtaining this fruition of habituation (*abhyāsa-phala*).
However, because the untainted is not a dharma that draws forth rebirth, it lacks retribution-fruition.
Regarding the manifestation of the signs arising from *dāna* (generosity) within the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of those six perfections:

if, while in seated meditation, one suddenly sees fields of merit, sublime environments, or the physical forms of the Triple Gem, these are all manifestations arising from the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*).

Next, if one perceives none of these signs at all, yet feels a profound yearning within the mind to practice giving and make offerings to the Triple Gem, these are all manifestations arising from the cause of habitual cultivation (*vāsanā-hetu*). Thus it is said.

Regarding these [precepts, patience, and so forth] (as detailed above), the next six obscurations are as follows: if one sees that the Three Jewels, teachers, monks, parents, or their images appear haggard, or are naked and exposed, or that temples and monasteries are desolate and ruined, these are all signs of the retributive fruits of the obscuration of stinginess.

The three types of penetration are: penetration of past lives, which reaches the past; penetration of the divine eye, which reaches the future; and penetration of the exhaustion of outflows, which reaches the present.
In the commentary, these are sometimes condensed into five analogies by combining the third with the analogy of the dense clouds over the lands of the world.

The commentary explains the distinctions as previously stated: the mountain is a metaphor for the five aggregates (*skandha*) of a bodhisattva, while the valley is a metaphor for the five aggregates of an ordinary person.
Regarding the light illuminating the hells, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata emits light that illuminates the suffering and affliction of sentient beings in the hells."
Birth spans the six heavens; furthermore, the *Xuánwén* states that "the elimination of suffering is the fruit" and "benefiting birth in the heavens is the cause.
The preaching of the Vaipulya sutras refers to the deeds of the seer Vāsava.

Taking this as an illustration, the cases of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) aspects of suffering and happiness are combined without distinction; they are analogous to a single characteristic,
a single flavor, unified within a single stage, and a single rain.
This refers to the lower section, which provides a dual explanation: first, that there is but one ground and one rain;

second, that although there are various sentient beings, they are like grasses and trees, which are differentiated. Regarding the first [point], it unifies sentient beings with the fact that they do not know [the truth]. As for the second, "Why is this so? raises the person who is capable of knowing;
from "one mark" and "one flavor" downward, it expresses the intent that there is no differentiation, thereby unifying the single ground and the single rain.
Regarding the fact that there are sentient beings whose lower, differentiated minds correspond to the superior grasses and trees: why is this?
It is because the following explains and establishes these two points concerning the extent of their opening and closing.
Herein, the three objects, three causes, and three fruits are distinguished vertically according to their respective stages.

If one discusses the horizontal [classification] based on the vertical [structure], the objective realm belongs to the Dharma-body; the three causes belong to Prajñā; and the three fruits belong to Liberation.

When these three are expanded into the six natures for cultivation, they are numerous; when condensed into two natures for cultivation, they are few. When condensed into one nature for cultivation, they are even fewer.
The *Original Threefold Path Signpost* states: "Although turbidity arises from conditions, turbidity is inherently present. The *Essential Points* states:
"Because one has never awakened from the beginning, turbidity is inherently present."
Furthermore, the reality of the fruit-ground within delusion—the mutual integration of the environment and its inhabitants—is based on the fundamental nature of the capacities of sentient beings.
Although the commentary does not follow a sequential order, it should logically conclude with the grounds before explaining them; here, however, both are combined and explained together.

In the seventh fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), it states: "Ignorance and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) universally respond to various conditions through two gates: arising and abiding.
Regarding this, some say that abiding refers to the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), while arising refers to the gate of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

Others say that abiding is the nature and arising is cultivation; this is the gate of the nature of cultivation. Now, I suspect that the gate of arising refers back to the preceding statement in the *Sūtra*: "The seeds of the Buddha arise from conditions."
The commentary states: "When ignorance serves as a condition, sentient beings arise; when the true teaching serves as a condition, perfect enlightenment arises.

This arising encompasses both the defiled and the pure. Regarding the "gate of abiding," it refers back to the preceding [point]: this is the dharma-nature and the dharma-position. The sub-commentary explains:

"Conditions have both the defiled and the pure, yet they equally take the nature of moisture to form waves; therefore, all take Suchness as their position, and equally take the waves as the manifestation of that nature."
Therefore, all take *tathatā* (suchness) as their characteristic; this dwelling also penetrates both the defiled and the pure. This current explanation also provides a detailed analysis.
Alternatively, if one later observes that the two gates of arising and dwelling have separate sources elsewhere, then one should remove this [section].

The commentary analyzes each sentence according to the principles of "difference" (*bhedā*) and "non-difference" (*abhedā*). For example, regarding liberation, there is both difference and non-difference:

"All noble ones (*ārya*) are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). This non-difference is itself difference. The seven kinds of skillful means (*upāya*) are all of one nature;
this difference is itself non-difference. This extends even to the single departure from opposition, the seven departures from oneness, and the extinction of one.

Regarding the seven methods of cessation (*saptabhaṅginaya*), such as difference and non-difference, they generally possess three dharmas and one characteristic according to both principle and teaching. The three dharmas being of one flavor refers to the discourse on the three dharmas;
if one were to say, "I too shall soon abide within them," it should be stated that one has reached the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Regarding the statement "up to the seeds of gnosis":

because one apprehends objects through gnosis, these three [seeds] arise from distinct categories of seeds—the causal seeds for lowering the head and raising the hand, the causal seeds for understanding the three vehicles, and the causal seeds for the mind that acts as the Buddha with a mind.
When compared to those nature-seeds, the three causal bodies are identical in essence; this now clarifies their classification.
The three causes are distinguished from one another.
If that is so, then regarding *prajñā* (wisdom) and *vimukti* (liberation), this refers only to the two aspects of the *dharmakāya*: its nature (*svabhāva*) and its category (*jāti*). A doubt arises:
if *prajñā* and *vimukti* possess these two distinct meanings of nature and category, this may indeed be seen; however, it is not yet clear what constitutes the "nature-seed" (*prakṛtibīja*).

Whether the Dharma-body and the Dharma-body as seeds of its own kind are identical or distinct, the various teachings and realms—namely the four teachings and ten realms—each distinguish their natures and categories; it would be difficult to present them in full detail. If one were to briefly distinguish them according to the four teachings, it is as explained in the *Ji* (Commentary).

The factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) constitute two types of seeds for liberation. Regarding these "factors conducive to penetration," the preceding five records state that *nirvāṇa* is called "liberation" (*vimukti*).

The wholesome roots cultivated therein, which do not abide in saṃsāra, are termed "penetration" (*nirveda*). For Śrāvakas, this occurs in three lifetimes; for Pratyekabuddhas, it takes a hundred kalpas.

These factors conducive to liberation are what are known as the "factors conducive to penetration. They consist of the two types of liberation: with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).

The hidden (*yin*) and the manifest (*xian*) are distinct; when the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) are within the entanglements (*saṃkleśa*), they are called "hidden," and when they emerge from the entanglements, they are called "manifest. When all three reside in the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), they are identical;
when they arise from cultivation (*bhāvanā*), they are distinct. This has already been annotated in detail above.

Since the three—marks (*lakṣaṇa*), substance (*dravya*), and nature (*svabhāva*)—pervade both the beginning and the end, and since the seeds (*bīja*) pervade all categories and the ten realms, these three factors of marks and so forth fully embody both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).
For instance, regarding the marks of the four evil destinies: they represent, from afar, places that are undesirable;
their substance consists of crushed and coarse physical forms and minds; and their nature is the dark portion (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) which is difficult to transform. And so on.
The marks of the Buddha are identical to the marks of bodhi; the causal conditions constitute the marks. As for the essence, it is the intrinsically pure mind (*svabhāva-viśuddha-citta*);

the direct cause constitutes the essence. As for the nature, it is the non-forgetting of wisdom and vows; the enabling cause constitutes the nature. This interpretation from the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) distinguishes these by means of the phenomena of the ten realms.
If one speaks in terms of principle, the three—marks, essence, and nature—are simply the three virtues (*tri-dharma*), beginning from the hells and ending with the [Buddha] realm.
The Tathāgata, having attained wondrous enlightenment, is able to know their mutual fusion and mutual inclusion;

one should likewise understand by analogy that they may also be explained by means of the nature (xing) being subsumed under the characteristics (xiang), or the characteristics being subsumed under the nature— namely, the category of nature and characteristics, the essence of characteristics and nature,
the essence of nature, the category of nature, and the nature of categories.

It is not necessary to restrict this to a single thought-moment; rather, let us distinguish them for now in terms of the fruit being separated by one thought-moment and the cause being pervasive. Alternatively, if we refer to the Three Truths:

the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) involves differentiation, while the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is without differentiation; the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*) is neither differentiated nor undifferentiated.

If we refer to the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*), the nine realms are differentiated while the Buddha-fruit is without differentiation; since the nature of the ten realms is identical, they are not differentiated.
It is not that there is no difference.
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*) as objects, the number varies; the Four Teachings clarify these realms as follows:

in the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation), the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teach seven or eight, while the *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) teach nine or ten. Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas of the *Zang* and *Tong* may have six, seven, eight, nine, or ten [realms] remaining undestroyed.
1. Because of delusion; 2. because the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are empty; 3–7. because of the great vows; 8. because the fruit is fulfilled; 9.

because there is no person at the head of the fruit—all these [stages] correspond to the ninth [category], which uses the real to manifest the provisional. All [stages] from 3 to 7 correspond to the eighth [category], which opens the provisional to reveal the real.

Now, regarding the tenth [category], one should explain it by means of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*) as they are entrusted to the realms (*dhātu*); in brief, stages 3 through 7 are "few," while stages 9 and 10 are "many. One should explain it thus.

Bring it forth. Observe the skill or clumsiness of the method; skill and clumsiness are understood through analogy. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "For example, employing needles and medicinal herbs is called the clumsy means (*upāya*), while employing incantations and arts is called the skillful means (*upāya*).
It is also like the two types of crossing a river: using a raft of grass is called the clumsy means."
One who uses a raft for crossing is said to cross skillfully.
Through mindfulness and so forth, one is able to hear and so forth. By means of what dharma does one mindfully hear which dharma? By means of what dharma does one contemplate which dharma?

By means of what dharma does one cultivate which dharma? One should know that taking what has been heard as the cause, there arise mindfulness and so forth, as well as the capacity to hear and so forth.
Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana*): there are three types of objects—those heard, those contemplated, and those cultivated.
An object is necessarily designated by its essence; because it is the cause for knowledge, it is called an "object" (*viṣaya*).
The essence (*tattva*) must be established by name according to its object; because it depends on the object, it is "wisdom" (*jñāna*).

To prevent the misconception that [the essence] does not depend on the essence itself, [it is said]: the object does not exist because it does not depend on the object; the essence arises spontaneously.

Because the essence depends on the essence, the object is produced from another; because the object depends on the object, the essence is produced from another. Thus, essence and object mutually support one another in co-arising. That which does not mutually support is not so.
It arises without cause. Furthermore, regarding the establishment of its functional divisions and the realization of its essence, there are immeasurable names.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Just as it is called *nirvāṇa*, it is also called 'non-arising' (*anutpāda*) and also called 'non-existence' (*abhāva*)."
Emergence is also called non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as well as the refuge, the cave-dwelling, the light, and so forth.
As it is said that there are many names for a single thing, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that liberation is likewise manifold in its nomenclature;
thus, one speaks of the "one hundred phrases of liberation."
All of Guangzhai’s writings refute the [theory of] three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, as cited in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), which states that "narrowness, inferiority, and brevity" refers to this:

it says that the Bodhisattva suppresses afflictions but has not yet emerged from the triple world; at this stage, he only suppresses the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*), which constitutes "brevity," and so forth.
"Phenomena and principles encompass all things: 'phenomena' refers to grass and water, while 'principles' refer to earth and rain.
In the commentary, this is not as it is in the prose; for example, whereas the prose is inconsistent in its expansion and condensation, the verses are orderly in their expansion and condensation."
Even according to the new sutras, it is not yet considered one's own retribution (*vipāka*).
They criticize the Tang translation of the *Avataṃsaka* for its poor Sanskrit phonology, claiming that if Vairocana were simply equated with "one sound," then Vairocana would be the retribution.

However, they fail to realize that "Vairocana" translates as "pervading all places," which is the Dharma-body itself. Furthermore, since even the "other-enjoyment body" is not the self-enjoyment [body], how could it possibly be the retribution?
The Dharma-body is cool and refreshing; this "coolness" is essentially the benefit of the fruition, such as, for example, those in the eight hot hells obtaining a cool breeze.
If, according to the commentary, the ninety-eight kinds of feverish afflictions are removed, this constitutes the benefit of the intermediate stage.

Therefore, the Master of the Records (Jizhu) points to the six sense organs; because they are identical in being free from the heat of view and thought and in possessing coolness, he says "also" and "moreover.
Regarding the hundred grains, Yang Quan states that millet, sacrificial grain, hemp, beans, and wheat constitute the five grains, and twenty varieties of each grain make up the hundred grains.
Regarding the two interpretations of "advancing" and "retreating," the term "grass" (*tṛṇa*) refers to the *Tripiṭaka* Bodhisattvas.
If one takes the meaning of "wood" (*kāṣṭha*) as an analogy for the categories of grass—namely superior, middling, and inferior—then the "small wood" represents the *Tripiṭaka* Bodhisattvas.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* presents the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and the four stages of the bodhisattva’s attainment of enlightenment;
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* presents the fifty-two stages common to the three vehicles of the exoteric teachings; the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (or *Bodhisattvabhūmi*) presents the forty-one stages;
and the old translations of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* present four different systems for the bodhisattva stages. Recent scholars have conflated these into one.

The "two trees" cannot be taken literally; they exist only as metaphors for the three stages (*tri-kalpa*) and represent both the general and specific Bodhisattvas, used to rebuke those who are deluded regarding the teachings.
Regarding the two interpretations—the general and the specific—the "three grasses and two trees" represent the specific, while the "trees" being opened up into three represents the general.
Regarding the power of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states that it "universally conforms up to the ultimate":

this refers to proceeding from the desire realm into the first dhyāna, continuing in sequence up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and then descending from the Peak of Existence back to the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). It receives the name "ultimate limit" as fully explained in the previous commentary.
The commentary merely misinterprets the meaning. Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* composed by Vasubandhu:

if one claims that it intends for the segmented body (*paricchinna-kāya*) to be extended until the transformation body (*pariṇāmi-kāya*), or if one asserts that the Master of the Great Commentary or the translators have misinterpreted the meaning, this does not reflect Vasubandhu’s intent.

Regarding the abiding in the four stages of the body: if one speaks of three stages, this includes humans and devas; if one distinguishes humans and devas and further includes both the general and specific bodhisattvas, there are four stages.

As for the other three [stages], they are already clearly and explicitly explained in the texts. Regarding humans and devas, it is said that they practice gradually; regarding the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), it is said that they seek [enlightenment].
In the distinct teaching (biejiao) of the Unsurpassed Vehicle, it is said that "delivering all sentient beings" does not refer to those in their final body (*paścima-kāya*).

Regarding the increase of both the common (tong) and the distinct (bie): the increase of the common refers to those who were previously matured; the increase of the distinct refers to the opening of the provisional (kaiquan) in this present sutra.
Furthermore, according to various teachings, there are two types: the Cloud-Rain [teachings] of the three vehicles concerning the resultant Buddha and the causal Bodhisattva.
Regarding the five hundred Arhats, there are seven Bodhisattvas whose views differ; this is established by the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which was composed by the five hundred Arhats.
As for the "seven Bodhisattvas," the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* (Fǎbǎo jīng) records that the Buddha told Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Dharmamati: [the names of the seven].
Guṇakānanaketu, Vajradhvaja, Vajragarbha, and Sudhana: do you see this Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī within the assembly,

who asks about the threefold contemplation of the dharma-realm, the path of the self-nature purity of all Buddhas, and the dharma-gate of the threefold contemplation practiced by a single Bodhisattva?
Since Yoga is distinct [from other systems], it cannot be interpreted by judging it according to the stages and practices of the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the opening of the analogy, the verse already states: "O Kāśyapa, you, O Kāśyapa! This was originally in prose and is the text that reiterates the core doctrine;
the *Jì* (Record/Commentary) states that this refers to the beginning of the verse.
First, the analogy of the sun and moon is used to illustrate the joy of the Buddha’s wisdom. As the *Sūtra* states:
"For example, the light of the sun and moon illuminates the world; whether it be good or evil, high or low, fragrant or foul, they shine equally upon all places without partiality.
In this same way, Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses all-knowledge."
The light of the mind of wisdom, within the births of sentient beings throughout the five destinies,
turns the wheel of the sublime Dharma equally for those who have faith and understanding in the Mahāyāna, the Pratyekabuddhayāna, and the Śrāvakayāna; likewise,
the Tathāgata’s wisdom neither increases nor decreases.

The five practices encompass all practices; for instance, regarding the holy practice of ethical discipline (*śīla-ārya-caryā*), it encompasses the precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the holy practices of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The Practice (*caryā*) subsumes the noble practices of concentration and wisdom of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; the Heavenly Practice (*deva-caryā*) subsumes the wisdom of the fourfold Four Noble Truths;
the Brahma Practice (*brahma-caryā*) subsumes all principles of reason; the Illness Practice (*vyādhi-caryā*) subsumes all cessation of evil;

and the Infant Practice (*bāla-caryā*) subsumes all production of goodness. Furthermore, it subsumes the seven categories of objective truths and the seven types of knowledge regarding those truths, and so forth.

The ten vehicles and ten objects encompass all things through their horizontal and vertical dimensions. Regarding these horizontal and vertical aspects, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) states:

"As in the 'Inconceivable Realm,' reaching the bottom of the true reality is called vertical; encompassing the ten dharma-realms is called horizontal. Seeking upward from the mind is called vertical; transforming downward is called horizontal.

Furthermore, seeking upward and transforming downward is called vertical; relying on the objects to give rise to vows is called horizontal. This extends to the "settling of the mind" (*anxin*), which reaches its ultimate depth.
Principle is called "vertical"; the sixty-four stages are called "horizontal. Penetrating and exhausting all delusions is vertical; the mutual comparison of various gates is horizontal.

Reaching the precious destination is vertical; examining and blocking obstructions is horizontal. From the "Chapter on the Path" onwards is vertical; the mutual comparison of various chapters is horizontal.
The primary and auxiliary teachings reaching their conclusion is vertical; the mutual comparison of various dharmas is horizontal. The sequence of stages is vertical.

The "extreme" (*anta*) refers to the vertical dimension (*ūrdhva*), while the "stages" (*sthāna*) encompassing all [levels] refer to the horizontal (*tiryak*). Patience (*kṣānti*) and exertion (*vīrya*) constitute the subsequent vertical sequence, whereas the mutual relation between the adverse (*pratikūla*) and the favorable (*anukūla*) constitutes the horizontal.
Non-attachment (*asaṅga*) in entering and abiding constitutes the vertical, while the departure from the three semblances (*pratirūpaka*) constitutes the horizontal.

Furthermore, in a general discussion, within each individual stage, the ten aspects relate to one another horizontally; yet, as each reaches its ultimate limit, they progress deeper vertically. Thus, the ten objects (*ālambana*) are both horizontal and vertical.

There are cases of horizontal possession and horizontal non-possession, as well as vertical possession and vertical non-possession. For example, developing the four dhyānas up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is vertical possession;

reaching the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is vertical non-possession. Developing the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the clear knowledges (*vidyā*), and so forth is horizontal possession;

developing the seven types of aversion (*pratikūla*) is horizontal non-possession. Furthermore, developing from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna is vertical possession; returning to the third dhyāna is vertical non-possession.
Furthermore, regarding the nine grades of the first dhyāna: if eight grades are present, it is "vertically complete"; if not, it is "vertically incomplete.
If one grade possesses all five factors (*pañcāṅga*), it is "horizontally complete"; if only four factors are present, it is "horizontally incomplete. This principle may be understood by analogy.

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains that the term "horizontal dharmas" (*tiryag-dharma*) used here to clarify the *prātipakṣika-vimokṣa* (liberations through opposition) refers to looking from one dhyāna to another, which is termed "horizontal. Moreover, within the first dhyāna, there are faculties (*indriya*).

The intrinsic flavors (*svabhāva-rasa*), purity (*śubha*), and so forth are called "horizontal" (*tiryak*) designations; the seven liberations (*vimokṣa*) are also called "horizontal. Regarding those that are not complete:

within the sphere of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), this one [liberation] is missing. (And so forth. To explain briefly: in the initial entry into the aggregates (*skandha-praveśa*), horizontal and vertical distinctions are not discussed.

Next, regarding afflictions (*kleśa*), the completeness of the sharp and dull proclivities (*anuśaya*) is termed "horizontal completeness"; from the single and multiple instances within the sharp and dull until reaching the "beyond words" (*anabhilāpya*), it is termed "vertical."

The presence within illness of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the five viscera (*pañca-kostha*), as well as ghosts and demons, is termed "horizontal" (*tiryak*). The mutual overcoming and mutual carving of these factors is termed "vertical.

Within karma, the obstruction of the *pāramitās* relative to one another is called "vertical obstruction," while those same factors viewed in relation to each other individually are called "horizontal.

Among the three types of Māras, the first two are horizontal; the subsequent evil followed by goodness, as well as falling into the Two Vehicles, are termed "vertical. This is fully present within the [obstruction of] views.
Regarding the arising of external phenomena and the Buddha-dharma, these are called the "vertical" four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and four gates; regarding pride, these are called the "horizontal.
Within the Two Vehicles, attaining the various *dhyānas* is called "horizontal," while attaining the first fruit up to the fourth fruit is called "vertical.

Furthermore, within the Four Noble Truths, viewing them in pairs is "horizontal," while viewing them in terms of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is "vertical. Moreover, within the Four Noble Truths, viewing them in pairs, as well as within the context of causes and conditions, is done by means of wisdom.

The realm of objects of expectation is also termed "horizontal" (*tiryak*). Within the realm of the Bodhisattva, one's own practice at a particular stage is termed "horizontal," while the mutual comparison of the three teachings is termed "vertical" (*ūrdhva*).

Furthermore, regarding the horizontal and vertical dharma-gates within the "Pervasive Destruction" (*pòbiàn*): that which is vertical and destroys the pervasive refers to the single gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*), which universally destroys [all delusions].

Commentary: Regarding the first entry, within the category of the "sphere of mental objects" (*dharmāyatana*), there are two kinds of phenomena:
first, mental phenomena (*cittadharma*), which exclude the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and include only the associated mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*);

second, non-mental phenomena, which consist of past and future matter (*rūpa*), all formations dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). The sound of this current abuse belongs to the category of formations dissociated from the mind.

This is because "umbrella" (chattrā) is a designation for a name. Within the [Abhidharma] *Paryāya*, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is one of the five aggregates; within the bases (*āyatana*), it is the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*);
and within the elements (*dhātu*), it is the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*). All of these constitute a small portion of abusive speech.

Regarding the sound element (*śabdadhātu*), there are eight types: those that are appropriated (*upātta*) and those that are non-appropriated (*anupātta*). As for the appropriated, the treatise states:

"That which is collectively grasped and maintained by the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) is called 'appropriated. For example, because they serve as the causes for sensations such as pain and itching, one should know that pleasure and pain are what the mind appropriates;
since they arise as the causes for the three types of feeling (*vedanā*), they are termed 'appropriated. The five sense faculties, such as the eye, are precisely these."
Sound produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) from this [cause] is called "sentient" (*sattva*), such as [the sound of] nails, hair, and so forth;

these are not "appropriated" (*upātta*) by the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and are thus called "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*), meaning they are not sentient. Regarding the statement that there are eight types of sound:
among those that are appropriated, there are those designated as "sentient" and those designated as "non-sentient," each of which may be either agreeable or disagreeable.

The mind has no appropriation (*anupāttaka*); sentient beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are called both "sentient" and "non-sentient," and each of these also has that which is agreeable and that which is disagreeable.
Thus, there are eight [categories]. Those that possess expressive meaning are names, phrases, and so forth; those that lack expressive meaning are wind, rivers, and so forth.

Regarding the four appropriated [elements],
the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that the speech of sentient beings is twofold:
that which is agreeable, such as praise and eulogy, and that which is expressive of meaning.
"Unpleasant" refers to things such as verbal abuse and the like, which have expressive meaning;
"sentient" names are of two kinds.
"Pleasant" refers to things such as gentle speech and the snapping of fingers, which do not have expressive meaning.
"Unpleasant" refers to such things as startling the assembly or clapping hands; these are not expressions [of the mind].
There are two names for the four types of sentient beings who lack physical appropriation (*anupāttaka*).
"Agreeable" refers to the meaningful expressions of a manifested person’s praise;
"disagreeable" refers to the meaningful expressions of a manifested person’s abuse.
These are designated as "non-sentient" because it is recorded that they include such things as wind, forests, and rivers.
"Agreeable" refers to things such as lutes and zithers, which are not expressive;

"disagreeable" refers to things such as explosions and the like, which are also not expressive—one should consider other examples accordingly. Among those that are expressive, praise is agreeable while abuse is disagreeable; for instance, clapping one's hands [is agreeable].

Although there is no praise or abuse [in this context], the principle that there may be what is agreeable and what is disagreeable can be understood through analogy. Regarding form (*rūpa*) and visible appearance (*varṇa*), when one abuses the form, one does not abuse the visible appearance; when one abuses the visible appearance, one does not abuse the form. Similarly, regarding feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, when one abuses the feeling, one does not abuse the mental object (*ālambana*); when one abuses the mental object, one does not abuse the feeling. Thus, it should be known through such analogies.

Mañjuśrī spoke thus to refute that claim: "In this great trichiliocosm, there is a continent named Aparagoyānī.

Regarding such a straight river, the Buddha has never spoken of various trees made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and jewels; these too are called forests. There are indeed [such forests].

because they consist of the three types of grass and two types of wood, they are not the ultimate truth. [The river of] golden sand flows directly into the Western Sea," and so on, concluding with: "Therefore, it is not..."

The *Fěishì* commentary states: "Now, 'winding paths' and 'forests' and the like are used as metaphors for the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, while the 'Golden Sands River' and the like are used as metaphors for the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says that the "Noble Practice" (*ārya-caryā*) realizes the three stages (*bhūmi*), and the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) says that the "Brahma Practice" (*brahma-caryā*) realizes two [stages].
The Grounds (*bhūmi*) are the cause, and thus they are established by treatises; the Sicknesses (*vyādhi*) arise from the fruit, and thus they are not established by treatises.

The practice of precepts (*śīla-caryā*) is realized from shallow to deep; the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi-caryā*) on the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) is realized from shallow to deep;

and the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*) through endurance is realized from shallow to deep. Upon ascending to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), one is not moved by the two extremes; this is called [the Immovable].
The stage of Immovability (Akṣobhyabhūmi) is called the "Stage of Endurance" (*Kṣāntibhūmi*) because it upholds the Buddha-dharma above while bearing the burden of sentient beings below.

It is called the "Stage of Fearlessness" (*Abhayabhūmi*) because one attains mastery over both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and so forth. Furthermore, it is said: "If, prior to the [first] bhūmi, one transforms others, this is termed 'Brahmacarya.

Compassion, joy, and equanimity are the activities of others; the Stage of the Only Son (*Ekaputraka-bhūmi*) is its realization; and the mind of relinquishment (*upekṣā-citta*) is the transformation of others."

The equality of principle and practice is the realization of ascending the stages (*bhūmi*). Because it is compassion for [all beings as] one's only child, it is said that this compassion is identical to the essence;

thus, it is called the "equality of emptiness" (and so forth). However, in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Texts), it is stated that the practice of precepts realizes the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), whereas the present commentary cites a sūtra stating that the practice of precepts dwells in the Stage of Endurance (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) and the practice of concentration dwells in the Immovable Stage. This may perhaps be the case.

The statement that "the essence of the stages (bhūmi) is fused" may be a scribal error; upon consulting the sūtras for verification, it is found that in the sūtras, ethical conduct (śīla-caryā) corresponds to the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi), while meditative concentration (samādhi-caryā) corresponds to the Stage of Patience (Kṣānti-bhūmi). This is consistent with [Master] Xuánzàng’s interpretation.
The *Ekaputrabhūmi-mahāsūtra* states: "After a bodhisattva has cultivated loving-kindness and compassion, they attain the stage of 'Extreme Affection for an Only Son.
Just as parents feel great joy when they see their child safe and sound, so too does the bodhisattva;

observing all sentient beings as being identical to an only son, they experience great joy upon seeing those who cultivate wholesome qualities. Furthermore, seeing sentient beings afflicted by the afflictions..."
Bound by the afflictions of illness, the mind gives rise to sorrow and distress; therefore, this stage is called "The Only Son" (*ekaputraka*).
Some versions of the sūtra read "many" (*bahu*) instead of "one" (*eka*);

both terms are applicable. It is the sphere of practice for both the profound and the shallow, where one gives birth to the two types of patience (*kṣānti*) regarding phenomena and their arising. Being close to these states, one is able to distance oneself from the three views, all of which are universally accessible.
Because they are both results, they are both profound; because they are all contained within the five grades, they are both shallow.

Regarding "both shallow" and "both profound" as in the commentary: "both profound" refers to the practice of the Bodhisattvas of the preceding grades, while "both shallow" refers merely to the practice of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*).

Below, according to the stages, the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*) resides in the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), while the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*) resides in the first dwelling (*prathamā bhūmi*); nevertheless, both also extend to the beginning.

This is as cited in the *Yìzhōng* (Exposition of Meaning), where the patience of quiescent extinction is correlated with ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*); the text from the *Shíbā kōng chāo* (Notes on the Eighteen Emptinesses) cited below is as follows:
It is said that all phenomena are "ultimately empty" (*atyanta-śūnya*) because they lack anything remaining;

being ultimate, they are empty and non-existent. Each [explanation] speaks from one side, yet it is not that there is no point of arrival. Although each arrives at the principle through its respective basis, they all have a point of arrival;

therefore, it is said that it is "not without. Because one proceeds by way of practice and dwells in proximity, there is always a point of arrival; thus, one should explain according to this standard.
Regarding the two aspects of speech and mind, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* clearly explains them within the context of verbal karma:
"Not delighting in speaking of the faults of others or of the sūtras" refers to *śamatha*; "skillfully cultivating such a mind of peace and happiness" refers to *vipaśyanā*. Regarding mental karma:
"Being free from harboring envy, flattery, or deceit" refers to *śamatha*; "arousing the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings" refers to *vipaśyanā*.
