The Commentary states that good and evil must combine to constitute the "trigger" (*ki*); neither pure good nor pure evil alone can serve as the trigger. The *Mysterious Text* says:
"From the beginning in the hells up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment, all take the intermingling of good and evil as the trigger."
Regarding the passage, "Hearing this, one invokes the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva with single-mindedness," the *Sūtra Commentary* states that there are four meanings of "hearing.

If one can thoroughly comprehend these four meanings of hearing, then the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is such that the mind has no basis, no dwelling, and no attachment; the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is single-minded invocation of the name;
and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is likewise single-minded invocation of the name.
Some people place the three characters "Guanshiyin" at the beginning of the second line, so that "Guanshiyin" immediately observes their sounds.
Xinghuang places them at the end of the first line, so that one single-mindedly invokes the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Regarding the second phrase, one may also read it by adding the three characters "Guanshiyin" (Avalokiteśvara) from above; in that case, the recitation would be:
"Single-mindedly call upon the name of Guanshiyin Bodhisattva, and he will immediately behold [you]," and so forth.
Regarding the fires of retribution from the Avīci Hell above up to the First Dhyāna below, the Commentary states:

"The Avīci sub-hells number eighty-four thousand; they are transparent inside and out, with flames blazing from top to bottom. In the realm of hungry ghosts, smoke rises from their limbs; among animals, there is the suffering of being boiled and roasted on glowing coals;
the asuras likewise face the perils of fire; and in the human realm, burning is seen manifestly. As for the conflagration at the end of a kalpa, it must [be discussed] when it arrives."
It is perfectly clear that from the first dhyāna downward, none are exempt from the calamity of fire.

Wherever there is a place for reforming evil and cultivating goodness, the fires of unwholesome karma follow; yet, even where the five precepts and ten wholesome paths are practiced, they are often obstructed by many evil karmas.
As the Sūtra says: "Nothing surpasses anger in burning away all roots of goodness. Even Śukra was consumed by the fire of desire.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The intense fire of sorrow now comes to burn me; all that can destroy wholesome karma is called 'fire.
When a practitioner cultivates the Path, they are universally afflicted by the fires of delusion—the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling."
When the skillful means for burning away [afflictions] have not yet been perfected, the peril of fire constantly oppresses.

As the teachings of all Buddhas state regarding the difference in merit, as in the *Yankou Jing* (Flaming Mouth Sūtra), when offering food to spirits and deities, one causes them to recite the names of the four Buddhas;
by causing them to recite the name of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, one causes the spirits and deities to transform their afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).
If one recites the name of the Tathāgata Wondrous Form Body, Vast and Broad Body, Free from Fear, it causes both ghosts and spirits to simultaneously eliminate their karmic obstacles.
[Question: How is it that there must be sixty-two [times] or the like, as in the passage "sixty-two billion *Ganges-sand* bodhisattvas"? [Answer: It is because... (text fragment).

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In this trichiliocosm, there currently dwell among the world various Dharma Princes numbering sixty-two Ganges-sands, who cultivate the Dharma and establish models to teach and transform sentient beings."

The *Shu-ge* (Commentary on the Structural Framework) explains this within the *Byōng-haeng-so* (Commentary on the Separate Practices) of the One Perfect Bodhisattva, stating that it may differ from that [other view] by saying:

"It is caused by the differences in the quality of the field—whether high or low, fertile or barren. Thus, making offerings to a hundred persons who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) is not equal to making offerings to one or two who have attained the second fruit, up to those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). This, however, does not intend to praise their virtues; rather, it is a comparison of the lower to the higher.
The Dharma may appear to have distinctions of superior and inferior; however, it is now clarified that neither the nature of unity nor multiplicity can be apprehended.
There are no two distinct characteristics: duality is not unity, and multiplicity is not plurality. Both enter equally into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) without difference.

Because one understands the immeasurable within the one, it is said that there are sixty-two billion [forms of Avalokiteśvara]; because one understands the one within the immeasurable, it is said that Avalokiteśvara is "Right Equality" (*samyak-samatā*). This is what constitutes Right Equality.

Regarding the commentary stating that "the mind and its objects are both inferior," etc., it says: "That the mind has degrees of intensity or dullness is entirely due to the mental power of the person before;
what does it have to do with Avalokiteśvara? (The main text) takes the mutual identity of the one and the many as the correct principle."

The *Jiānánjiě nánzhī jīng* (Sūtra on the Difficult to Understand and Difficult to Know) states "difficult to understand and difficult to enter. The *Shù* (Commentary) states that the Ten Abidings (*daśabhūmi*) are the beginning of understanding, while the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) constitute entry.
In the *Lùn* (Treatise), three additional phrases are added before this: "difficult to see," "difficult to awaken to," and "difficult to know. The *Jì* (Record) states:

"This 'difficult to understand' refers to the skillful means (*upāya*) corresponding to hearing, reflection, and cultivation; the character 'understand' (*jiě*) is an error and should be read as 'see' (*jiàn*)."
He then added three phrases, saying: "To erect the great Dharma-banner, to kindle the great Dharma-torch, and to beat the great Dharma-drum without ceasing.

Those who claim that [the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*] teaches the Three Vehicles are in error; although Master Gushan classified the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* within the category of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, within the sutra itself the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara speaks of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, as when he says: "If there are those in training (*śaikṣa*) who are tranquil, wondrously luminous..."
If there are those for whom the supreme and wondrous manifests its perfection, I manifest the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them;
if there are those on the path of learning who have severed the twelve links of dependent origination, I manifest the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them;

if there are those on the path of learning who have attained the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths, I manifest the body of a Śrāvaka and preach the Dharma for them. The reader must harmonize these passages so that no contradictions arise.
The *Jingjie jingzhen zhuanliu yingluo shu* (Commentary on the Pearl Necklace Adorning the Neck) states: "The 'neck' symbolizes the principle of the single reality of the Middle Way;

'adorned' symbolizes that because the Bodhisattva cultivates the practice of constant relinquishment, they neither dwell upon nor cling to any of the merits of vows and practices, up to and including Buddha-wisdom, bodhi, and nirvana."
Regarding this Dharma-gift, the commentary states: "Precisely because wealth penetrates the Dharma, wealth is named Dharma; that is, the Dharma is the wealth.

This refers to the phenomena born of causes and conditions, which are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—the three truths within one mind, all fully present. Being equal regarding the Dharma, one is also equal regarding wealth;
this is called the Dharma-gift."
Curses and various poisons return to their source. In the *Piyū-jīng* (Sutra of Similes), there was a lay follower and a brahmin who were asked for a drink;
being unable to give it, they rose up a corpse and sent a ghost to kill [the petitioner].
At that time, an arhat in the mountains instructed them to return and take refuge in the Triple Gem. Thus, by dawn, the ghost found no opportunity and all the ghosts turned back.

The *Bie xing ji* (Record of Separate Practices) states that when the Brahmin who harmed the Arhat was obscured so that the ghost could not see him, and the pure-faith layman attained awakening while the Brahmin was restored to life, these instances involve "true contemplation" (*zhenguān*) and "pure contemplation" (*qingjing guān*).
Regarding the five characters for "contemplation" (*guān*) therein, they are all pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). True contemplation is [defined as follows].

The contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) purifies; the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) causes the ground to be pure; and the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama*) is the wisdom that both negates and illuminates simultaneously, being the great wisdom of equality.
As for the contemplation of compassion (*karuṇā*), one observes sentient beings with unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*).

Furthermore, the dharma of compassion must employ the three contemplations. [Note: The character "霅" (xià) has the same pronunciation as "五" (wǔ), and all characters in this phrase are pronounced in the level tone.]
Regarding the constant aspiration and constant veneration [of the Buddha], the character "shàng" (上) in the phrase "cháng shàng" (常上) is,
according to the oral instructions of the monk Xuánjì, found as the character "dāng" (當) in the Tripitaka and in ancient manuscripts from various sources.
This is analogous to such expressions as "may all beings always aspire," "should aspire," "should fix their mindfulness," and "should abandon negligence."

The *Pīti-ti-kye-rae-jin-gi* (Record of the Thunderous Resonance of the Compassionate Body and Precepts) states: "Regarding the line 'the compassionate body' (*pīti-ti*), the first two lines of the verse refer to the oral karma (*mukha-karma*).

Although it is said that the two wheels [of the Dharma] are the basis for transformation, they reside in the mouth; yet this necessarily relies upon the body and mind as the basis for bestowing the Dharma.

Because this body manifests its form for the sake of the Dharma and is fundamentally intended to save sentient beings from suffering, the Dharma-body is named the 'compassionate body. This body first employs the virtue of the precepts to awaken people."

Just as when the heavenly thunder resounds, there is nothing that does not become solemn, so too is the one whose compassionate mind universally covers all called "Great Cloud. Once the two wheels have been bestowed, it is then appropriate to transmit the Dharma.
The *Sutra on the Prophecies of Miaoyin and Guanshiyin* states: "The five tones and characters are all sounds chanted by sentient beings."

Because Samantabhadra observes through wondrous wisdom, he accomplishes the realm of the three truths: "Double-negation of emptiness and existence" corresponds to Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound), and "Simultaneous illumination of emptiness and existence" corresponds to Shizhuyin (World-Sound).
Within these two characters lies the realm of wisdom. "Brahma-sound" refers to the four contemplations of compassion, mercy, joy, and equanimity;

this is the illumination of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that accords precisely with the capacities of sentient beings, and is thus called Haichaoyin (Ocean-Tide Sound). Within these two characters lies the realm of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

The wisdom of ultimate emptiness transcends the nine realms of emotion; its illumination of the voices of sentient beings gives rise to the characteristics of the two periods of time, which is named the "Victorious Worldly Voice.
This single sound and character is the realm of the wisdom of emptiness.

Alternatively, some chapters appear to have great benefit, yet they possess both large and small degrees of benefit. For example, in the "Chapter on Purifying Buddha-lands," five hundred elders attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

this benefit is great. In [the section where] thirty-two thousand people seeking the vehicle of the śrāvakas realized that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are impermanent and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*); this benefit is small.
Some chapters appear to offer minor benefits, yet there are both great and small [benefits], as stated in the chapter on Maudgalyāyana within the *Śrāvaka-varga*:
"Because the Dharma abides in reality, removing all extremes and remaining unshakable; because the Dharma is without fluctuation, it does not rely upon the six heretical views.

When this Dharma was being taught, eight hundred lay devotees (*gṛhapati*) at that time resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta—this is a great benefit. Furthermore, in the chapter on Subhūti, it says: "No..."

"When one realizes that the nature of written characters is devoid of the nature of characters, this is liberation. When this Dharma was being taught, two hundred devaputras attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "This is the realization of the principle of 'emptiness' according to the Shared Teaching; it constitutes entry into the Path of Seeing. Within the division of the True and the Middle, the Shared [Teaching] is also called 'Small'."

Alternatively, it may encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, benefiting both as well; for example, the "Chapter on Repentance" in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* provides repentance common to the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

Since the three vehicles subsume the four teachings (*catuḥśāsana*), when the three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) are extinguished, each vehicle attains its respective benefit. Furthermore, the *Paramādya-rāja-sūtra* states:

"If one desires to seek the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), or the fruit of an arhat (*arhatphala*), one should likewise practice repentance."
Those who seek to eliminate karmic obstructions and attain the three clarities and six supernatural powers— whether as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas,

or bodhisattvas seeking mastery up to the ultimate stage and the attainment of all-knowledge— should likewise repent to eliminate their karmic obstructions; this chapter fully contains the fourfold teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
All of these are explained away by the three previous meanings as being of the same category—esoteric and indeterminate.

In the "Dhāraṇī" chapter, they are reinforced by means of incantations; that is, by employing spells to facilitate understanding, so that those of shallow insight may receive and uphold [the teachings] with reverence and diligence.
"Supported by both the hidden and the manifest" means that they provide assistance; "the hidden" refers to ghosts and spirits, while "the manifest" refers to bodhisattvas.
The shamans and sorcerers who distort worldly customs are full of deception;
the layman Shunada has not yet been examined.
Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mantra* and other mantras, there are two types of *dhāraṇī-praṇidhāna* (vows of incantation): namely, the Exoteric and the Esoteric.
The Exoteric refers to the three [mantras] beginning with the *Mahāprajñā*; the Esoteric refers to those that preserve the original Sanskrit sounds today.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there is a question and answer concerning why Śakra Devendra considers the *Prajñā* to be the unsurpassed *vidyā-mantra*. The answer states: "Among the various non-Buddhist sages..."
Various incantations and arts benefit the people; those who recite this mantra shall attain great fame and renown, and the people will enter [the path] and submit.
Because this mantra is noble, it is called Prajñā, and it is used as a mantra. Śakra addressed the Buddha:

"This Prajñā mantra constantly bestows upon sentient beings the joy of virtue and the Way, whereas other incantations and arts can only increase evil; the divine mantra of Prajñā can [only increase goodness]."
It extinguishes all Buddhas’ nirvana and all attachments; what incantation could [overcome] greed and the like? For this reason, it is called the Great Bright Incantation (*mahā-vidyā-mantra*).

It is "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) because there is nothing greater than it, or because there is nothing superior to it. It is "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*); that which is equal to this "unequaled" is called "equal to the unequaled.
Because they all destroy ignorance, they are collectively termed "bright" (*vidyā*). Furthermore, among all sentient beings, the Buddhas—
Because it is peerless, *prajñā* is called "peerless. Furthermore, "the peerless and equal" (*asamasama*) refers to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Since there is nothing capable of equalling this peerless stage, it is named "the peerless and equal. The above is from the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*.
The *Fuxing* (Explanatory Notes) states that "using [the mantra] as a whole" means to obstruct evil, which constitutes *śīla* (restraint), and to maintain goodness, which constitutes *dhāraṇī*.

This clarifies that the use of this vidyā-mantra to obstruct evil and maintain goodness brings joy to those who hear it; these are the three remaining worlds, sequentially corresponding to the three *siddhis*.
Specifically, "greatly illuminating the breaking of the three teachings" refers to the breaking of the non-illumination of the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) and the Lesser Outsiders;

"breaking the superior" refers to the breaking of the superiority of those prior to the distinct stages (Pratyekabuddhas); "breaking the equal-to-the-unequal" refers to the breaking of the equality of those prior to the mind of the Vajra-stage of the Perfect Teaching.
As for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* stating that it "breaks ignorance," all three delusions are collectively designated by this term.

For averting calamities, increasing merit, and summoning: averting calamities is like the *Candraguhyatilaka* (The Blazing Light); increasing merit is like the *Śrīdevī* (Goddess of Merit) mantra for fulfilling all requests;
and summoning is like the *Abhiṣeka* (Consecration) mantra. Furthermore, one may reprimand spirits and deities.
Furthermore, it is called a "true mantra" because it entrusts the divine spell to contemplate the true mind. It is like reciting the Great Compassion Mantra while seeking wisdom;
as the sutra says, one should contemplate the mind within a precious mirror. When the mirror is bright, the images of the ten realms arise;
by cultivating these ten realms, it is therefore called "true."
Furthermore, there are the vidyās such as the Vidyā of Illumination, the Unsurpassed Vidyā, and the Vidyā Equal to the Unequaled;
these seed-syllables are the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇīs, known as the "Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Seeds. Those who recite them possess the seeds of the Buddha, which are the cause of realization.
The *Śāstra* states: In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are four things called *śātava*: salt, water, a vessel, and horse dung; these are named *śātava*.
In the *Sūtra*, the term *kṣānti* is sometimes pronounced as *qian* instead of *yan*; this should be understood according to the *Chanyao mimi yaojue jing* (Secret Essentials of Dhyāna Sūtra).
In the Qieyun, "zhou" is read with the phonetic "shū-ān".
The commentaries both state that there are two types of *vetāla*: those used by humans to raise corpses, and those used by *yakṣas* to raise corpses.

In the commentary on the "Chapter on King Wondrous Adornment," the character *qín* (親) is read with the phonetic *xiǎo* (小) and the tone *qiè* (切), meaning "to change facial expression. This is incorrect; it should be *jiāo* (湫), read with the phonetic *liáo* (了) and the tone *qiè* (切), meaning "narrow" or "constricted."
*Ka-ka-yin* (喀喀音) means to miss a meal. *Men-lu* (門閭):
*lu* is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *ju* (居). According to the *Liji* (Rituals of the Zhou), five households constitute a *bi* (比); they are made to compare and protect one another.
Five *bi* constitute a *lu* (閭); they are made to love one another as neighbors.

Whether experiencing sweetness or bitterness, there is neither joy nor resentment; "yùn" (慍) is pronounced as *yùn* (於運切) and means anger. When I serve my master according to the rules for treating guests with excellence, I feel sweet satisfaction and joy;
when I am overworked, I feel bitter hardship but remain without resentment.

"Xi-he-xi" (噏赫噏)—the first "xi" is pronounced with the initial *x* and the final *-ji* (切). This refers to the internal breath; it should actually be written as "xi" (翕), meaning "to gather" or "to fill.

"Adorned with a thousand merits upon his body," and so forth.

Observing both master and disciple together—this refers to Miaoyin (Ghoṣa)—he cautioned him, saying: "Do not look down upon that land or those who accompany you."

The *Śāstra* explains other sūtras as the Great Treatise on the Right Path, stating: "The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the Great Chapter on Bodhi. It further states:

"Those who wish to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) by means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)—the dharma-realm of the foundations of mindfulness encompasses all phenomena;

The practices that assist the Path include the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*), the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), and so forth;
